sections.title: Content provenance and generation boundaries

sections.html:
Read the full checked source context

The lecture rejects a single inevitable route from tradition to feudalism to capitalism or from central planning to one market model. It uses China and Russia to illustrate different, politically shaped transition paths toward forms it calls state capitalism. Path dependence means that earlier arrangements alter the resources, expectations, and power of later decision makers; a reform starts from that inherited position. A related survivorship bias arises if we infer the original form of all traditional societies only from those that still survive. A system change may lack a deliberate starting decision or a clear start date; where there was a decision, the new system could have been imposed rather than voluntarily chosen, as with Soviet-bloc central planning. The design and survival of a system can also serve political goals, so political control can help stabilize it even when its economic results are poor for much of the population. These are interpretive claims from the slides, not proof that one historical path is universal. Week I lecture, PDF slides 31–36

The lecture's Narrow Corridor schematic places state power vertically and society's power horizontally. It labels a corridor where state capacity is constrained by organized society as the Shackled Leviathan; outside it are a Despotic Leviathan where state power dominates, an Absent Leviathan with weak state capacity, and a weak-both Paper Leviathan. The country labels are illustrative placements in a qualitative model, not measured coordinates or a necessary sequence of development. This visual connects political constraints to economic institutions; the course's uploaded Why Nations Fail chapter supplies a different historical argument, so one should not pretend that chapter itself contains this figure. Week I lecture, PDF slides 34–35

The lecture's Acemoglu–Robinson (2006) feedback diagram links today's political institutions to de jure (legally assigned) power, and today's distribution of resources to de facto (effective) power. Together those forms of power help shape today's economic institutions and tomorrow's political institutions. Economic institutions affect economic performance and the next resource distribution, which feeds back into later power. The arrows express a conceptual causal mechanism and endogeneity, not measured coefficients or algebraic identities. Week I lecture, PDF slides 43–44

Why a striking comparison may still mislead

Austria–Czechoslovakia comparison. The chart plots GDP per person in 1990 international Geary–Khamis dollars over 1820–2010 using the Maddison Project 2013 version. The visible gap later in the series motivates a question about divergent institutions and systems. It does not isolate a causal effect of socialism: war, borders, industrial structure, measurement, and other historical differences also require analysis. The slide retains a “Czecho-slovakia” series for 2000 and 2010, after the state's dissolution, without explaining how those observations were constructed. Read its units, source date, and this labeling limit before using it as evidence. Week I lecture, PDF slide 40

Germany measurement example. For 1950–1989, the slide reports West German GNP and GNP-per-person growth figures of \(4.2\) and \(3.6\), while its East German official NMP series reports \(5.6\) and 5.9. Two re-estimates of East German GNP using different 1989 Mark/DM conversions report \(1.6\)/\(1.9\) and \(-2.2\)/\(-1.9\) respectively. The table's labels do not print a unit for these rates, and NMP and GNP are different aggregates. The key lesson is sensitivity to accounting and conversion, not a precise uncontested ranking from unlike numbers. Week I lecture, PDF slide 41, table attributed there to Pohl (1991)

The lecture surveys geography, culture, and leaders' ignorance as proposed explanations of prosperity, then poses Nogales and other counterexamples to simple one-factor accounts. It argues that trust and cooperation can themselves be shaped by institutions. These examples show why competing explanations must be examined; they do not mean geography or culture never matters. The Nogales and colonial-history note explains the uploaded chapter's own evidence and its limits in detail. Week I lecture, PDF slides 37–43

Finally, the lecture's Lagos insecurity scenario, Adam Smith quotation, and China discussion all point to the same decision mechanism: if property claims, contract enforcement, or predictable treatment are doubtful, an investor has reason to protect or conceal resources, seek personal connections, or use shorter-horizon opportunities. The China slide specifically names inconsistent rules, weak independent judicial checks, and reliance on guanxi networks; those are lecturer claims for discussion, not a blanket characterization of every Chinese transaction. The uploaded Roland chapter explains the contracting problems behind that intuition. Week I lecture, PDF slides 46–52 Institutions and economic development

The lecture's final example is a screenshot of a September 2024 article describing a debated practice in which a relative's conviction can restrict access to certain public jobs, university programs, or military service. It illustrates an indirect effect of legal rules on people who were not convicted and why households may care about predictability and equal application. The screenshot reports nearly 25 million recorded offenders during 2000–2022 and states that some 100 million people could be at risk if each has three affected relatives. That multiplication gives about 75 million relative instances before any overlap; the article does not explain the difference. Neither number is an observed count of people actually penalized. The slide presents this as an article excerpt, not as independently verified course data. Week I lecture, PDF slide 52

Explain the chapter’s Nogales puzzle and compare Spanish extraction with the unsuccessful coercive strategy in Virginia. Define encomienda/mita precisely, connect outside options to land/voice incentives, and distinguish a historical mechanism from an isolated causal effect while interpreting the two maps’ boundaries/units.

Study conditions, assessment scope and sources

sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

sections.html: Nogales Arizona/Sonora share nearby geography and broadly similar ancestry/culture, yet the authors report different income, services, security and political accountability in the book’s period. Institutional incentives are their proposed explanation; Sonora benefits from US-linked manufacturing and is relatively prosperous within Mexico. An encomienda is a grant of Indigenous people’s tribute/labor obligations to an encomendero with formal conversion duty, not just land title or ordinary paid work. Colonial mita adapted an earlier Inca compulsory-labor turn to mining extraction after population concentration into reducciones. Political hierarchy/dense settlements/resources can make coercive appropriation feasible. An outside option is the next best feasible alternative to accepting an arrangement.
sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. State the Nogales outcome differences before explanation: historical income about 30,000 versus a third, plus schooling/services/security/accountability. Similar local geography challenges simple one-factor explanations, not all geography/culture effects.
  2. Spanish conquerors sought labor/tribute; Buenos Aires lacked a readily controllable centralized labor base/gold and faced resistance. Asunción allowed appropriation of farming Guaraní organization. Capturing rulers such as Moctezuma/Atahualpa could place conquerors over tribute systems; this was coercion, not consent.
  3. Define encomienda obligations and mita mining catchment. Colonial mita drew one-seventh of male inhabitants across roughly 200,000 square miles until 1825; taxes payable in silver, forced purchases and carrying labor reinforced extraction. The earlier Inca arrangement had different purposes/reciprocal provisions.
  4. The mita map identifies a historical catchment, not an estimated economic effect; Calca/Acomayo contrast is the authors’ persistence illustration (roads/markets/consumption), not formal identification ruling out all other differences.
  5. Virginia Company first sought to coerce Indigenous people but could not commandeer a comparably centralized rich tribute base. It then imposed harsh company labor on English settlers: similar extraction goal, different legal form and targets from encomienda. Settlers could exit to Indigenous communities/frontier, limiting coercion.
  6. Headrights/land incentives in 1618 and assembly 1619 increased returns and voice; they were relative inclusion, not universal democracy. Later Maryland/Carolina hierarchy attempts also faced exit. Women, enslaved and propertyless people lacked votes; Indigenous dispossession persisted. Population map legend uses \(\text{people}/\mathrm{km}^{2}\), nearby prose \(\text{people}/\mathrm{mi}^{2}\); keep units distinct and no-data separate from low density. Mechanisms are conditional, not an inevitable national destiny.
sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Colonial institutions and divergence: Why Nations Fail, chapter 1; fingerprint d4bf9c4cdad229430e95558fa87fd4edcf657d0b2820a100f9160c229a5b3f3a. Heading depth and required relative figure-path relocation alone are adapted.

Colonial institutions and divergence: Why Nations Fail, chapter 1

Question: Why can places with similar geography and people have very different living standards? Acemoglu and Robinson argue that political and economic institutions create different incentives to work, invest, innovate, provide public goods, and exercise power. This chapter introduces an institutional explanation of comparative economic performance through the history of the Americas. It belongs with the introductory discussion in the Comparative Economics course hub: to compare economic systems, we need to ask who sets the rules, whose actions those rules reward, and how the rules persist. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 38–41

All page references below are physical PDF pages; this extracted chapter does not show printed book page numbers. The examples and historical interpretations are the authors' arguments, not independent causal estimates supplied by this chapter. The source is Acemoglu & Robinson, “So Close and Yet So Different”.

Topic map

The solid arrows map the authors' proposed mechanism, not a mechanical law that every country must follow. The dotted connections identify illustrations and limits. Colonial conditions shaped what conquerors could extract; political institutions then influenced economic rules, while those who benefited from the rules had reasons to defend them. The two Nogaleses pose the question, the colonial histories suggest how different paths began, and later finance and business cases show how the paths might still matter. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 3–23, 27–41

Nogales: the question that motivates the chapter

Nogales is divided by the United States–Mexico border. The authors describe an average annual household income of about $30,000 on the Arizona side and about one-third of that on the Sonora side. They also contrast education, health, roads, public utilities, security, and the practical ability to start a business. The figures describe the period of the book; they should not be read as current statistics. For the authors, political accountability matters as well as income: residents in Arizona could replace elected officials, whereas residents of Sonora lived under the long rule of Mexico's PRI until the political reforms of 2000. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 1–2

The neighboring cities share climate and a similar disease environment, and the authors describe their residents as having broadly similar ancestry and culture. They therefore argue that the border's political and economic rules are more convincing explanations for the disparity than local climate or a simple cultural difference. On their account, rules and public services in the United States make schooling, occupational choice, investment, and adoption of technology more rewarding; political institutions also give citizens leverage over officials. The comparison makes their hypothesis vivid, but this chapter does not turn it into a controlled statistical experiment or establish that no other factor matters. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 2–3

There is an important qualification within the authors' own account. Nogales, Sonora, is more prosperous than much of Mexico because it benefits from proximity to the United States and from maquiladora factories using US capital and know-how. Thus the story is about different institutional incentives and opportunities, not an assertion that no productive activity can occur on the Mexican side or that the border cuts off all economic influence. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 37–38

Spanish colonization: creating rules for extraction

Why the first Buenos Aires failed while Asunción prospered for conquerors

The first Spanish settlement at Buenos Aires had a favorable climate, but the Charrúa and Querandí resisted attempts to obtain their food and labor. The region offered neither easily accessible gold nor a large, centralized population that the colonists could control through its leaders. The Spaniards had planned to extract resources and compel others to work, so a place where they would have to produce food themselves was unattractive to them. An expedition instead encountered the sedentary, farming Guaraní. After overcoming resistance, Spanish settlers placed themselves above existing systems of tribute and forced labor in Asunción; Buenos Aires was abandoned and not resettled until 1580. This contrast illustrates conquerors' incentives: a colony could be attractive to its rulers because people and resources were easy to appropriate, regardless of its long-run potential for broad prosperity. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 4–5

Capturing leaders and appropriating existing organization

The authors describe a recurring conquest strategy in Mexico and Peru. Conquerors captured a ruler, demanded wealth and provisions, then installed themselves as the new elite over existing systems of taxation, tribute, and compelled labor. Cortés's seizure of Moctezuma and Pizarro's capture of Atahualpa at Cajamarca illustrate the method. The account of Atahualpa includes a ransom of one room of gold and two rooms of silver; he was executed despite its delivery. Capturing a ruler was useful precisely because an existing political hierarchy could transmit orders and organize resources. These are historical cases of violent appropriation, not evidence that the affected populations consented to the new rules. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 5–10

The encomienda was a colonial grant assigning Indigenous people to a Spanish holder, the encomendero. Those assigned owed tribute and labor; the holder was formally charged with converting them to Christianity. In practice, the authors' examples from Bartolomé de las Casas describe severe coercion, seizure of land and food, and work for the settler's benefit. The legal description and the observed power relationship need to be kept separate: an encomienda was neither ordinary wage employment nor simply a grant of land. It gave the holder control over people's obligations and the surplus from their work. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 7–9

The Potosí mita and its local legacy

The discovery of Potosí silver made access to mine labor especially valuable. Viceroy Francisco de Toledo first concentrated much of the Indigenous population into reducciones, settlements that made labor easier to organize and control. He then adapted the earlier Inca mita, a turn of compulsory labor. The authors distinguish the earlier Inca use of labor for plantations supplying temples, elites, and armies, with famine relief and security in return, from Toledo's colonial mining mita. The latter drew workers from a catchment of about 200,000 square miles in present-day Peru and Bolivia and required one-seventh of its male inhabitants to work in Potosí's mines. It lasted until 1825. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 10–11

The chapter's Map 1 shows the Inca realm, road network, colonial cities, modern borders, and the mining-mita catchment. Its value is to make clear that the compulsory-labor zone covered a large part of the Inca heartland rather than an isolated mine. The map marks a historical boundary; by itself it does not quantify the later economic effect of being inside it. Acemoglu & Robinson, Map 1, PDF p. 12

Map 1. Shading identifies the Inca Empire, while separate lines mark the Inca road network and the Potosí mita catchment; dots mark colonial cities. The catchment overlaps the former imperial heartland, including the region around Cusco. Acemoglu & Robinson, Map 1, PDF p. 12

The authors compare nearby Quechua-speaking provinces: Acomayo, inside the former mita zone, and Calca, outside it. They say inhabitants of Acomayo consume about one-third less, its road is worse, and farmers there produce more for subsistence, while Calca farmers more often sell to markets. The example gives an intuition for institutional persistence: past coercion may leave less infrastructure and fewer market opportunities. The chapter presents this as a historical interpretation, not a formal identification strategy that rules out every other difference between the provinces. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 12–13

Toledo's system extended beyond the mine. A fixed head tax payable in silver pushed households toward paid labor so they could obtain cash; the repartimiento de mercancías forced locals to buy goods at prices set by Spaniards; and the trajín compelled people to carry loads for elite businesses. Together with the encomienda and mita, these rules transferred land, labor, and income to colonial rulers and constrained Indigenous people's ability to choose work and accumulate resources. The authors argue that this enriched the Crown and colonial elites while reducing the scope for broad economic development. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 13–14

Jamestown: why attempts at coercion changed course

England entered American colonization later than Spain. The authors say the regions with dense populations and precious metals had already been claimed, and the English arrived in a northern territory where the Spanish model was harder to operate. Roanoke failed; Jamestown was founded in 1607. The Virginia Company nevertheless initially sought provisions, treasure, and labor from Indigenous people. The Powhatan Confederacy had political organization, but its ruler Wahunsunacock did not command the same centralized, resource-rich empire as the rulers in Mexico and Peru. Colonists could not seize a leader and thereby obtain a ready-made tributary workforce. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 14–17

Food shortages made this failure costly. John Smith arranged trade for supplies and argued that settlers would need practical skills and would have to work themselves. The colonists' search for gold continued; their attempt to make Wahunsunacock subordinate to the English king failed, and he imposed a trade embargo. Smith's departure preceded the winter of 1609–10, during which only about 60 of 500 colonists survived. The chapter treats this sequence as evidence that the Spanish extraction strategy was not viable in Virginia. Its Pocahontas rescue story is expressly qualified as appearing only “according to some accounts”; it is not needed for the economic explanation. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 16–19

The company then tried to compel its own settlers to work. Gates and Dale imposed severe rules, including death penalties for escape and some theft. Land belonged to the company; workers received assigned rations and worked in supervised gangs. This resembled the encomienda in its aim of extracting labor through coercion, but it was not an encomienda: no Spanish grant of Indigenous people to an encomendero operated in Jamestown. The immediate targets of this later system were English settlers under company authority. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 19–21

The company's power was limited because settlers had outside options: they could leave for Indigenous communities or try to live on the frontier. An outside option is the next best available action if one rejects an imposed arrangement. It makes harsh terms harder to enforce because the person can exit. The authors also contrast relatively sparse population in much of North America with dense areas of central Mexico and Andean Peru. Map 2 visualizes estimated population density around 1500; its legend is in people per square kilometer, while the neighboring prose offers examples per square mile. Those numbers must not be equated without converting units. The map supports a broad contrast in settlement patterns, not a claim that all of North America had the same population density. Acemoglu & Robinson, Map 2 and discussion, PDF pp. 20–21

Map 2. Estimated population density around 1500. The legend separates no data from four density bands—0–0.75, 0.75–2.5, 2.5–10, and 10–400 people per square kilometer. The darker areas in central Mexico and the Andes help explain why taking over existing tribute and labor systems was more feasible there than in Virginia. Acemoglu & Robinson, Map 2, PDF p. 20

Unable to compel either Indigenous people or settlers on the desired terms, the company shifted to incentives. In 1618 it began the headright system: a male settler received 50 acres, plus 50 acres for each family member and servant brought to Virginia. Settlers were released from contracts and received houses; in 1619 the General Assembly gave settlers a political say. Land and voice raised the return to cultivating and investing in the colony. This was a change in economic rights accompanied by a change in political rights, not an immediate arrival at modern universal democracy. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF p. 21

English elites later tried to create landed hierarchies in Maryland and Carolina. Lord Baltimore's Maryland scheme assigned large manors to lords; Carolina's proposed constitution placed hereditary leet-men below an aristocracy of landgraves and caziques. Settlers' ability to seek land and other options made these schemes difficult to impose. By the 1720s the thirteen colonies had governors and elected assemblies, generally based on male property ownership. These assemblies helped establish a tradition of political participation and limits on rulers, but women, enslaved people, and the propertyless did not vote. The authors' comparison is one of relative breadth of rights, not a claim that colonial America was egalitarian. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 22–23

Different paths after independence

The authors trace the US constitutional order of 1787 back to the colonial assemblies that began at Jamestown in 1619. In their account, broader political participation constrained arbitrary power and made more broadly usable economic rights possible. This was still profoundly limited: the US Constitution accepted slavery, counted an enslaved person as three-fifths for allocating House seats, and left voting rules to states; women and enslaved people were excluded. Later conflict over slavery culminated in the Civil War. The point is not that US institutions were fully free, but that political power and economic opportunity were distributed more broadly for a substantial part of the population than in the authors' Mexican comparison. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 23–26

Mexico's independence had a different political starting point in the authors' narrative. Napoleon's invasion of Spain created a constitutional crisis, and the 1812 Cádiz Constitution proposed popular sovereignty, limits on privilege, and equality before the law. Mexican elites, shaped by colonial hierarchies and alarmed by Hidalgo's revolt, feared that wider political participation would threaten their position. When Spanish constitutional reform returned in 1820 with proposals to end coerced labor and special privileges, these elites supported independence under Iturbide's 1821 Plan de Iguala, which removed the provisions they found threatening. Iturbide then concentrated power and dismissed the constitutionally authorized congress. Independence therefore did not necessarily end colonial economic privileges. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 24–26

Political turnover and coercion continued: the authors report that Antonio López de Santa Ana occupied the presidency eleven times and that Mexico had 52 presidents between 1824 and 1867. Their mechanism is that insecure government and property rights, weak tax and service capacity, and retained monopolies made investment and initiative risky for many people. Later Porfirio Díaz restored a measure of order and opened trade, but also used expropriation and political favors to benefit allies. Political stability alone is therefore not sufficient in this account; one must ask who can use state power, who receives property and market access, and who can challenge privilege. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 26–27, 30–33

The authors call this path-dependent change. New opportunities such as late nineteenth-century export trade and valuable frontier land did not erase earlier power relations. US land laws gave many settlers access to frontier holdings, while in much of Latin America connected elites received land. The US story also involved the dispossession of Indigenous people; “broader access” did not include them. Díaz's export-oriented modernization brought some growth, yet the authors describe continued exclusion and the deportation of possibly 30,000 Yaqui people between 1900 and 1910. Institutions can change in form while preserving who captures the gains. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 32–33

Persistence is not permanence. The chapter recounts revolutions, civil wars, reforms, and eventual movement toward democracy in Latin America, showing that rules can change, albeit often through conflict. Its discussion of repression draws on different reports and estimates, which should not be merged into a single precise count: for example, it reports 2,279 political killings in Chile in a truth commission report, 42,275 named Guatemalan victims in a clarification commission report with higher estimates elsewhere, and 9,000 Argentine deaths in an official commission count with higher human-rights estimates. These events underline the human cost of struggles over power; they do not by themselves prove every economic link in the authors' theory. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 33–34

From political rules to invention, firms, and finance

The Industrial Revolution increased productivity through mechanization and new inventions. An inventor who expects to benefit from an idea has a reason to develop and commercialize it; a patent protects some rights to that idea. But a patent alone does not finance a factory or a new firm. Entrepreneurs also need entry into markets, a workforce, and credit. The authors use this sequence to show why the same individual talent can yield different outcomes under different rules. Their examples include Thomas Edison, who had limited formal schooling, sold an early patent to raise capital, and later founded businesses. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 28–29, 39

The chapter reports that among US patentees in 1820–45, only 19% came from professional or major landowning families and 40% had primary schooling or less. It also reports growth from 338 US banks with $160 million in assets in 1818 to 27,864 banks with $27.3 billion in assets in 1914. The authors argue that competitive finance helped people with inventions obtain capital at lower rates. As a contrast, they report 42 banks in Mexico in 1910, with two controlling 60% of banking assets; concentrated lending favored wealthy insiders and higher rates. These figures refer to different dates and national contexts, so they illustrate the institutional argument rather than serving as a matched quantitative causal test. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 28–30

The authors do not claim that US bankers were naturally less interested in profits. They argue that the same profit motive was channeled differently by political rules. US politicians also attempted to create bank monopolies for allies, but voters could remove officeholders who used regulation in ways harmful to a wider electorate. Where rulers and their allies could sustain monopoly privileges, banking remained concentrated and potential competitors struggled to borrow. The proposed causal chain is: distribution of political power → rules and enforcement for banking → access to finance → who can start and grow a firm. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 30–32

Carlos Slim, Bill Gates, and the limits of business power

The chapter contrasts two wealthy entrepreneurs to make the effect of rules concrete. In the United States, Bill Gates could build Microsoft using a skilled workforce, finance, markets, and enforceable property rights. His wealth did not exempt Microsoft from public antitrust action: US authorities investigated the company and the Department of Justice filed a case in 1998 over its alleged abuse of monopoly power, with a settlement in 2001. The authors do not portray the US market as free of monopoly attempts; they emphasize constraints that can operate even against a powerful firm. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 34–35, 39

Carlos Slim had succeeded in investments and turning around firms, but the chapter identifies his acquisition of Telmex as the decisive opportunity. During privatization in 1990, a Slim-led consortium won control of 51% of the voting stock, equivalent to 20.4% of total stock, although it had not submitted the highest bid. The authors say payment could be delayed and financed using Telmex dividends. A former public telecommunications monopoly became a highly profitable private monopoly. The broader environment included licenses, red tape, political connections, and scarce finance that could keep competitors out. This is an account of how access to a protected market can generate wealth; it should not be reduced to a claim that Slim lacked ability. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF p. 35

The Mexican Competition Commission found substantial Telmex monopoly power in several telephone markets, but the authors say regulatory efforts failed. They highlight the recurso de amparo, originally a constitutional protection of individual rights, as a legal instrument Telmex could use to resist regulation. In a separate CompUSA/COC dispute litigated in Dallas, Slim's side lost and was fined $454 million. The authors interpret this as evidence that a business strategy successful under one set of legal and political rules can fail under another. These cases are illustrations of institutional constraints and advantages, not a complete assessment of either entrepreneur's career or of every antitrust system. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 35–36

What the authors mean by institutions

Economic institutions are the rules and their enforcement that affect economic choices: property and contract security, freedom to enter occupations and markets, access to land and credit, competition, schooling, and incentives to save, invest, and adopt technology. Political institutions determine who can make and change those economic rules, how rulers are constrained, how state power is exercised, and whether citizens or groups can act collectively to hold officials accountable. The category includes constitutions and elections, but also the state's capacity to govern and the real distribution of political power. A written constitutional promise alone is insufficient when rulers can ignore it. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 38–39

The authors' explanation has two linked parts. Economics: institutions alter the expected return and risk of schooling, work, innovation, investment, and entrepreneurship, so they affect prosperity. Politics: power determines which institutions are adopted and whether they survive. An arrangement that lowers total welfare can still be valuable to an incumbent who collects monopoly profit or controls land and labor. That person has a reason to resist reforms even if a broader population would gain. This feedback explains why unequal rules can persist and why knowledge of a better policy is not enough to implement it. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 39–41

The chapter states a broad theory rather than presenting a complete statistical identification of it. Nogales, Acomayo–Calca, banking, and the two entrepreneurs give historically specific reasons to take the theory seriously, but their contrasts are not by themselves proof that institutions are the only cause of prosperity. Equally, institutional paths are not fixed forever: the chapter itself describes reforms, conflict, and change. The careful reading is that incentives, enforcement, political power, and feedback must be examined together for each comparison. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 3, 13, 31–34, 38–41

Answers to the six assigned reading questions

These questions are transcribed from the Week 1 course screenshot. The answers use this chapter alone.

  1. What seem to be the main differences between the two Nogaleses? The authors report much higher income, schooling, health, public-service quality, security, and political accountability in Nogales, Arizona. Nogales, Sonora, has lower average income and weaker services, and starting a firm is exposed to crime, bureaucracy, and corruption. The cities' proximity makes the institutional difference across the border their proposed explanation. The Sonora side is nevertheless relatively prosperous within Mexico because of US-linked manufacturing. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 1–3, 37–38

  2. What was the encomienda and how did it work? It was a grant assigning Indigenous people to an encomendero. They owed tribute and labor; the holder was formally responsible for Christian conversion. The authors' examples show the arrangement functioning as a means of coerced labor and extraction, including seizure of land, food, and output. It was a rule over people's obligations rather than simply a land title or a normal employment contract. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 7–9

  3. Was the encomienda or a similar system used in Jamestown? There was no encomienda as such in Jamestown. The Virginia Company first tried to exploit the Powhatan population but could not reproduce the Spanish conquest strategy. It later imposed a harsh company-run labor regime on English settlers, with company land, rations, supervised work, and severe penalties. That was similar in its coercive goal, but differed in its legal form and target. Settlers' outside options helped force a shift toward headright land grants and an assembly. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 15–23

  4. What important historical differences between Mexico and the USA are explained? In the authors' account, densely populated and organized parts of Spanish America enabled colonizers to take over systems of tribute and forced labor; efforts to impose comparable coercion in Virginia failed, leading to land incentives and colonial assemblies. At independence, US constitutional constraints grew out of that assembly tradition, while Mexican elites sought to preserve privileges threatened by Cádiz reforms. Later instability, land and bank monopolies, and politically allocated favors restricted economic entry in Mexico; broader rights and competitive finance supported invention and firms in the United States. The US path also included slavery, exclusion from voting, and Indigenous dispossession, so it is a relative contrast. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 5–33

  5. How did Carlos Slim become rich? The authors say Slim made gains in securities and firm acquisitions, then greatly increased his wealth by winning the privatized Telmex monopoly through a Slim-led consortium. Political access, barriers to entry, limited competition, favorable payment terms, and the ability to challenge regulation helped protect its profits. The answer is about how institutions shaped an opportunity available to a skilled and ambitious entrepreneur, not a claim that a single law or transaction explains his entire fortune. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 35–36

  6. How do the authors understand institutions? They are the economic and political rules made and enforced collectively through the state and society. Economic rules shape incentives to acquire skills, invest, innovate, enter markets, and use credit. Political rules and the actual distribution of power determine who chooses economic rules, how officials are constrained, and whether favored groups can preserve benefits at others' expense. Institutions include enforcement and state capacity, not only written laws. Their interaction can make a prosperous or unequal path persistent. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 38–41

Synthesis

The chapter's central claim is a chain of incentives and power: colonial circumstances influenced which rules conquerors could impose; the resulting distribution of political power shaped economic rights, entry, and finance; and beneficiaries of those rules often defended them. This helps explain why the authors see lasting differences between the two Nogaleses and between the United States and Mexico. The claim is strongest as a framework for asking who has power, which economic choices are rewarded, and why reform is hard. Its historical contrasts are informative illustrations, while the exclusions and violence within both national histories prevent a simple story of one uniformly “good” society and one uniformly “bad” one. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 37–41

sections.title: Practice with fading assistance

sections.html:
Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks

The prepared keys operationalize each component; all are essential. Pass requires an explicit mechanism and justified application plus every specified limit. Partial applies to an incomplete argument or isolated arithmetic transcription error with otherwise correct setup; teach gives feedback and obtains a fresh check. An arithmetic slip is not itself proof of conceptual failure, but a numerically wrong result does not count as a complete pass. Fail applies to any critical conceptual error identified below. Unscorable applies to missing response or ambiguous/unknown help conditions; do not infer acquisition.

Full role coverage: I1, I2, D1, and D2 each test all components C1 Nogales hypothesis and limit, C2 extraction institutions and local legacy, C3 Jamestown incentives and outside options, C4 comparative qualifications and map limits. Normal acquisition is two distinct passes on I1 and I2, same revision/criterion and known unassisted conditions. Permitted repair/entry substitution: use a previously unseen D1 or D2 as a full_scope_independent check; record that immediate use explicitly and do not count it as delayed retention. Only combinations of two different unexposed I/D items are permitted. Supported, worked, diagnostic, and C items do not fill this role. Correction items are deliberately narrower and cannot substitute for acquisition or delayed checks. If both delayed variants are consumed during repair, request new prepared delayed items from plan before claiming delayed readiness.

Each delayed pass independently requires the same entire criterion after at least 24 elapsed hours from the last instruction/solution exposure for this objective, with current tuple, fresh item and known intervening exposure. The 24-hour guard is an operational minimum; recall owns dates. A previously seen question can be used for practice only.

Produce a critical explanation of the chapter’s chain from political constraints to entry/property/finance incentives, comparing post-independence paths, invention and banking, and Gates/Slim. Distinguish talent from the opportunities/constraints rules create and include exclusions, dated comparisons and limits on causal identification.

Study conditions, assessment scope and sources

Essential criterion components are C1 political-economic incentive chain, C2 independence and finance mechanisms, C3 Gates-Slim institutional comparison, C4 exclusions and causal-evidence limits. Primary finished-note locations: Different paths after independence; From political rules to invention, firms, and finance; Carlos Slim, Bill Gates, and the limits of business power; What the authors mean by institutions; Answers to the six assigned reading questions; Synthesis.

Instruction and supported practice may use the selected notes. Independent checks are closed-note: show the stated prompt and its supplied data only, with no explanation, model answer, hints, web search, other people, AI help, or solution-bearing figure access before the response. A simple calculator is allowed for arithmetic after the learner states the reasoning; no symbolic or generative tools. If notes, item keys, or matching solutions were accessed, record the exposure and do not call that attempt independent. No timing or confidence threshold replaces a complete answer. No biography outside the chapter, present antitrust/legal advice, modern bank counts or causal identification method is added. Historical financial quantities are evidence context; reproduction of every count is not an independent outcome criterion.

sections.title: Prerequisites and checks

sections.html: Economic institutions are rules/enforcement governing property, contracts, entry, skills, land, credit and innovation incentives. Political institutions distribute power to choose/change those rules and constrain officials; state capacity and effective power matter beyond constitutional text. A patent can protect an invention yet commercialization also needs entry, workforce and finance. The chapter compares opportunities offered to skilled ambitious people, not national innate motives or a complete accounting of every fortune. Privately owned firms can still enjoy protected monopoly; privatization alone is not competitive entry.
sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
1. Trace post-independence power: US constitutional constraints developed from assemblies but accepted slavery and excluded many voters. Mexican elites opposed threatening Cádiz reforms and supported independence retaining privileges; Iturbide concentrated power. Instability can weaken rights/services, but Díaz shows stability/export growth can coexist with favoritism/expropriation. Ask who benefits, not merely whether rulers are stable.
  2. Link power to financial rules: the authors say electoral constraints could frustrate US politicians’ bank-monopoly attempts, while favored Mexican insiders sustained concentration. Same profit motive, different rule constraints. Banking access changes who can finance/commercialize ideas; patents alone are insufficient. US/mexican bank counts/assets use different dates and contexts, so not a matched causal test.
  3. Interpret Gates: skilled workforce, finance, markets/rights helped Microsoft, and public antitrust action constrained a powerful firm. This is not absence of US monopoly attempts.
  4. Interpret Slim: prior investment/turnaround success plus Telmex privatization supplied protected market access; consortium control of 51% voting stock equaled 20.4% total stock, not 51% of all shares. Political access, entry/finance barriers, payment terms and regulatory resistance shaped monopoly profit. Amparo’s rights-protecting origin differs from its strategic use. A different US litigation context constrained his side in the Dallas dispute; do not infer a universal national legal ranking.
  5. Connect feedback: incumbents receiving rents can defend rules, while market opportunity/power also changes over time. US slavery, restricted voting and Indigenous dispossession; Mexican export growth/reforms/conflict qualify simple good/bad stories. Historical repression counts from distinct reports/estimates cannot be merged as one precise count. Narratives illustrate a theory, not identify institutions as the exclusive cause of prosperity.
sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
Reading context

Deliver these complete reused passages before the worked example; earlier concise prompts are checkpoints, not substitutes. Necessary prerequisites use the complete prepared lessons specified above.

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Different paths after independence; fingerprint d4bf9c4cdad229430e95558fa87fd4edcf657d0b2820a100f9160c229a5b3f3a. Heading depth and required relative figure-path relocation alone are adapted.

Different paths after independence

The authors trace the US constitutional order of 1787 back to the colonial assemblies that began at Jamestown in 1619. In their account, broader political participation constrained arbitrary power and made more broadly usable economic rights possible. This was still profoundly limited: the US Constitution accepted slavery, counted an enslaved person as three-fifths for allocating House seats, and left voting rules to states; women and enslaved people were excluded. Later conflict over slavery culminated in the Civil War. The point is not that US institutions were fully free, but that political power and economic opportunity were distributed more broadly for a substantial part of the population than in the authors' Mexican comparison. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 23–26

Mexico's independence had a different political starting point in the authors' narrative. Napoleon's invasion of Spain created a constitutional crisis, and the 1812 Cádiz Constitution proposed popular sovereignty, limits on privilege, and equality before the law. Mexican elites, shaped by colonial hierarchies and alarmed by Hidalgo's revolt, feared that wider political participation would threaten their position. When Spanish constitutional reform returned in 1820 with proposals to end coerced labor and special privileges, these elites supported independence under Iturbide's 1821 Plan de Iguala, which removed the provisions they found threatening. Iturbide then concentrated power and dismissed the constitutionally authorized congress. Independence therefore did not necessarily end colonial economic privileges. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 24–26

Political turnover and coercion continued: the authors report that Antonio López de Santa Ana occupied the presidency eleven times and that Mexico had 52 presidents between 1824 and 1867. Their mechanism is that insecure government and property rights, weak tax and service capacity, and retained monopolies made investment and initiative risky for many people. Later Porfirio Díaz restored a measure of order and opened trade, but also used expropriation and political favors to benefit allies. Political stability alone is therefore not sufficient in this account; one must ask who can use state power, who receives property and market access, and who can challenge privilege. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 26–27, 30–33

The authors call this path-dependent change. New opportunities such as late nineteenth-century export trade and valuable frontier land did not erase earlier power relations. US land laws gave many settlers access to frontier holdings, while in much of Latin America connected elites received land. The US story also involved the dispossession of Indigenous people; “broader access” did not include them. Díaz's export-oriented modernization brought some growth, yet the authors describe continued exclusion and the deportation of possibly 30,000 Yaqui people between 1900 and 1910. Institutions can change in form while preserving who captures the gains. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 32–33

Persistence is not permanence. The chapter recounts revolutions, civil wars, reforms, and eventual movement toward democracy in Latin America, showing that rules can change, albeit often through conflict. Its discussion of repression draws on different reports and estimates, which should not be merged into a single precise count: for example, it reports 2,279 political killings in Chile in a truth commission report, 42,275 named Guatemalan victims in a clarification commission report with higher estimates elsewhere, and 9,000 Argentine deaths in an official commission count with higher human-rights estimates. These events underline the human cost of struggles over power; they do not by themselves prove every economic link in the authors' theory. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 33–34

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage From political rules to invention, firms, and finance; fingerprint d4bf9c4cdad229430e95558fa87fd4edcf657d0b2820a100f9160c229a5b3f3a. Heading depth and required relative figure-path relocation alone are adapted.

From political rules to invention, firms, and finance

The Industrial Revolution increased productivity through mechanization and new inventions. An inventor who expects to benefit from an idea has a reason to develop and commercialize it; a patent protects some rights to that idea. But a patent alone does not finance a factory or a new firm. Entrepreneurs also need entry into markets, a workforce, and credit. The authors use this sequence to show why the same individual talent can yield different outcomes under different rules. Their examples include Thomas Edison, who had limited formal schooling, sold an early patent to raise capital, and later founded businesses. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 28–29, 39

The chapter reports that among US patentees in 1820–45, only 19% came from professional or major landowning families and 40% had primary schooling or less. It also reports growth from 338 US banks with $160 million in assets in 1818 to 27,864 banks with $27.3 billion in assets in 1914. The authors argue that competitive finance helped people with inventions obtain capital at lower rates. As a contrast, they report 42 banks in Mexico in 1910, with two controlling 60% of banking assets; concentrated lending favored wealthy insiders and higher rates. These figures refer to different dates and national contexts, so they illustrate the institutional argument rather than serving as a matched quantitative causal test. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 28–30

The authors do not claim that US bankers were naturally less interested in profits. They argue that the same profit motive was channeled differently by political rules. US politicians also attempted to create bank monopolies for allies, but voters could remove officeholders who used regulation in ways harmful to a wider electorate. Where rulers and their allies could sustain monopoly privileges, banking remained concentrated and potential competitors struggled to borrow. The proposed causal chain is: distribution of political power → rules and enforcement for banking → access to finance → who can start and grow a firm. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 30–32

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Carlos Slim, Bill Gates, and the limits of business power; fingerprint d4bf9c4cdad229430e95558fa87fd4edcf657d0b2820a100f9160c229a5b3f3a. Heading depth and required relative figure-path relocation alone are adapted.

Carlos Slim, Bill Gates, and the limits of business power

The chapter contrasts two wealthy entrepreneurs to make the effect of rules concrete. In the United States, Bill Gates could build Microsoft using a skilled workforce, finance, markets, and enforceable property rights. His wealth did not exempt Microsoft from public antitrust action: US authorities investigated the company and the Department of Justice filed a case in 1998 over its alleged abuse of monopoly power, with a settlement in 2001. The authors do not portray the US market as free of monopoly attempts; they emphasize constraints that can operate even against a powerful firm. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 34–35, 39

Carlos Slim had succeeded in investments and turning around firms, but the chapter identifies his acquisition of Telmex as the decisive opportunity. During privatization in 1990, a Slim-led consortium won control of 51% of the voting stock, equivalent to 20.4% of total stock, although it had not submitted the highest bid. The authors say payment could be delayed and financed using Telmex dividends. A former public telecommunications monopoly became a highly profitable private monopoly. The broader environment included licenses, red tape, political connections, and scarce finance that could keep competitors out. This is an account of how access to a protected market can generate wealth; it should not be reduced to a claim that Slim lacked ability. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF p. 35

The Mexican Competition Commission found substantial Telmex monopoly power in several telephone markets, but the authors say regulatory efforts failed. They highlight the recurso de amparo, originally a constitutional protection of individual rights, as a legal instrument Telmex could use to resist regulation. In a separate CompUSA/COC dispute litigated in Dallas, Slim's side lost and was fined $454 million. The authors interpret this as evidence that a business strategy successful under one set of legal and political rules can fail under another. These cases are illustrations of institutional constraints and advantages, not a complete assessment of either entrepreneur's career or of every antitrust system. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 35–36

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage What the authors mean by institutions; fingerprint d4bf9c4cdad229430e95558fa87fd4edcf657d0b2820a100f9160c229a5b3f3a. Heading depth and required relative figure-path relocation alone are adapted.

What the authors mean by institutions

Economic institutions are the rules and their enforcement that affect economic choices: property and contract security, freedom to enter occupations and markets, access to land and credit, competition, schooling, and incentives to save, invest, and adopt technology. Political institutions determine who can make and change those economic rules, how rulers are constrained, how state power is exercised, and whether citizens or groups can act collectively to hold officials accountable. The category includes constitutions and elections, but also the state's capacity to govern and the real distribution of political power. A written constitutional promise alone is insufficient when rulers can ignore it. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 38–39

The authors' explanation has two linked parts. Economics: institutions alter the expected return and risk of schooling, work, innovation, investment, and entrepreneurship, so they affect prosperity. Politics: power determines which institutions are adopted and whether they survive. An arrangement that lowers total welfare can still be valuable to an incumbent who collects monopoly profit or controls land and labor. That person has a reason to resist reforms even if a broader population would gain. This feedback explains why unequal rules can persist and why knowledge of a better policy is not enough to implement it. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 39–41

The chapter states a broad theory rather than presenting a complete statistical identification of it. Nogales, Acomayo–Calca, banking, and the two entrepreneurs give historically specific reasons to take the theory seriously, but their contrasts are not by themselves proof that institutions are the only cause of prosperity. Equally, institutional paths are not fixed forever: the chapter itself describes reforms, conflict, and change. The careful reading is that incentives, enforcement, political power, and feedback must be examined together for each comparison. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 3, 13, 31–34, 38–41

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Answers to the six assigned reading questions; fingerprint d4bf9c4cdad229430e95558fa87fd4edcf657d0b2820a100f9160c229a5b3f3a. Heading depth and required relative figure-path relocation alone are adapted.

Answers to the six assigned reading questions

These questions are transcribed from the Week 1 course screenshot. The answers use this chapter alone.

  1. What seem to be the main differences between the two Nogaleses? The authors report much higher income, schooling, health, public-service quality, security, and political accountability in Nogales, Arizona. Nogales, Sonora, has lower average income and weaker services, and starting a firm is exposed to crime, bureaucracy, and corruption. The cities' proximity makes the institutional difference across the border their proposed explanation. The Sonora side is nevertheless relatively prosperous within Mexico because of US-linked manufacturing. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 1–3, 37–38

  2. What was the encomienda and how did it work? It was a grant assigning Indigenous people to an encomendero. They owed tribute and labor; the holder was formally responsible for Christian conversion. The authors' examples show the arrangement functioning as a means of coerced labor and extraction, including seizure of land, food, and output. It was a rule over people's obligations rather than simply a land title or a normal employment contract. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 7–9

  3. Was the encomienda or a similar system used in Jamestown? There was no encomienda as such in Jamestown. The Virginia Company first tried to exploit the Powhatan population but could not reproduce the Spanish conquest strategy. It later imposed a harsh company-run labor regime on English settlers, with company land, rations, supervised work, and severe penalties. That was similar in its coercive goal, but differed in its legal form and target. Settlers' outside options helped force a shift toward headright land grants and an assembly. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 15–23

  4. What important historical differences between Mexico and the USA are explained? In the authors' account, densely populated and organized parts of Spanish America enabled colonizers to take over systems of tribute and forced labor; efforts to impose comparable coercion in Virginia failed, leading to land incentives and colonial assemblies. At independence, US constitutional constraints grew out of that assembly tradition, while Mexican elites sought to preserve privileges threatened by Cádiz reforms. Later instability, land and bank monopolies, and politically allocated favors restricted economic entry in Mexico; broader rights and competitive finance supported invention and firms in the United States. The US path also included slavery, exclusion from voting, and Indigenous dispossession, so it is a relative contrast. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 5–33

  5. How did Carlos Slim become rich? The authors say Slim made gains in securities and firm acquisitions, then greatly increased his wealth by winning the privatized Telmex monopoly through a Slim-led consortium. Political access, barriers to entry, limited competition, favorable payment terms, and the ability to challenge regulation helped protect its profits. The answer is about how institutions shaped an opportunity available to a skilled and ambitious entrepreneur, not a claim that a single law or transaction explains his entire fortune. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 35–36

  6. How do the authors understand institutions? They are the economic and political rules made and enforced collectively through the state and society. Economic rules shape incentives to acquire skills, invest, innovate, enter markets, and use credit. Political rules and the actual distribution of power determine who chooses economic rules, how officials are constrained, and whether favored groups can preserve benefits at others' expense. Institutions include enforcement and state capacity, not only written laws. Their interaction can make a prosperous or unequal path persistent. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 38–41

Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Synthesis; fingerprint d4bf9c4cdad229430e95558fa87fd4edcf657d0b2820a100f9160c229a5b3f3a. Heading depth and required relative figure-path relocation alone are adapted.

Synthesis

The chapter's central claim is a chain of incentives and power: colonial circumstances influenced which rules conquerors could impose; the resulting distribution of political power shaped economic rights, entry, and finance; and beneficiaries of those rules often defended them. This helps explain why the authors see lasting differences between the two Nogaleses and between the United States and Mexico. The claim is strongest as a framework for asking who has power, which economic choices are rewarded, and why reform is hard. Its historical contrasts are informative illustrations, while the exclusions and violence within both national histories prevent a simple story of one uniformly “good” society and one uniformly “bad” one. Acemoglu & Robinson, PDF pp. 37–41

O008-W1

Item/version: O008-W1 / 1. Role: worked example. Components: C1 political-economic incentive chain, C2 independence and finance mechanisms, C3 Gates-Slim institutional comparison, C4 exclusions and causal-evidence limits.

Prompt: Construct a source-grounded critical paragraph connecting assemblies/Cádiz-independence politics, banking and invention, and Microsoft/Telmex; include the meaning of economic/political institutions and limits.

Prepared key and essential reasoning: Political institutions distribute/constrain rule-making power, economic rules/enforcement alter entry/property/credit/innovation returns. US assembly-based constraints versus Mexican elite-preserving independence are the authors’ relative power paths, with severe US exclusions and later Mexican changes. Patents plus workforce/entry/credit enable commercialization; voter constraints could check bank privileges, not less-profit-seeking bankers; dated unequal bank comparisons are illustrations. Gates benefited from enabling conditions yet Microsoft faced antitrust; Slim was skilled but Telmex protected-market acquisition/regulatory barriers aided wealth, with voting/total stock distinct. Rent beneficiaries can resist reform. Neither entrepreneurs nor histories form a controlled causal test or universal institutional ranking.

sections.title: Practice with fading assistance

sections.html:
Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks

The prepared keys operationalize each component; all are essential. Pass requires an explicit mechanism and justified application plus every specified limit. Partial applies to an incomplete argument or isolated arithmetic transcription error with otherwise correct setup; teach gives feedback and obtains a fresh check. An arithmetic slip is not itself proof of conceptual failure, but a numerically wrong result does not count as a complete pass. Fail applies to any critical conceptual error identified below. Unscorable applies to missing response or ambiguous/unknown help conditions; do not infer acquisition.

Full role coverage: I1, I2, D1, and D2 each test all components C1 political-economic incentive chain, C2 independence and finance mechanisms, C3 Gates-Slim institutional comparison, C4 exclusions and causal-evidence limits. Normal acquisition is two distinct passes on I1 and I2, same revision/criterion and known unassisted conditions. Permitted repair/entry substitution: use a previously unseen D1 or D2 as a full_scope_independent check; record that immediate use explicitly and do not count it as delayed retention. Only combinations of two different unexposed I/D items are permitted. Supported, worked, diagnostic, and C items do not fill this role. Correction items are deliberately narrower and cannot substitute for acquisition or delayed checks. If both delayed variants are consumed during repair, request new prepared delayed items from plan before claiming delayed readiness.

Each delayed pass independently requires the same entire criterion after at least 24 elapsed hours from the last instruction/solution exposure for this objective, with current tuple, fresh item and known intervening exposure. The 24-hour guard is an operational minimum; recall owns dates. A previously seen question can be used for practice only.

sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Comparability, data reliability and reading questions; fingerprint edb8887ee683dab0eac786b8cbb319555883374c9c39b4b7b770e66a110e7055. Heading depth and required relative figure-path relocation alone are adapted.

Comparability, data reliability and reading questions

Source: Week II - lecture - large slides Source: Week III - lecture - large slides

  • Measurement can change what a comparison means
  • Source chronology and the first summary
  • Acemoglu–Robinson reading questions and answer routes
  • Earlier lecture questions and the boundary of supplied readings
  • What the source leads add to the map

Comparative economics asks positive questions about how institutions and economic systems work. Meaningful comparisons need a defined outcome, credible units and a defensible counterfactual; a large difference alone does not establish its cause. Countries supply a limited and heterogeneous sample, and qualitative features such as informal institutions are difficult to compress into comparable numbers. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 6–7

The data checks are a necessary foundation for the synthetic-control case and institutional narratives. They do not imply that every official statistic is false or every alternative proxy is superior. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 6–15

Measurement can change what a comparison means

A series can change over time because the economy changes, because its definition changes, or because collection/reporting changes. Cross-country differences can likewise mix true differences with measurement conventions. Record the unit, price basis, coverage, reference date and missing observations before explaining a gap. Political pressure, censorship, self-censorship and incentives within statistical agencies can affect data production and availability. That motivates scrutiny of the specific measurement process, rather than a blanket rejection based on the country’s political label. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 6–10

The lecture reports Li Keqiang’s older skepticism about Chinese GDP and his interest in electricity, rail freight and loans as alternative activity indicators. Such indicators can triangulate an official series but each measures a particular part of the economy; a shift toward services can weaken a historical proxy relationship. Its Chen et al. (2019) graph places the official provincial GDP growth rate on the horizontal axis and the researchers’ adjusted provincial GDP growth rate on the vertical, both in percent, with a 45-degree equality line. Circle size separately represents the relative size of provincial GDP. Points below the line indicate adjusted growth below officially reported growth, not a direct estimate of the GDP-level gap. The chart is not a newly audited correction of current national GDP. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 8–9

The axes compare growth rates in percent; the vertical discrepancy at a given official growth rate is a difference in percentage points. Circle size represents relative provincial GDP level. Growth-rate differences and relative economic size are distinct information. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 9

The youth-unemployment chart reports a 21.3% June 2023 value for ages 16–24 and a later 18.8% August 2024 value for the series excluding students. Those figures straddle a definitional/publication break. Subtracting them and calling the result an improvement in one unchanged population would be invalid. The accompanying land-sales figure measures area in billions of square feet, over 2010–2020; it is not land-sale revenue, an asset price, or a current property-market indicator. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 10–12

The annotation marks the reporting/definition discontinuity; retaining that context prevents a false before/after comparison. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 11

The lecture also points to North Korean nighttime lights as a proxy, and to removals or alterations of US government datasets. Its Freilich et al. (2025) example reports CDC datasets declining from 1,519 to 1,316 between January 21 and February 11, 2025; the Guardian chart reports nearly 400 deleted or altered datasets in a distinct August 18, 2026 report. These are separate source-attributed claims with different dates and coverage. Neither count measures all data quality, and a deleted webpage does not automatically mean underlying observations were destroyed. The articles are references cited on the lecture slide, not independently ingested full sources or a live inventory checked here. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 13–14

The source’s topic and agency counts describe its classified set of affected datasets. Agency totals and topic totals group the same reported events differently; they should not be added together as independent removals. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 14

Source chronology and the first summary

The Week II lecture’s next-session assignment is dated October 16. It asks students to discuss five questions on The Narrow Corridor, chapter 1, and six on Paths of Economic and Political Development (2006), without submitting written answers. The supplied assignment image repeats those reading prompts and points toward synthetic-control resources; it contains no learner responses or results. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 3

For the first “summary,” the lecture names Roland chapter 7 and Acemoglu–Robinson (2006). It states that the summary takes the final twenty minutes of the third seminar on October 16, with several multiple-choice questions and one or two open questions. That is the source’s dated course instruction, not an inferred expansion of examination scope to every additional reading. The existing Week 1 institution note supplies the checked Roland foundations. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 4

The Week III lecture’s next-session assignment is dated October 23 and asks for oral discussion of Polanyi chapter 4 and Rosser–Rosser chapter 4 (or its named alternative title). The files are inside the selected Week 3 folder and are covered as supplied; the date does not authorize ingestion of a separate later folder. Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 3

Acemoglu–Robinson reading questions and answer routes

The six supplied questions can be answered from Institutions, power and democratization:

  1. Driving force: economic institutions shape incentives and performance, while their political selection responds to distributional conflict and power. This is the authors’ explanation, not a one-variable causal estimate.
  2. Model: political institutions supply de jure power; resources and organization supply de facto power; together they shape current economic rules and future political institutions; economic rules affect current outcomes and future resources.
  3. De facto power: resources and the ability to solve collective-action problems, organize, protest or use force; wealth is one input rather than the definition itself.
  4. Credible commitment: a future transfer or reform promise may be reneged on once the other side’s leverage fades. Durable political-rule changes can alter tomorrow’s incentives where a revocable policy promise cannot.
  5. Repression: elites choose it when retaining their advantages is valuable and repression is sufficiently feasible/cheap relative to concessions; destruction, failure and empowerment of the military can make it unattractive.
  6. Britain: growth and political reform interact through institutional protection, investment, industrial/urban change and the organization of excluded groups. Early parliamentary constraints were not yet universal democracy; the narrative is joint evolution rather than proof that income alone automatically causes democracy.

The detailed explanation and historical limits appear in the linked note, grounded in the complete supplied chapter. Acemoglu–Robinson (2006), physical PDF pp. 1–19 Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 3, 44–50

The five Narrow Corridor prompts have their full answers in Liberty, Leviathans and the cage of norms: Warre discourages commerce/investment through persistent threats; order is valuable but statelessness need not imply constant violence and state strength need not protect liberty; the three Leviathans differ in capacity and effective societal constraint; the cage enforces unequal customary roles; the Asante protection/dependency account shows a norm protecting against danger while binding a person to subordination. The Narrow Corridor, chapter 1, physical PDF pp. 7–26 Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 3

Earlier lecture questions and the boundary of supplied readings

The Week II lecture repeats questions on Why Nations Fail, chapter 1. Its supplied slides answer the Nogales, encomienda, Jamestown, colonial divergence and institutional-definition prompts; the complete book chapter itself is a reference lead, not another supplied source in this pass. Nogales contrasts are dated examples. Spanish extraction used tribute/labour claims under encomienda; failed coercion in Jamestown led toward land and work incentives rather than successful adoption of the same Spanish regime. Institutions are the rules governing incentives and power, which can be inclusive or extractive, rather than a synonym for a building or organization. Existing Week 1 checked notes develop the colonial context. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 37–43

Carlos Slim prompt—bounded clarification: the institutional mechanism relevant to the question is control of a protected telecommunications incumbent. The OECD’s 2012 Review of Telecommunication Policy and Regulation in Mexico, Table 1.3 and the following Telmex paragraph, printed pp. 21–22 (physical PDF pp. 23–24), describes Slim-family control of América Móvil, its Telmex stake, and the 1990 sale of controlling Telmex shares to a Grupo Carso-led consortium. Telmex received exclusive long-distance/international service rights until 1997 alongside expansion and regulatory obligations. Ownership and entry rules can therefore create concentrated income opportunities. This verifies that mechanism; it does not claim that those pages reconstruct Slim’s entire fortune or that all his earnings were explained by one event.

The full Why Nations Fail chapter’s finer biographical/legal narrative is not certified here. The publisher’s accessible excerpt was checked for the prompt but did not contain Slim’s discussion; no unsupported quotation or invented chapter answer is supplied. The separate 2006 chapter and lecture already support the general distinction between selective protection and broad institutional inclusion. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 37–43

What the source leads add to the map

The lecture bibliography includes Abadie, Korolev, other synthetic-control articles, an R-bloggers example and other empirical references. The two supplied full papers establish the method and Russia case; a link alone is not evidence that code was run or every cited article was read. Likewise, Week III’s later-book-chapter pointers, Murphy–O’Reilly empirical illustration, Irfan references, S&P/UK reports and two YouTube links have the bounded treatment stated in their relevant notes. No later-week material, unavailable book chapter, video content or unexecuted replication result is silently promoted into checked course coverage. O009-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: A hypothetical provincial graph reports official GDP growth 8% and adjusted growth 6%, while circle area indicates relative GDP size. Compute the adjusted-minus-official growth discrepancy and distinguish its units from a GDP-level difference. A second graph reports youth unemployment of 21.3% in June 2023 and 18.8% in August 2024 after excluding students; may their difference measure improvement for one unchanged population? A land-sales observation is 2 billion square feet. Interpret the quantity, alternative electricity/rail/loan/night-light proxies and reporting incentives. Explain why CDC \(1519\to1316\) and nearly 400 deleted/altered datasets are distinct reports, summarize the dated October 16/23 assignments/first-summary scope, and distinguish checked readings, lecture interpretations, bounded Slim verification and unexecuted bibliography leads.

Complete solution and essential rubric: The growth discrepancy is \(6-8=-2\) percentage points. The axes contain growth rates in percent, not GDP levels; circle size contains separate relative-level information. The youth series crosses a population/definition and publication break, so subtracting the two rates cannot isolate improvement in one unchanged series. \(2\) billion square feet is land area, not revenue, price or a current market reading. Activity proxies each cover a subset and can lose relevance with structural change; political/reporting incentives require specific scrutiny, not rejection of every official statistic.
