sections.html:
Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Synthetic control: design, fit and inference; fingerprint f68abe39a544b3e0073189cf0d3543276edd30d9d1b78718c7ff6a94a34dee87. Heading depth and required relative figure-path relocation alone are adapted.

Synthetic control: design, fit and inference

Source: Abadie 2021 jel.20191450 Source: Week II - lecture - large slides

  • The missing counterfactual and convex weights
  • Selecting predictors and weights
  • Why fit can help and when it misleads
  • Context, data and feasibility
  • Placebos, inference and robustness
  • How the surveyed extensions change the estimator
  • Distinct inferential reference distributions

Synthetic control is the core method behind the lecture’s Russia case. Understanding the missing counterfactual, weight constraints and diagnostic limits comes before interpreting a post-treatment gap.

A synthetic control estimates what would have happened to one treated aggregate unit after an intervention by constructing a comparison from untreated units. Its central idea is that a weighted combination can resemble the treated unit more closely than any single comparison unit. That matters when interventions are rare and the available sample contains only a few regions, countries, or other large units. Many standard comparative designs are most informative with many units; a single-unit time series can be sensitive to other shocks; and informal comparative case studies do not formalize how comparison units were chosen. The synthetic-control design makes that choice explicit and lets readers inspect the fit and the units contributing to it (§§1–2, PDF pp. 1–3) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 1–3.

The missing counterfactual and convex weights

Let unit \(1\) be treated after period \(T_0\), with \(J\) untreated donor units. Write \(Y^N_{1t}\) and \(Y^I_{1t}\) for the treated unit’s untreated and treated potential outcomes. After treatment, the observed outcome is \(Y_{1t}=Y^I_{1t}\), so the effect is

\[\tau_{1t}=Y^I_{1t}-Y^N_{1t},\qquad t>T_0.\]

The treated outcome is observed, but the untreated counterfactual is not. Synthetic control estimates it as

\[\widehat Y^N_{1t}=\sum_{j=2}^{J+1}w_jY_{jt},\qquad \widehat\tau_{1t}=Y_{1t}-\widehat Y^N_{1t}.\]

The effect can vary over post-treatment time; the estimator does not impose a constant effect. With \(w_j\geq0\) and \(\sum_{j=2}^{J+1}w_j=1\), the synthetic outcome is a convex weighted average of donor outcomes. Thus the estimate avoids extrapolation beyond the donor outcomes’ support. Relaxing these restrictions can allow extrapolation; regression weights may sum to one while still being negative or larger than one. The paper illustrates this distinction with West Germany’s regression weights, including four negative weights (eqs. (1)–(6), PDF pp. 4–5; §4 and Table 3, PDF pp. 15–16) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 4–5 Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 15–16.

Selecting predictors and weights

Weights are selected using pre-intervention predictors. Let \(X_1\) collect the treated unit’s predictor values and \(X_0\) the corresponding donor values. For a chosen diagonal predictor-weight matrix \(V=\operatorname{diag}(v_1,\ldots,v_k)\) with nonnegative entries \(v_h\geq0\), canonical synthetic control solves

\[W(V)\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{W\geq0,\;\mathbf1^\top W=1}(X_1-X_0W)^\top V(X_1-X_0W).\]

The article writes the equivalent weighted norm objective in equation (7). The nonnegative entries of \(V\) determine how heavily each predictor mismatch counts; conditional on \(V\), the problem is convex constrained quadratic optimization. Negative diagonal entries would no longer define a nonnegative squared-distance objective. One simple choice scales predictors by inverse variance. Another chooses V to minimize pre-treatment outcome prediction error. The two-stage version of Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller (2015) divides pre-treatment time into training and validation windows: compute weights from training predictors, score their validation-period outcome mean squared prediction error (MSPE), select V, then refit using the final pre-treatment predictor window. This only helps when a choice of V produces both useful pre-treatment outcome prediction and acceptable predictor balance. Cross-validation solutions need not be unique, and fit to a selected period is not proof that the post-treatment relationship remains valid (eqs. (7)–(9), PDF pp. 6–7) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 6–7.

The German reunification example makes these mechanics concrete. West Germany is compared with a donor pool of 16 OECD countries. A simple donor average fails to reproduce West Germany’s pre-1990 GDP trajectory; the synthetic control tracks it closely (Figure 1, PDF p. 8). Its listed weights are Austria 0.42, Japan 0.16, Netherlands 0.09, Switzerland 0.11, and United States 0.22; all other listed donor weights are zero (Table 2, PDF p. 9). Selected covariate means are also close: for example, GDP per capita is 15,808.9 for West Germany and 15,802.2 for its synthetic comparison (Table 1, same page). This is an example, not a guarantee that a convex combination exists or that a close fit implies an unbiased counterfactual.

Why fit can help and when it misleads

The factor-model argument explains why fit is diagnostic. For untreated outcomes the article uses

\[Y^N_{jt}=\delta_t+\theta_t Z_j+\lambda_t\mu_j+\varepsilon_{jt},\]

where \(\delta_t\) is a common time component, \(Z_j\) observed predictors, \(\mu_j\) unobserved factor loadings, \(\theta_t\) and \(\lambda_t\) time-varying coefficients, and \(\varepsilon_{jt}\) mean-zero unit-specific transitory shocks (eq. (10), PDF pp. 10–11). Difference-in-differences is a special restriction with time-invariant \(\lambda_t\) ; fixing the latent-factor coefficient removes that source of differential trends, while observed predictor effects must still be matched or controlled for in a parallel-trends interpretation. The unrestricted model need not satisfy parallel trends.

If a synthetic comparison exactly matches observed predictors and pre-treatment outcomes, it matches \(Z_1\) , while the extended pre-treatment outcome trajectory can provide evidence about the unobserved \(\mu_1\) . The cited bias-bound result depends on assumptions including this match and a linear factor structure; the bound worsens with transitory-shock scale and the number of latent factors and improves with more pre-treatment periods. A large donor pool can make it easier to overfit a short pre-period, creating a close observed fit even when latent loadings differ. Consequently, more pre-periods do not rescue a materially poor fit, and increasing the donor pool can raise overfitting risk. The factor model is a working approximation; under nonlinear outcome processes, even close linear interpolation may have substantial bias. A poor convex-hull fit is a reason to reject the conventional estimator, not to hide mismatch behind extrapolating regression weights (§3.3, PDF pp. 10–11; §5, PDF pp. 18–21) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 10–11 Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 18–21.

Predictor choice is part of the design. Pre-treatment outcomes matter because they can proxy for latent factors and allow checking trajectory fit. Other predictors matter too: omitting relevant observed predictors effectively leaves them among the unobserved components. A holdout pre-period can assess whether the chosen predictors predict outcomes beyond the period used to construct the weights. Post-treatment outcomes must not drive design choices if the researcher wants a clean safeguard against specification searches; the pre-treatment design and weights can be set before post-treatment outcomes are observed (§3.4, PDF pp. 11–12; §4, PDF pp. 16–17) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 11–12 Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 16–17.

Synthetic controls are often sparse because the solution projects the treated predictor vector onto the donor convex hull. When that vector is outside the hull and donor points are in general position, the solution is unique and uses at most \(k\) positive weights for \(k\) predictors. If it lies inside the hull, solutions may be non-unique; sparse solutions with at most \(k+1\) positive weights exist. Sparsity is useful for interpretation and contextual scrutiny, not by itself a bias cure. With multiple treated units, non-uniqueness and distant contributing donors can become practical problems. Abadie and L’Hour add a penalty for pairwise predictor distances of contributing donors; as its tuning parameter grows, the estimator approaches one-to-one matching, while smaller values emphasize aggregate fit. Their extension yields a unique sparse solution under stated geometric conditions (§4 and Figure 2, PDF pp. 17–18; §8, eqs. (13)–(14), PDF pp. 26–27) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 17–18 Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 26–27.

Context, data and feasibility

The design also needs contextual plausibility. Donors should not receive the treatment or be affected by it; units with large idiosyncratic shocks may be unsuitable; and there must be enough unaffected donors to form a comparison. Anticipation can bias estimates, so the intervention may need to be backdated to before responses begin. Spillovers violate no-interference assumptions: excluding exposed donors can reduce contamination but may worsen fit. The direction of contamination may sometimes be reasoned through from transparent weights. In the German example, if donor countries’ GDP were themselves negatively affected by reunification, the estimated negative effect for West Germany would be attenuated (§5, PDF pp. 19–22) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 19–22.

Feasibility depends on whether the treated unit lies near the donors’ convex hull in substantively important predictors and outcomes. If only trends can be matched but levels cannot, demeaned or differenced outcomes, or a constant-shift variant, may help in suitable settings; such transformations can also increase noise and need not be valid when levels affect growth or when the underlying process is nonlinear. A researcher should not use conventional synthetic control when no credible donor combination approximates the treated unit. The paper further requires aggregate outcomes and predictors for treated and donor units, adequate pre-treatment history, and enough post-treatment observations to capture relevant effects. Longer pre-periods improve information but risk structural breaks; weighting more recent pre-period measures may help address instability. Highly volatile outcomes, small effects, and short or delayed post-period effects limit detectability; filtering may reduce common or unit-specific noise, though it changes the target and requires justification (§§5–6, PDF pp. 19–23) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 19–23.

Placebos, inference and robustness

Inference in the canonical approach is often permutation-based: reassign treatment to each donor, reconstruct its synthetic control, and compare its placebo effect with the treated effect. One statistic is the ratio of post-period to pre-period root mean squared prediction error (RMSPE):

\[R_j(t_1,t_2)=\left[\frac{1}{t_2-t_1+1}\sum_{t=t_1}^{t_2}(Y_{jt}-\widehat Y^N_{jt})^2\right]^{1/2},\qquad r_j=\frac{R_j(T_0+1,T)}{R_j(1,T_0)}.\]

Large pre-treatment placebo errors make those placebos weak comparisons; one can report the distribution of ratios or gaps and, with transparent rules, exclude placebos whose pre-fit is substantially worse. One-sided statistics can focus power on a specified direction. This procedure does not automatically approximate a sampling distribution or turn observational treatment assignment into random assignment. Its interpretation depends on a defensible assignment benchmark; placebo rankings are a way to contextualize evidence, not a universal causal p-value. Other proposals include generalized permutation tests and confidence sets, end-of-sample instability tests, residual permutation under exchangeability conditions, bias-corrected synthetic control, and predictive intervals (§3.5, PDF pp. 12–15; §8 “Inference,” PDF pp. 29–32) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 12–15 Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 29–32.

Diagnostics should include backdating/in-time placebos, donor-placebo comparisons, leave-one-out donor checks, and sensitivity to predictors and donor-pool definitions. In the reunification illustration, a ten-year backdating exercise finds close fit before the true intervention and a gap emerging near it (Figure 3, PDF p. 24); removing contributing donors leaves a negative estimate around the baseline (Figure 4, PDF p. 26). Those are design-specific checks rather than proof that every application is robust. Relevant extensions surveyed include multiple treated units, donor matching penalties, time weights, matrix completion/low-rank factor methods for missing outcomes, synthetic difference-in-differences, and alternative inferential procedures (§7, PDF pp. 23–25; §8, PDF pp. 25–33) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 23–25 Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 25–33.

The source's permutation ranking can be written

\[p=\frac{1}{J+1}\sum_{j=1}^{J+1}\mathbf1\{r_j\geq r_1\}.\]

Including the treated unit gives a minimum attainable rank fraction of \(1/(J+1)\), so a small donor pool limits resolution. This fraction is called a permutation p-value under the stated assignment benchmark; it does not manufacture randomized assignment or a repeated-sampling model. The researcher must state the reference distribution and any exclusions of badly fitted placebo units. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 13–14

How the surveyed extensions change the estimator

The extensions are contextual reading: each relaxes or augments a particular design feature; the article does not claim every extension is interchangeable. With \(I\) treated units and donors \(j=I+1,\ldots,I+J\), the Abadie–L’Hour objective for treated unit \(i\) is

\[\min_{W_i\geq0,\;\mathbf1^\top W_i=1}\left\{\left\|X_i-\sum_jw_{ij}X_j\right\|^2+\lambda\sum_jw_{ij}\|X_i-X_j\|^2\right\},\quad\lambda>0.\]

The first term rewards a good aggregate predictor match; the second penalizes giving weight to individually distant donors even if their differences cancel in the aggregate. The treatment estimate remains \(\widehat\tau_{it}=Y_{it}-\sum_jw_{ij}Y_{jt}\); a simple average across treated units estimates their average effect. The penalty does not add post-treatment outcomes to the weight-fitting stage. These are equations (13)–(14), with sums written over the donor set. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 27

A regression bias adjustment estimates an untreated prediction function \(\widehat\mu_{0t}(X)\) using donors, then subtracts the weighted predicted discrepancy:

\[\widehat\tau_{it}=\left(Y_{it}-\sum_jw_{ij}Y_{jt}\right)-\sum_jw_{ij}\left[\widehat\mu_{0t}(X_i)-\widehat\mu_{0t}(X_j)\right].\]

Equivalently, compare treated and weighted donor residuals after removing their predicted outcomes. This can address imperfect balance but adds dependence on the prediction model; estimated pre-period bias can instead support a constant-shift adjustment only if its stability is credible. Equations (15)–(16) are not an automatic guarantee that poor overlap is harmless. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 29

The regression extension writes \(\widehat Y^N_{1t}=\widehat\alpha+\sum_{j=2}^{J+1}\widehat w_jY_{jt}\). Its weights may be negative and need not sum to one. An elastic-net fit minimizes pre-period squared residuals plus

\[\lambda_1\left[\frac{1-\lambda_2}{2}\sum_jw_j^2+\lambda_2\sum_j|w_j|\right],\quad\lambda_1\geq0,\quad0\leq\lambda_2\leq1.\]

The squared-weight part shrinks dispersed large coefficients; the absolute-weight part can set coefficients to zero. Cross-validation chooses regularization. Such a model trades convex-interpolation transparency for flexibility and possible extrapolation; unpenalized regression is the zero-penalty limit, not proof of credible identification. Equations (17)–(18) state this version. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 29–30

Matrix methods view untreated outcomes as a matrix with common latent structure. A low-rank approximation estimates a small number of common patterns, denoises observed entries and imputes treated post-period entries; variants first denoise donors and then fit ridge weights. Some methods add covariates or fixed effects. Synthetic difference-in-differences adds weights over pre-period times as well as donor units. These methods still require their own stability/identification and inference assumptions; sharing a predictive target does not make those assumptions identical. The final discussion leaves large open questions about small-sample inference, model sensitivity, multiple interventions and prospective experimental design. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 30–35

Figure 1: the left panel compares West Germany with the simple OECD donor mean; the right uses the fitted synthetic comparison. The vertical line is reunification in 1990. Good pre-fit makes the comparison interpretable but does not independently establish no spillovers or stable latent relations. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 8

Tables 1–2 preserve predictor balance, the five positive weights and the eleven zero-weight donors. Weights sum to one at the displayed precision; a weight is a statistical contribution, not evidence that the donor was unaffected. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 9

Figure 2 projects the treated predictor vector onto the donors’ convex hull. Only the red donor vertices contribute in this illustration; geometric proximity must be paired with substantive comparability. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 17

Figure 3 pretends reunification happened in 1980. The large divergence emerges around the actual intervention, which is supportive in-time evidence, rather than a proof that any other event has been excluded. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 24

Figure 4 removes positively weighted donors one at a time. The family of resulting paths displays this application’s sensitivity; robust pre-fit and sign do not remove all identification assumptions. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 26

Distinct inferential reference distributions

The article’s surveyed alternatives differ from simply moving the treatment label across donor units. An end-of-sample instability test compares estimates over the post-treatment window with estimates computed over same-length consecutive pre-treatment windows. Its repeated-sampling justification uses stationary data and a large pre-period \(T_0\); merely labelling an early date a placebo does not supply that justification. Generalized donor-permutation tests can instead generate confidence sets by test inversion: collect effect values whose null hypotheses are not rejected. Physical PDF pp. 31

A time-residual permutation approach writes untreated outcomes as \(Y^N_{1t}=P^N_t+u_t\), with mean-zero stationary, weakly dependent errors. Under a candidate post-treatment effect sequence \(a_t\), subtract \(a_t\) from observed treated outcomes to construct null-adjusted outcomes. The article first explains unrestricted permutation under an i.i.d. simplification; valid inference requires estimated residuals to be exchangeable under the null. Stationarity and weak dependence alone do not imply arbitrary exchangeability. This proposal fits constrained weights under the null using all periods, including the adjusted post-period, unlike canonical pre-only weight construction. It is a distinct null-testing procedure, not permission to fit canonical weights to untreated-looking post outcomes chosen after seeing results. The source also distinguishes a regression orthogonality restriction from the linear factor model; an unbiased factor-model synthetic control need not automatically satisfy that restriction. Physical PDF pp. 31–32

Another surveyed procedure forms bias-corrected mean post-treatment effects with confidence intervals centred on \(K\)-fold cross-fitted estimates, using large pre- and post-periods and an asymptotically pivotal statistic. Cross-fitting constructs fits with held-out portions to reduce dependence between fitting and evaluation; it does not erase the underlying time-series requirements. In contrast, predictive intervals account both for uncertainty in estimated predictor parameters and irreducible uncertainty in the untreated outcome’s disturbance \(u_t\). An interval for an average effect, a confidence set obtained by inverting a particular test, and a predictive interval for a particular missing untreated outcome have different targets and cannot be read interchangeably. This is the supplied article’s bounded survey, not a full proof or implementation of each cited external paper. Physical PDF pp. 32
sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
O010-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: For a hypothetical canonical synthetic control, two donors have one pre-treatment predictor 2 and 6; the treated predictor is 3. Solve the nonnegative sum-one weights that exactly match it. Donor post-outcomes are 10 and 14; observed treated outcome is 11. Compute the synthetic untreated outcome and actual-minus-counterfactual gap. If the treated predictor instead lay below 2, could a convex fit match it exactly? Explain potential outcomes, \(W(V)\) and nonnegative diagonal \(V\), pre-only training/validation/refit, the factor-model fit argument and its restrictions, sparse/nonunique geometry, and the contextual feasibility/anticipation/spillover/stability checks needed before interpreting the gap causally. Contrast unrestricted regression weights and explain why excellent fit alone is insufficient.

Complete solution and essential rubric: \(w_1=(6-3)/(6-2)=0.750000\) and \(w_2=1-w_1=0.250000\); both are nonnegative and sum to one. The untreated prediction is \(0.750000(10)+0.250000(14)=11.000000\) and estimated gap is \(11-11.000000=0.000000\). The observed treated potential outcome is available after intervention; its untreated potential outcome is missing. A target below the donor minimum cannot be exactly matched by a convex combination; negative/excess weights or an intercept can extrapolate but change the estimator. Canonical weights minimize \((X_1-X_0W)^\top V(X_1-X_0W)\) subject to nonnegative sum-one weights; nonnegative diagonal \(V\) weights predictor mismatches as squared distances. Use pre-period data to fit/design; pre training/validation can choose \(V\) then refit, without tuning to post gaps. The linear factor model separates common time effects, observed predictors, latent loadings/time-varying coefficients and transitory shocks. Matching predictors/pre outcomes can approximate latent loadings under the stated linear/stability/noise assumptions; more latent factors/noise and short prehistories can undermine it, and a huge donor pool can overfit. DID is a restricted time-invariant latent-coefficient case with relevant observed effects matched/controlled. Outside-hull/general-position projections can be unique with at most \(k\) positive weights; inside-hull solutions may be nonunique, with a sparse solution using at most \(k+1\). Neither sparsity nor fit proves identification. Donors must be untreated/uncontaminated and substantively comparable, with no anticipation or justified backdating, adequate history, stable post relation and credible overlap. Excluding spillover donors can impair fit; for negative donor spillovers the estimated negative treated effect can be attenuated. Long histories risk breaks, volatility reduces precision, demeaning requires a credible level shift, and nonlinear processes can defeat linear interpolation. The reported gap remains conditional on those checks, not a randomized comparison or universal SCM advantage. Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks

Required components: potential_outcomes_convex_weights_and_gap, pre_only_design_factor_fit_and_geometry, donor_context_feasibility_and_stability. Each full prompt/key below elicits every component; all are necessary for a pass on every permitted pair. Accept algebraically equivalent expressions and clearly defined opposite cash-flow signs with correct interpretation. A pass requires all requested outputs/reasons, correct units/assumptions and no critical conceptual error. Partial means a missing component or an unresolved isolated arithmetic slip with an otherwise valid method; independent correction is required for a pass. Fail means a critical mechanism/condition is wrong. Unscorable means a response or its help/exposure conditions cannot be established. Unknown help conditions are never independent evidence.

Critical errors: Negative weights called convex; post outcomes tune canonical design; perfect fit called proof of causal identification; contaminated donors ignored.

sections.html:
Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Synthetic control: design, fit and inference; fingerprint f68abe39a544b3e0073189cf0d3543276edd30d9d1b78718c7ff6a94a34dee87. Heading depth and required relative figure-path relocation alone are adapted.

Synthetic control: design, fit and inference

Source: Abadie 2021 jel.20191450 Source: Week II - lecture - large slides

  • The missing counterfactual and convex weights
  • Selecting predictors and weights
  • Why fit can help and when it misleads
  • Context, data and feasibility
  • Placebos, inference and robustness
  • How the surveyed extensions change the estimator
  • Distinct inferential reference distributions

Synthetic control is the core method behind the lecture’s Russia case. Understanding the missing counterfactual, weight constraints and diagnostic limits comes before interpreting a post-treatment gap.

A synthetic control estimates what would have happened to one treated aggregate unit after an intervention by constructing a comparison from untreated units. Its central idea is that a weighted combination can resemble the treated unit more closely than any single comparison unit. That matters when interventions are rare and the available sample contains only a few regions, countries, or other large units. Many standard comparative designs are most informative with many units; a single-unit time series can be sensitive to other shocks; and informal comparative case studies do not formalize how comparison units were chosen. The synthetic-control design makes that choice explicit and lets readers inspect the fit and the units contributing to it (§§1–2, PDF pp. 1–3) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 1–3.

The missing counterfactual and convex weights

Let unit \(1\) be treated after period \(T_0\), with \(J\) untreated donor units. Write \(Y^N_{1t}\) and \(Y^I_{1t}\) for the treated unit’s untreated and treated potential outcomes. After treatment, the observed outcome is \(Y_{1t}=Y^I_{1t}\), so the effect is

\[\tau_{1t}=Y^I_{1t}-Y^N_{1t},\qquad t>T_0.\]

The treated outcome is observed, but the untreated counterfactual is not. Synthetic control estimates it as

\[\widehat Y^N_{1t}=\sum_{j=2}^{J+1}w_jY_{jt},\qquad \widehat\tau_{1t}=Y_{1t}-\widehat Y^N_{1t}.\]

The effect can vary over post-treatment time; the estimator does not impose a constant effect. With \(w_j\geq0\) and \(\sum_{j=2}^{J+1}w_j=1\), the synthetic outcome is a convex weighted average of donor outcomes. Thus the estimate avoids extrapolation beyond the donor outcomes’ support. Relaxing these restrictions can allow extrapolation; regression weights may sum to one while still being negative or larger than one. The paper illustrates this distinction with West Germany’s regression weights, including four negative weights (eqs. (1)–(6), PDF pp. 4–5; §4 and Table 3, PDF pp. 15–16) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 4–5 Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 15–16.

Selecting predictors and weights

Weights are selected using pre-intervention predictors. Let \(X_1\) collect the treated unit’s predictor values and \(X_0\) the corresponding donor values. For a chosen diagonal predictor-weight matrix \(V=\operatorname{diag}(v_1,\ldots,v_k)\) with nonnegative entries \(v_h\geq0\), canonical synthetic control solves

\[W(V)\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{W\geq0,\;\mathbf1^\top W=1}(X_1-X_0W)^\top V(X_1-X_0W).\]

The article writes the equivalent weighted norm objective in equation (7). The nonnegative entries of \(V\) determine how heavily each predictor mismatch counts; conditional on \(V\), the problem is convex constrained quadratic optimization. Negative diagonal entries would no longer define a nonnegative squared-distance objective. One simple choice scales predictors by inverse variance. Another chooses V to minimize pre-treatment outcome prediction error. The two-stage version of Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller (2015) divides pre-treatment time into training and validation windows: compute weights from training predictors, score their validation-period outcome mean squared prediction error (MSPE), select V, then refit using the final pre-treatment predictor window. This only helps when a choice of V produces both useful pre-treatment outcome prediction and acceptable predictor balance. Cross-validation solutions need not be unique, and fit to a selected period is not proof that the post-treatment relationship remains valid (eqs. (7)–(9), PDF pp. 6–7) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 6–7.

The German reunification example makes these mechanics concrete. West Germany is compared with a donor pool of 16 OECD countries. A simple donor average fails to reproduce West Germany’s pre-1990 GDP trajectory; the synthetic control tracks it closely (Figure 1, PDF p. 8). Its listed weights are Austria 0.42, Japan 0.16, Netherlands 0.09, Switzerland 0.11, and United States 0.22; all other listed donor weights are zero (Table 2, PDF p. 9). Selected covariate means are also close: for example, GDP per capita is 15,808.9 for West Germany and 15,802.2 for its synthetic comparison (Table 1, same page). This is an example, not a guarantee that a convex combination exists or that a close fit implies an unbiased counterfactual.

Why fit can help and when it misleads

The factor-model argument explains why fit is diagnostic. For untreated outcomes the article uses

\[Y^N_{jt}=\delta_t+\theta_t Z_j+\lambda_t\mu_j+\varepsilon_{jt},\]

where \(\delta_t\) is a common time component, \(Z_j\) observed predictors, \(\mu_j\) unobserved factor loadings, \(\theta_t\) and \(\lambda_t\) time-varying coefficients, and \(\varepsilon_{jt}\) mean-zero unit-specific transitory shocks (eq. (10), PDF pp. 10–11). Difference-in-differences is a special restriction with time-invariant \(\lambda_t\) ; fixing the latent-factor coefficient removes that source of differential trends, while observed predictor effects must still be matched or controlled for in a parallel-trends interpretation. The unrestricted model need not satisfy parallel trends.

If a synthetic comparison exactly matches observed predictors and pre-treatment outcomes, it matches \(Z_1\) , while the extended pre-treatment outcome trajectory can provide evidence about the unobserved \(\mu_1\) . The cited bias-bound result depends on assumptions including this match and a linear factor structure; the bound worsens with transitory-shock scale and the number of latent factors and improves with more pre-treatment periods. A large donor pool can make it easier to overfit a short pre-period, creating a close observed fit even when latent loadings differ. Consequently, more pre-periods do not rescue a materially poor fit, and increasing the donor pool can raise overfitting risk. The factor model is a working approximation; under nonlinear outcome processes, even close linear interpolation may have substantial bias. A poor convex-hull fit is a reason to reject the conventional estimator, not to hide mismatch behind extrapolating regression weights (§3.3, PDF pp. 10–11; §5, PDF pp. 18–21) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 10–11 Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 18–21.

Predictor choice is part of the design. Pre-treatment outcomes matter because they can proxy for latent factors and allow checking trajectory fit. Other predictors matter too: omitting relevant observed predictors effectively leaves them among the unobserved components. A holdout pre-period can assess whether the chosen predictors predict outcomes beyond the period used to construct the weights. Post-treatment outcomes must not drive design choices if the researcher wants a clean safeguard against specification searches; the pre-treatment design and weights can be set before post-treatment outcomes are observed (§3.4, PDF pp. 11–12; §4, PDF pp. 16–17) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 11–12 Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 16–17.

Synthetic controls are often sparse because the solution projects the treated predictor vector onto the donor convex hull. When that vector is outside the hull and donor points are in general position, the solution is unique and uses at most \(k\) positive weights for \(k\) predictors. If it lies inside the hull, solutions may be non-unique; sparse solutions with at most \(k+1\) positive weights exist. Sparsity is useful for interpretation and contextual scrutiny, not by itself a bias cure. With multiple treated units, non-uniqueness and distant contributing donors can become practical problems. Abadie and L’Hour add a penalty for pairwise predictor distances of contributing donors; as its tuning parameter grows, the estimator approaches one-to-one matching, while smaller values emphasize aggregate fit. Their extension yields a unique sparse solution under stated geometric conditions (§4 and Figure 2, PDF pp. 17–18; §8, eqs. (13)–(14), PDF pp. 26–27) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 17–18 Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 26–27.

Context, data and feasibility

The design also needs contextual plausibility. Donors should not receive the treatment or be affected by it; units with large idiosyncratic shocks may be unsuitable; and there must be enough unaffected donors to form a comparison. Anticipation can bias estimates, so the intervention may need to be backdated to before responses begin. Spillovers violate no-interference assumptions: excluding exposed donors can reduce contamination but may worsen fit. The direction of contamination may sometimes be reasoned through from transparent weights. In the German example, if donor countries’ GDP were themselves negatively affected by reunification, the estimated negative effect for West Germany would be attenuated (§5, PDF pp. 19–22) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 19–22.

Feasibility depends on whether the treated unit lies near the donors’ convex hull in substantively important predictors and outcomes. If only trends can be matched but levels cannot, demeaned or differenced outcomes, or a constant-shift variant, may help in suitable settings; such transformations can also increase noise and need not be valid when levels affect growth or when the underlying process is nonlinear. A researcher should not use conventional synthetic control when no credible donor combination approximates the treated unit. The paper further requires aggregate outcomes and predictors for treated and donor units, adequate pre-treatment history, and enough post-treatment observations to capture relevant effects. Longer pre-periods improve information but risk structural breaks; weighting more recent pre-period measures may help address instability. Highly volatile outcomes, small effects, and short or delayed post-period effects limit detectability; filtering may reduce common or unit-specific noise, though it changes the target and requires justification (§§5–6, PDF pp. 19–23) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 19–23.

Placebos, inference and robustness

Inference in the canonical approach is often permutation-based: reassign treatment to each donor, reconstruct its synthetic control, and compare its placebo effect with the treated effect. One statistic is the ratio of post-period to pre-period root mean squared prediction error (RMSPE):

\[R_j(t_1,t_2)=\left[\frac{1}{t_2-t_1+1}\sum_{t=t_1}^{t_2}(Y_{jt}-\widehat Y^N_{jt})^2\right]^{1/2},\qquad r_j=\frac{R_j(T_0+1,T)}{R_j(1,T_0)}.\]

Large pre-treatment placebo errors make those placebos weak comparisons; one can report the distribution of ratios or gaps and, with transparent rules, exclude placebos whose pre-fit is substantially worse. One-sided statistics can focus power on a specified direction. This procedure does not automatically approximate a sampling distribution or turn observational treatment assignment into random assignment. Its interpretation depends on a defensible assignment benchmark; placebo rankings are a way to contextualize evidence, not a universal causal p-value. Other proposals include generalized permutation tests and confidence sets, end-of-sample instability tests, residual permutation under exchangeability conditions, bias-corrected synthetic control, and predictive intervals (§3.5, PDF pp. 12–15; §8 “Inference,” PDF pp. 29–32) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 12–15 Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 29–32.

Diagnostics should include backdating/in-time placebos, donor-placebo comparisons, leave-one-out donor checks, and sensitivity to predictors and donor-pool definitions. In the reunification illustration, a ten-year backdating exercise finds close fit before the true intervention and a gap emerging near it (Figure 3, PDF p. 24); removing contributing donors leaves a negative estimate around the baseline (Figure 4, PDF p. 26). Those are design-specific checks rather than proof that every application is robust. Relevant extensions surveyed include multiple treated units, donor matching penalties, time weights, matrix completion/low-rank factor methods for missing outcomes, synthetic difference-in-differences, and alternative inferential procedures (§7, PDF pp. 23–25; §8, PDF pp. 25–33) Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 23–25 Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 25–33.

The source's permutation ranking can be written

\[p=\frac{1}{J+1}\sum_{j=1}^{J+1}\mathbf1\{r_j\geq r_1\}.\]

Including the treated unit gives a minimum attainable rank fraction of \(1/(J+1)\), so a small donor pool limits resolution. This fraction is called a permutation p-value under the stated assignment benchmark; it does not manufacture randomized assignment or a repeated-sampling model. The researcher must state the reference distribution and any exclusions of badly fitted placebo units. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 13–14

How the surveyed extensions change the estimator

The extensions are contextual reading: each relaxes or augments a particular design feature; the article does not claim every extension is interchangeable. With \(I\) treated units and donors \(j=I+1,\ldots,I+J\), the Abadie–L’Hour objective for treated unit \(i\) is

\[\min_{W_i\geq0,\;\mathbf1^\top W_i=1}\left\{\left\|X_i-\sum_jw_{ij}X_j\right\|^2+\lambda\sum_jw_{ij}\|X_i-X_j\|^2\right\},\quad\lambda>0.\]

The first term rewards a good aggregate predictor match; the second penalizes giving weight to individually distant donors even if their differences cancel in the aggregate. The treatment estimate remains \(\widehat\tau_{it}=Y_{it}-\sum_jw_{ij}Y_{jt}\); a simple average across treated units estimates their average effect. The penalty does not add post-treatment outcomes to the weight-fitting stage. These are equations (13)–(14), with sums written over the donor set. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 27

A regression bias adjustment estimates an untreated prediction function \(\widehat\mu_{0t}(X)\) using donors, then subtracts the weighted predicted discrepancy:

\[\widehat\tau_{it}=\left(Y_{it}-\sum_jw_{ij}Y_{jt}\right)-\sum_jw_{ij}\left[\widehat\mu_{0t}(X_i)-\widehat\mu_{0t}(X_j)\right].\]

Equivalently, compare treated and weighted donor residuals after removing their predicted outcomes. This can address imperfect balance but adds dependence on the prediction model; estimated pre-period bias can instead support a constant-shift adjustment only if its stability is credible. Equations (15)–(16) are not an automatic guarantee that poor overlap is harmless. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 29

The regression extension writes \(\widehat Y^N_{1t}=\widehat\alpha+\sum_{j=2}^{J+1}\widehat w_jY_{jt}\). Its weights may be negative and need not sum to one. An elastic-net fit minimizes pre-period squared residuals plus

\[\lambda_1\left[\frac{1-\lambda_2}{2}\sum_jw_j^2+\lambda_2\sum_j|w_j|\right],\quad\lambda_1\geq0,\quad0\leq\lambda_2\leq1.\]

The squared-weight part shrinks dispersed large coefficients; the absolute-weight part can set coefficients to zero. Cross-validation chooses regularization. Such a model trades convex-interpolation transparency for flexibility and possible extrapolation; unpenalized regression is the zero-penalty limit, not proof of credible identification. Equations (17)–(18) state this version. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 29–30

Matrix methods view untreated outcomes as a matrix with common latent structure. A low-rank approximation estimates a small number of common patterns, denoises observed entries and imputes treated post-period entries; variants first denoise donors and then fit ridge weights. Some methods add covariates or fixed effects. Synthetic difference-in-differences adds weights over pre-period times as well as donor units. These methods still require their own stability/identification and inference assumptions; sharing a predictive target does not make those assumptions identical. The final discussion leaves large open questions about small-sample inference, model sensitivity, multiple interventions and prospective experimental design. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 30–35

Figure 1: the left panel compares West Germany with the simple OECD donor mean; the right uses the fitted synthetic comparison. The vertical line is reunification in 1990. Good pre-fit makes the comparison interpretable but does not independently establish no spillovers or stable latent relations. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 8

Tables 1–2 preserve predictor balance, the five positive weights and the eleven zero-weight donors. Weights sum to one at the displayed precision; a weight is a statistical contribution, not evidence that the donor was unaffected. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 9

Figure 2 projects the treated predictor vector onto the donors’ convex hull. Only the red donor vertices contribute in this illustration; geometric proximity must be paired with substantive comparability. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 17

Figure 3 pretends reunification happened in 1980. The large divergence emerges around the actual intervention, which is supportive in-time evidence, rather than a proof that any other event has been excluded. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 24

Figure 4 removes positively weighted donors one at a time. The family of resulting paths displays this application’s sensitivity; robust pre-fit and sign do not remove all identification assumptions. Abadie (2021), physical PDF pp. 26

Distinct inferential reference distributions

The article’s surveyed alternatives differ from simply moving the treatment label across donor units. An end-of-sample instability test compares estimates over the post-treatment window with estimates computed over same-length consecutive pre-treatment windows. Its repeated-sampling justification uses stationary data and a large pre-period \(T_0\); merely labelling an early date a placebo does not supply that justification. Generalized donor-permutation tests can instead generate confidence sets by test inversion: collect effect values whose null hypotheses are not rejected. Physical PDF pp. 31

A time-residual permutation approach writes untreated outcomes as \(Y^N_{1t}=P^N_t+u_t\), with mean-zero stationary, weakly dependent errors. Under a candidate post-treatment effect sequence \(a_t\), subtract \(a_t\) from observed treated outcomes to construct null-adjusted outcomes. The article first explains unrestricted permutation under an i.i.d. simplification; valid inference requires estimated residuals to be exchangeable under the null. Stationarity and weak dependence alone do not imply arbitrary exchangeability. This proposal fits constrained weights under the null using all periods, including the adjusted post-period, unlike canonical pre-only weight construction. It is a distinct null-testing procedure, not permission to fit canonical weights to untreated-looking post outcomes chosen after seeing results. The source also distinguishes a regression orthogonality restriction from the linear factor model; an unbiased factor-model synthetic control need not automatically satisfy that restriction. Physical PDF pp. 31–32

Another surveyed procedure forms bias-corrected mean post-treatment effects with confidence intervals centred on \(K\)-fold cross-fitted estimates, using large pre- and post-periods and an asymptotically pivotal statistic. Cross-fitting constructs fits with held-out portions to reduce dependence between fitting and evaluation; it does not erase the underlying time-series requirements. In contrast, predictive intervals account both for uncertainty in estimated predictor parameters and irreducible uncertainty in the untreated outcome’s disturbance \(u_t\). An interval for an average effect, a confidence set obtained by inverting a particular test, and a predictive interval for a particular missing untreated outcome have different targets and cannot be read interchangeably. This is the supplied article’s bounded survey, not a full proof or implementation of each cited external paper. Physical PDF pp. 32

sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Russia without the Revolution: predictive counterfactuals; fingerprint fdca1e98732bf62614e87748ccaae494b4e87b9e06154c38b9eac5e257e63f40. Heading depth and required relative figure-path relocation alone are adapted.

Russia without the Revolution: predictive counterfactuals

Source: How Russia might have evolved without the revolution annaeconstat2009.144.0075 Source: Week II - lecture - large slides

  • Historical setting and policy sequence
  • Data and the prediction target
  • Competing estimators and regularization
  • Main scenarios and donor weights
  • War, population and comparability
  • Diagnostics and forecast uncertainty
  • Why close fit can forecast badly
  • Structural simulations and the stability assumption
  • Logs, levels, growth and welfare limits

This case applies synthetic-control reasoning; the design and inference foundations are explained in Synthetic control: design, fit and inference.

Korolev asks how Russia’s GDP per capita might have evolved without the 1917 Revolution. This is a predictive exercise: estimate pre-1917 relationships between Russia and other countries, then extend those relationships after 1917. It does not determine whether the Revolution could have been avoided, and it cannot isolate the Revolution from the Civil War, World War I, country-specific shocks, or Soviet policies (abstract and §§1, 4.4–5, printed pp. 75–76, 99–103; physical PDF pp. 2–3, 26–30) Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 2.

Historical setting and policy sequence

Korolev describes late-imperial Russia as predominantly agrarian and poorer than most European countries, with an expanding industrial and rail sector. His cited 1913 estimates put roughly three-quarters of workers in agriculture and more than half of GDP there. It was largely a market economy with a substantial state role. The 1905 Revolution prompted constitutional changes without ending the monarchy; Stolypin’s agrarian reforms began in 1906, and World War I interrupted the reform path. The paper distinguishes the February–March and October–November 1917 changes while acknowledging alternative historical periodizations. Physical PDF pp. 4

Civil War dating is not uniform in the cited histories. The Bolsheviks’ War Communism from 1918 involved nationalization, rationing, compulsory grain acquisition and market restrictions amid war and crises. The 1921 New Economic Policy (NEP) restored substantial market elements, including peasants’ ability to sell output, while large industry remained state-owned. From 1928, centralized industrialization emphasized capital goods alongside agricultural collectivization. The paper associates this period with famine and repression and later emphasizes that GDP comparisons omit those human costs. These are its historical account and cited estimates, not a claim that the counterfactual separately identifies each policy’s effect. Physical PDF pp. 4–5

Data and the prediction target

The panel uses the 2020 Maddison Project update and Russia’s GDP series completed by Markevich and Harrison. It covers 31 countries with complete GDP per capita series from 1885 to 1938. Russia is treated; there are 30 potential donors. The outcome is usually log GDP per capita. The pre-period is 1885–1916, \(T_0=32\); treatment starts in 1917 and the outcome window runs through 1938, 22 post-period years. The author notes territorial and population changes and possible data-quality concerns, while relying on the source series’ adjustments for consistent Russian/Soviet GDP per capita (§3, printed pp. 79; Table A1, printed p. 108 / physical PDF p. 35) Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 6.

Competing estimators and regularization

All candidate methods forecast the untreated Russian outcome from donor outcomes:

\[\widehat y^0_{1t}=\widehat\alpha+Y_{-1,t}^{\top}\widehat\beta.\]

The key finite-sample challenge is 30 possible controls for only 32 pre-treatment observations. Unrestricted regression can overfit and yield unstable forecasts. The article compares three approaches. HCW selects a subset of donor countries and estimates OLS; best-subset selection compares the best model at each size using BIC or AICc. Lasso minimizes pre-period squared error plus \(\lambda\sum_j|\beta_j|\), shrinking some coefficients to zero; post-lasso refits OLS on selected controls. The author tries leave-one-out and blocked 4-fold/8-fold cross-validation. Canonical synthetic control minimizes pre-period squared outcome gaps subject to nonnegative weights summing to one. The demeaned version matches deviations from each country’s pre-period mean and reconstructs the forecast by adding Russia’s mean, allowing a parallel level shift. Equations (3.1)–(3.2) and these estimators are in §3, printed pp. 79–82 / physical PDF pp. 6–9. Physical PDF pp. 6–9

Main scenarios and donor weights

The paper prefers synthetic control, especially the demeaned version, because its placebo exercises generally forecast better in this finite sample. Its Figure 2 shows the two synthetic specifications predicting a World War I-era decline, recovery and growth in the 1920s, a recession around the beginning of the 1930s, and eventual recovery. The counterfactual is above actual Soviet Russia in the 1920s and early 1930s; actual GDP per capita overtakes some counterfactuals in the second half of the 1930s (Figure 2, printed pp. 83) Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 10. This is a comparison of scenario paths, not a structurally identified treatment effect.

The donor weights reveal substantive concerns. In baseline synthetic control, Finland receives 0.332; India 0.206; Sri Lanka 0.289; Argentina 0.052; Peru 0.115; Norway 0.001; and Sweden 0.003. In the demeaned version the principal weights are Sri Lanka 0.410, Denmark 0.249, Finland 0.316, with smaller weights for Canada, Portugal, and Switzerland (Table II, printed pp. 85) Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 12. Finland was part of the Russian Empire before the Revolution, so its status as a donor is questionable, although it did not become communist. Dropping Finland changes donor composition but leaves the counterfactual path broadly similar. Non-European donors are also a concern because closer Eastern European countries are missing from the complete panel.

War, population and comparability

World War I comparability is another issue. Russia’s listed military losses are 1.7 million, or 1.09% of its 1913 population. The baseline synthetic units’ implied losses are much smaller: depending on specification and calculation, 0.03–0.30% (Table I, printed pp. 84) Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 11. Restricting donors to countries with at least 0.5% population losses leaves Austria, Finland, France, Germany, Italy, UK, Australia, New Zealand, and Canada. The ordinary synthetic control then cannot match pre-1917 Russia because all restricted donors are richer; the demeaned version fits better. The author interprets baseline results with the risk that World War I damage is understated in the counterfactual. Table I also shows a scaling assumption: the baseline synthetic control’s implied population (65.9 million) is far below Russia’s (156.2 million), so the comparison assumes economies are scalable and population size or density does not change growth (Table I, printed pp. 84–86) Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 11.

Diagnostics and forecast uncertainty

Robustness checks find similar synthetic paths through much of the 1920s and early 1930s when Finland is dropped or a demeaned model is used. The restricted-donor standard model fails pre-fit; its demeaned form works better. The 1930s paths diverge more across specifications. Leave-one-out estimates appear fairly robust to removing donor countries one at a time (Figures 4–6, printed pp. 86–88) Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 13. Russia backdating to 1905, 1909, and 1913 tests match-period sensitivity. 1905 is a poor placebo because Russia had a revolution and reforms then; the mismatch may reflect that event, and the author cautions against causal interpretation. At 1909 and 1913, some methods fail to reproduce the pre-1917 path or World War I downturn; the demeaned all-donor synthetic control performs more plausibly (Backdating discussion and Figures 7–9, printed pp. 88–91 / physical PDF pp. 15–18) Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 15.

The author does not conduct formal inference. Instead, he compares placebo gaps for each donor country treated as if it had experienced a 1917 intervention. Russia’s actual-minus-counterfactual log gap is negative and near the bottom of placebo gaps through much of the 1920s, consistent with higher predicted GDP absent the Revolution. In the 1930s it approaches zero and turns positive in some specifications, but lies near the middle of a dispersed placebo distribution. The placebo spread increases with the forecast horizon. Table III ranks Russia backdating MSEs (\(\times1{,}000\)): demeaned synthetic control is best for 1909 and 1913; demeaned restricted-donor synthetic is best for 1905. Table V’s other-country placebo MSEs (\(\times1{,}000\)) are 43.943 for canonical synthetic control and 43.697 for demeaned synthetic control, compared with 65.015 for a linear trend and much larger HCW errors. Placebo-based cross-validation performs better on those same placebo MSEs, but the paper cautions that it directly optimizes that metric (Figures 3 and 7–9; Tables III–V, printed pp. 84, 89–93 / physical PDF pp. 11, 16–20) Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 10.

Why close fit can forecast badly

HCW and lasso fit pre-1917 Russia very closely but often forecast implausibly volatile paths. HCW coefficient totals in the all-donor specifications are about 2.099 or 2.998, which implies two to three times the common growth if donors all grow at the same rate (Table VI, printed pp. 96) Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 23. Lasso/post-lasso totals range from about 1.25 to 2.36 in Table VII (printed pp. 101) Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 28. With restricted World War I donors, these totals move closer to one and forecasts become more moderate (Table VIII, printed pp. 102) Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 29. The article’s explanation is finite-sample bias–variance tradeoff: many regressors relative to 32 pre-observations make HCW and weakly regularized lasso vulnerable to overfit. Leave-one-out CV can under-regularize dependent time-series data; blocked folds do not consistently solve it here. These comparisons support this case’s method ranking, not a universal claim that synthetic control always wins (§§1, 4.2–4.4, printed pp. 76, 90–102 / physical PDF pp. 3, 17–29) Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 3.

Structural simulations and the stability assumption

Korolev contrasts his predictive relationship with earlier structural simulations, in which a model specifies how sectors, capital accumulation and policy distortions generate output. In his account, Hunter–Szyrmer’s KAPROST model considers detailed or aggregate production and alternative 1928–1940 policies; they conclude that less demanding policies, including avoiding collectivization, could have done better. Allen’s three-sector model assumes excess agricultural labour, and instead finds capitalist or continued-NEP counterfactuals below actual Soviet output. Those differences depend on the specified technologies, labour constraints and policies; their models are summarized in this supplied paper, not independently audited here. Physical PDF pp. 26–28

Cheremukhin and coauthors use a two-sector growth model with productivity paths and wedges representing distortions. Continuing pre-1913 productivity trends with fixed distortions gives a counterfactual below actual 1939 Soviet output; removing labour/capital wedges while holding other components at 1913 levels yields a much better counterfactual. Korolev’s preferred paths are nearer the former comparison in the late 1930s but remain uncertain across specifications. His reduced-form donor relationship covers 1917 onward and cannot decide which individual industrialization or agricultural policy was optimal. A fitted forecast and a structural policy simulation answer different questions under different maintained assumptions. Physical PDF pp. 28–29

Stability is a specific historical concern: the paper reports that Russian capital-goods industries were largely foreign-owned and that Russia depended heavily on grain exports and international trade. World War I disrupted world trade and finance; that exposure could have harmed Russia differently from the selected donors even without a Revolution. Missing comparable Eastern European data limits how well the donor pool can address this. Thus “the pre-1917 predictive relation would persist” is a substantive assumption threatened by a known structural break, not a consequence of small pre-period residuals. Physical PDF pp. 29

Logs, levels, growth and welfare limits

The appendix compares logs, levels, and growth rates. The author chooses logs because they substantially improve pre-period log-series fit relative to modeling first differences, while only slightly reducing fit for growth rates. Reconstructing log levels from fitted growth rates compounds past forecast errors, behaving like a random walk. Modeling GDP in levels gives qualitatively similar synthetic-control results, though some demeaned variants look optimistic and placebo fit is worse (Appendix A, printed pp. 103–110; Figures A2–A5; Tables A2–A5) Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 30. The article’s conclusion is carefully qualified: the counterfactual suggests a shorter downturn and stronger 1920s growth without the Revolution, while 1930s outcomes are specification-sensitive and increasingly uncertain. The paper cannot distinguish effects of the Revolution, Civil War, World War I, and other Russia-specific forces; nor can it evaluate individual policies or welfare costs. Its results are predictive, and economic outcomes omit deaths from famine and repression (printed pp. 99–103) Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 26.

The demeaned estimator makes the level shift explicit. Let \(\bar y_j=T_0^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{T_0}y_{jt}\) and \(\widetilde y_{jt}=y_{jt}-\bar y_j\). Fit nonnegative weights summing to one using the demeaned pre-period observations, then forecast

\[\widehat y^0_{1t}=\bar y_1+\sum_{j=2}^{J+1}\widehat\beta_j\,(y_{jt}-\bar y_j).\]

The estimated intercept is therefore \(\bar y_1-\sum_j\widehat\beta_j\bar y_j\). Ordinary convex weights cannot predict below every donor’s outcome level; demeaning can match changes while shifting the level. That is useful only if the shifted donor relation is credible after treatment. Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 9

Figure 2 compares actual and counterfactual log GDP per capita, standard (left) and demeaned (right) synthetic control. These vertical differences are log gaps, not raw-dollar GDP or directly measured welfare. Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 10

Figure 3 places Russia’s actual-minus-counterfactual log gap among donor placebo gaps; Table I records population and war-loss comparability. The author explicitly declines formal inference, and the placebo spread grows over the horizon. Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 11

Table II preserves standard/demeaned, no-Finland and WWI-restricted weights. Changing specification can change the contributing countries; none is simply a randomly chosen untreated twin. Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 12

Figure 5 is a range of selected counterfactual scenarios, not a confidence interval. Divergence is larger for the 1930s than for the central 1920s comparison. Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 14

Tables IV–V preserve cross-validated penalty choices and average other-country placebo MSE \(\times1{,}000\). Small differences between synthetic variants are sample results; placebo-based CV optimizes this same metric. Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 20

This page contains two distinct items: Table VI reports all-donor HCW coefficients, whose totals exceed two; Figure 12 below it displays the restricted-WWI HCW forecast paths. Adding unrestricted slopes can amplify a common donor trend rather than simply average it. Table VI also repeats \(J_{\max}=8\) in its final BIC header, while the discussion on physical PDF pp. 21–22 distinguishes maximum subsets of 8 and 28 controls. Preserve that source-header discrepancy; do not interpret the repeated header as an additional independently specified model. Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 23

Appendix Tables A2–A3 compare pre-period fit when models are estimated in logs or differences. A good growth fit does not guarantee a good reconstructed level path because errors accumulate. Korolev (2021), physical PDF pp. 36

sections.html:
O012-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: For a hypothetical demeaned log-GDP counterfactual, Russia’s pre-mean is 4; two donor post-minus-pre-mean deviations are 0.2 and 0.4 with weights 0.25 and 0.75. Compute the missing log outcome and actual-minus-predicted gap if actual is 4.1. An unrestricted forecast instead has donor coefficient sum 2; what common log-growth contribution does donor growth 0.1 imply? Explain canonical versus demeaned/HCW/lasso forecasts, the actual sample/timing/policy sequence, donor/WWI/population and foreign-trade comparability, diagnostics and the absence of formal inference. Interpret the 1920s versus 1930s scenario conclusions, logs/levels/growth reconstruction and structural policy simulations, including welfare limits.

Complete solution and essential rubric: The demeaned forecast is \(4+0.25(0.2)+0.75(0.4)=4.350000\); gap is \(4.1-4.350000=-0.250000\) log units, not raw dollars or exact percentage points. Demeaning adds the treated pre-mean to weighted donor deviations; its intercept is the treated mean minus weighted donor means. A common donor log increase \(0.1\) contributes \(2(0.1)=0.200000\) under the supplied coefficient sum, illustrating amplification rather than averaging. The actual panel is 31 countries/30 donors, 1885–1916 pre 32 years and 1917–1938 post 22 years. War Communism 1918, NEP 1921 and industrialization/collectivization from 1928 belong to a joint historical sequence, not separately identified effects. HCW subset OLS and lasso/post-lasso can overfit 30 controls/32 observations; blocked/leave-one-out CV do not universally solve dependent-data regularization. Standard SCM uses convex weights; demeaning allows a level shift only if post stability is credible. Finland’s imperial connection, missing comparable Eastern Europe, donor war losses far below Russia’s, richer restricted-WWI donors and population scaling all matter; ordinary restricted SCM fails prefit, while demeaned fit can improve without proving comparability. Foreign-owned capital/trade dependence plus WWI disruption threatens the predictive relation. Leave-one-out, Finland removal, restricted donors and backdating probe sensitivity; 1905 itself had revolution/reforms. The paper explicitly does not conduct formal inference; widening placebo gaps/scenario ranges are not confidence intervals. Preferred scenarios suggest shorter downturn/stronger 1920s growth absent Revolution; 1930s rank/sign depend more on specification with wider uncertainty. Growth errors cumulate when reconstructing log levels; logs improve relevant prefit here, not universally. Structural simulations encode sectors/productivity/wedges and answer different policy questions; conflicting conclusions depend on those assumptions. The predictive case cannot isolate Revolution/Civil War/WWI/individual Soviet policies or measure famine/repression deaths and welfare from GDP alone. All requested calculations, derivations and qualifications are essential; the component map above applies to every full form.

Self-assessment criteria and tutor checks

Required components: demeaned_log_gap_and_trend_amplification, historical_donor_war_and_sample_comparability, diagnostics_structural_targets_and_welfare_limits. Each full prompt/key below elicits every component; all are necessary for a pass on every permitted pair. Accept algebraically equivalent expressions and clearly defined opposite cash-flow signs with correct interpretation. A pass requires all requested outputs/reasons, correct units/assumptions and no critical conceptual error. Partial means a missing component or an unresolved isolated arithmetic slip with an otherwise valid method; independent correction is required for a pass. Fail means a critical mechanism/condition is wrong. Unscorable means a response or its help/exposure conditions cannot be established. Unknown help conditions are never independent evidence.

Acquisition requires two distinct unused unassisted full checks selected from the six exact metadata routes. sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Institutions, power and democratization; fingerprint bf0560feeb58d62c7ccfa01f533301f1666e3c7a968faa595c85d53afe507f1e. Heading depth and required relative figure-path relocation alone are adapted.

Institutions, power and democratization

Source: Acemoglu Robinson 2006 v2 Source: Week II - lecture - large slides

  • Rules, incentives and selective protection
  • Reconstructing the dynamic framework
  • Democratization and its reversal
  • Comparative statics and limits
  • Britain as an application
  • Lecture applications and interpretation

Why can institutions that discourage investment persist, and why do promises of reform sometimes fail? Acemoglu and Robinson's 2006 chapter treats economic rules and political power as jointly evolving. Economic institutions shape prosperity, but groups choose them under distributional conflict; the institutions that enlarge the total pie need not benefit those with power. This is the chapter's theoretical account, not a claim that a cross-country correlation alone identifies causation. Acemoglu–Robinson (2006), physical PDF pp. 1–3

This map preserves the two state variables, two power channels and distinct current/future outcomes. The source calls it schematic and simplified. In particular, resources are a major focus, but the ability to solve collective-action problems is also a source of de facto power. Acemoglu–Robinson (2006), physical PDF pp. 2–6 Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 44–50

Rules, incentives and selective protection

Institutions are humanly devised rules and constraints, rather than the organizations playing within them. Formal political rules govern leader selection and allocation of authority; formal legal rules govern rights, obligations and transactions; informal norms govern expected behaviour through social pressure, guilt and moral obligation. Effective institutions can reduce uncertainty, cheating and transaction costs, but “institutions” does not mean “efficient rules” by definition. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 30–32

The hold-up problem arises when one party makes a relationship-specific sunk investment and then faces worse terms from a partner, with limited alternatives. Anticipating that ex post vulnerability can discourage an otherwise useful investment. Credibly enforceable contracts may help if litigation/enforcement costs are low enough. A commitment problem is broader: a promise that is attractive now may be abandoned later when incentives change. Hold-up is a particular investment-based instance, not a synonym for every broken promise. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 33–34

The lecture distinguishes inclusive economic institutions—broad participation, broadly secure property rights, occupational choice, entry, competition and incentives to invest/innovate—from extractive institutions that channel resources toward privileged groups, selectively protect rights and restrict others through coercion or entry barriers. Inclusive political institutions combine pluralism and accountability with sufficient central authority to enforce rules; extraction can coexist with a powerful authoritarian state or an ineffective one. “Small state” is therefore not equivalent to inclusion. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 41–43

Reconstructing the dynamic framework

Economic institutions affect investments in physical and human capital and technology, organization of production, aggregate performance and the next period's distribution. They are endogenous collective choices because their distributive effects create conflicts. The authors emphasize institutions without claiming that geography and culture can never matter. Acemoglu–Robinson (2006), physical PDF pp. 2–3

De jure power comes from political institutions: constitutional rules, voting rights and constraints on rulers. De facto power comes from effective organization and resources, including protests, revolts, armed groups or military influence even without formal authority. A constitutional monarchy reallocates formal power relative to an unconstrained monarch; a disenfranchised organized group can still impose costs. Neither power channel is simply another name for income. Acemoglu–Robinson (2006), physical PDF pp. 3–4

Together they influence current economic rules and future political institutions. Political institutions and resource distribution are relatively durable state variables. An already wealthy group can use resources to preserve favourable rules and thereby reproduce its advantage; formal institutions also tend to persist until a sufficiently large power shift occurs. Persistence does not imply inevitability: technology, external conditions and critical junctures can alter the balance. Acemoglu–Robinson (2006), physical PDF pp. 4–5

Why not adopt efficient rules and compensate the losers? Promised transfers and protection may not be credible when tomorrow's powerful group can renege. A monarch can promise secure property rights today yet retain the ability to expropriate later. Merchants who gain temporary protest power want durable protection, but their organization may dissolve; converting de facto power into a change in formal political institutions can make future concessions more credible. This connects distribution, efficiency and political commitment rather than treating them as separable bargains automatically enforceable by a neutral third party. Acemoglu–Robinson (2006), physical PDF pp. 3, 6–7

The reproduced lecture diagram has current economic performance and future resources on its right, and future political institutions below. Those time labels explain the feedback: future resources and formal rules change the next round of power, not the past. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 50

Democratization and its reversal

In the chapter's simple “today/tomorrow” account, citizens temporarily overcome collective-action problems and threaten costly disorder or revolution. Elites can offer current policy concessions, promise future concessions, repress, or transfer durable political power. If citizens' temporary threat will fade, future elite promises may be noncredible. Extending voting rights changes who can choose policy tomorrow and therefore supplies a more credible commitment than a revocable policy promise. Acemoglu–Robinson (2006), physical PDF pp. 7–8

Democratization is not automatic. Elites may choose repression when retaining power is sufficiently valuable and repression is relatively cheap or feasible. Repression risks destroyed wealth, loss of life, sanctions, failure and empowerment of a military that could threaten elites themselves. In this framework democracy emerges when temporary concessions are insufficient, promises are noncredible and repression is too costly relative to conceding. Those are conditional mechanisms, not a universal numerical threshold supplied by the chapter. Acemoglu–Robinson (2006), physical PDF pp. 8–9

Consolidation means democratic institutions endure. A coup is the reverse conversion: elites with a temporary military/political opportunity can change formal institutions to secure future policies they favour. Promises by a democratic majority to remain moderate may also lack credibility after the coup threat subsides. The model therefore distinguishes creating democracy from sustaining it. Acemoglu–Robinson (2006), physical PDF pp. 9–10

Comparative statics and limits

The chapter gives three connected conditions favouring broad property protection and democratization: checks/balance of power; a relatively broad powerful group with investment opportunities; and limited rents available through coercive/extractive institutions. A small investor oligarchy may protect only its own assets, so investment interests alone are insufficient. Resource equality or effective organization can balance de facto power. Checks can also make democracy less threatening to elites by limiting what the majority can do. Acemoglu–Robinson (2006), physical PDF pp. 10–12

Economic structure changes those trade-offs. Land can be easier to tax/redistribute than mobile capital; resource rents raise the stakes of political monopoly; physical/human-capital economies may suffer greater destruction from repression and require less easily coerced effort. These mechanisms can make repression and coups more attractive in some agrarian/resource settings and less attractive in others. They are the authors' comparative arguments, not an assertion that all agrarian societies follow one path. Acemoglu–Robinson (2006), physical PDF pp. 11–12

Prosperity and democracy are jointly endogenous in the framework. Correlation does not by itself show that income causes democracy or that elections alone ensure growth. The chapter reports evidence against an automatic income-to-democracy causal interpretation after historical factors are considered; the claim is tied to that cited research, rather than a proof that every possible income effect is zero. Acemoglu–Robinson (2006), physical PDF pp. 12–13, 18–19

Britain as an application

The authors trace a sequence from seventeenth-century conflict and limits on the monarchy through more secure property rights and financial development, then industrialization/urbanization and stronger organization among previously excluded groups. Parliament's gains after the Civil War and 1688 were not mass democracy: voting remained narrow and corrupt. The 1832 reform removed many rotten-borough inequalities and expanded an electorate still limited to a minority of adult men; further organization and unrest preceded the 1867 and 1884 reforms. Secret ballots and anti-corruption measures also matter; formal suffrage alone did not immediately remove intimidation. Acemoglu–Robinson (2006), physical PDF pp. 13–15

Later changes included merit-based civil service, labour protections, social insurance/pensions, redistributive taxation and mass education. The chapter's narrative gives the 1918 Representation of the People Act and equal voting terms for women in 1928. Its opening reference to 1919 is internally inconsistent with that later chronology; use the body chronology, not the opening typo. Reform was gradual and strategic, with unrest, organization, electoral calculation and the costs of repression all relevant. Acemoglu–Robinson (2006), physical PDF pp. 15–18

This application answers why economic rise and democratization appear related without reducing the story to “richer people demand democracy.” Earlier institutions altered investment and growth; resulting structural changes altered de facto power; reform then changed de jure power and subsequent economic rules. Haiti is the authors' contrasting historical path, described as of the chapter's 2006 context, not a current country-status assessment. Acemoglu–Robinson (2006), physical PDF pp. 1–2, 16–19

Lecture applications and interpretation

The lecture's Nogales table contrasts annual household income (Arizona about USD 30,000 versus Sonora about one-third), education, health, services, security/business conditions and accountability across a border. These are the reading's historical comparisons, not current statistics. Encomienda granted tribute/labour claims over Indigenous populations with nominal conversion obligations, enabling elite extraction. Jamestown did not implement that Spanish institution: attempts to extract from Indigenous people and coercion of English settlers eventually gave way to land/incentive changes when the original strategy failed. The table and examples illustrate institutional incentives; a border narrative alone is not a controlled estimate of every difference. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 37–40

Institutions may remain inefficient because reform requires collective action, people can free ride, small groups with concentrated stakes may organize more effectively, and existing rules may obstruct challengers. The functionalist fallacy is to infer an institution's origin or automatic emergence from its useful function. These foundations connect the lecture to the chapter's persistence mechanism and the additional Olson reading. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 35–36

The full dynamic model and commitment mechanism are core because they explain endogenous institutions and answer the supplied seminar questions. Britain, Nogales and colonial contrasts support the reasoning; they do not establish a single inevitable development path or a forecast of present politics. Acemoglu–Robinson (2006), physical PDF pp. 18–19 Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 3, 44–50
