sections.html:
O013-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: In a hypothetical polity, workers gain temporary effective power through urban organization; formal rules favour landowners. Elites offer a current concession plus a revocable future promise, repression at uncertain cost, or broader voting rights. Reconstruct the complete dynamic institutional framework. Explain commitment versus hold-up, concessions/repression/democratization and later coups, conditional comparative statics and Britain’s sequence. Does income alone imply democracy or selective investor protection imply inclusion?

Complete solution and essential rubric: Political institutions at \(t\) allocate de jure power; current resources and collective organization create de facto power. Together they shape current economic institutions and political institutions at \(t+1\). Economic rules affect current performance and future resources, feeding the next round of power. Temporary mobilization is effective influence without formal votes, rather than simply wealth. Efficient rules can hurt incumbents; compensation may not be credible once leverage fades. Hold-up specifically requires a sunk relationship-specific investment; commitment is the broader future-incentive problem. Current concessions do not bind tomorrow, while voting rights alter future policy choice. Repression depends on rents, feasibility and destruction, failure and military-empowerment costs. Democratization can become attractive when temporary promises fail and repression is too costly; consolidation is separate because a temporary coup threat can become durable elite formal power. Balanced checks, a broad investing coalition and limited coercive rents can help; a narrow oligarchy may protect only itself. Land, resource rents, capital mobility, human-capital dependence and repression costs change the trade-offs without a universal threshold. Britain’s monarchy/parliament constraints preceded finance, investment and industrial/urban change, which strengthened excluded groups before 1832/1867/1884 and later reforms; early Parliament was not mass democracy. Use the body chronology of the 1918 Act and 1928 equal terms, retaining the opening 1919 discrepancy. Prosperity and democracy are jointly endogenous: correlation is not a one-way income effect. Broad rights, entry and accountability with capacity differ from selective protection or a small state. Historical Nogales/colonial cases remain dated illustrations; beneficiary and organization barriers explain persistence without inevitability or a functionalist origin claim. All requested calculations, derivations and qualifications are essential; the component map above applies to every full form.

interactions.prompt_html:
O013-I1

O013-I1, item_version 1, full_capability_check. Prompt: A constitution gives merchants no votes. An export boom finances their independent associations and a temporary boycott; no political law has yet changed. The ruler promises secure property next year but retains unilateral expropriation, while a small court-connected investor group already has protected assets. Diagnose the two power channels, reconstruct the full current/future feedback and explain which arrows the export shock initially changes. Compare the promise, durable voting reform and repression; explain why narrow investor protection need not produce inclusion, and how capital mobility, broad organization and coercive rents could alter the choice. If merchant voting reform is adopted, does that guarantee consolidation? Suppose the former court-connected elite later gains a temporary military opportunity and demands restrictions on the new electorate while the majority promises future moderation: explain how reversal can turn effective leverage into durable formal power. A commentator calls Britain’s 1832 reform universal democracy and treats its growth correlation as a one-way income effect: assess both claims.
interactions.solution_html:
Complete solution and essential rubric: The unchanged constitution fixes the current de jure allocation; export resources and association/boycott capacity change de facto power before formal votes change. Political institutions at \(t\) shape de jure power, current resources/collective organization shape de facto power, and both affect current economic institutions and political institutions at \(t+1\). Economic rules affect current performance and next-period resources. The boom first affects the resource/organization channel, not retroactively the constitution; later feedback can change formal rules. The ruler’s revocable property promise may fail once the boycott fades because expropriation remains attractive and feasible. Durable voting rights can change future policy control; a current concession alone does not do so. This is general commitment, whereas hold-up specifically requires a sunk relationship-specific investment. Protected court investors demonstrate selective rights, not broad entry/security; a small powerful investing group may defend its privilege. Balanced power and a broad investing coalition with limited extractive rents can favour broader protection; mobile capital or destructive repression can increase repression’s cost, while valuable coercive rents can increase resistance. No numerical threshold or inevitable democratization follows. Even if the merchants obtain voting reform, consolidation is a separate question of whether the new democratic rules endure. In the specified later military opportunity, the former elite gains temporary de facto coup leverage; restricting the franchise or replacing democratic rules can convert that temporary threat into durable de jure control over future policy. The majority’s promised moderation may be noncredible after the coup threat fades, so the same commitment logic can drive reversal. This is a conditional mechanism, not a prediction that the coup must occur or that the earlier reform itself failed. British parliamentary constraints supported finance/investment before industrialization and urban organization changed excluded groups’ power. The 1832 electorate remained a minority of adult men; later 1867/1884 changes, secret ballots and social reforms mattered. Income and democracy are jointly endogenous, so correlation alone does not identify a one-way income effect. Require the complete dated feedback, commitment/investment distinction, conditional political choice and historical correction; no learner result or historical causal estimate is implied.

I1/I2 are immediate checks; D1/D2 are distinct parallel variants reserved where possible for delayed checks. A delayed success requires an unused form before recap, no help/solution access, and at least 24 actual elapsed hours after acquisition and the most recent relevant teaching/solution exposure. Record intervening exposure. A calendar-date change alone is insufficient; an early D attempt is immediate evidence only.

interactions.prompt_html:
O013-I2

O013-I2, item_version 1, full_capability_check. Prompt: A democracy faces a temporary military coup threat. Its majority offers moderation this year and promises to keep future taxes low after the army withdraws; an elite faction demands permanent limits on who may vote. Compare this reverse transition with initial democratization, distinguishing effective military leverage, formal rights, credible commitment and consolidation. Reconstruct the complete two-state-variable feedback rather than drawing performance as a cause of past institutions. Contrast a landed/resource-rent elite with owners of mobile industrial capital, including repression/destruction/military risks and the danger of selective protection. Use Britain’s secret-ballot and 1918/1928 chronology to assess the statement “passing one suffrage law completes democracy and establishes growth causation.”
interactions.solution_html: Complete solution and essential rubric: The temporary military threat supplies de facto leverage; changing the franchise converts it into durable de jure power. A promise of low future taxes may be noncredible once that threat recedes, just as an elite promise of future concessions can fail after popular mobilization fades. Initial democratization transfers durable policy choice toward citizens; a coup can reverse that conversion. Consolidation is whether democracy endures, not merely whether it was once created. Political institutions and resource distribution are state variables: today’s institutions assign legal power, today’s resources/organization assign effective power, together they shape current economic institutions and future political institutions, and current economic rules affect current performance and future resources. No arrow changes the past. This is intertemporal political commitment without a necessary relationship-specific investment; a supplier’s sunk dedicated machine would add hold-up. Immobile land/resource rents can raise redistributive stakes and the value of political monopoly; mobile capital and dependence on skilled effort can make repression/destruction more costly. Repression may also empower the army against elites. Checks, balanced organization, a broad investing group and limited coercive rents can favour broad rights, while protecting only elite investors is not inclusion; these are conditional comparisons. Britain’s broader franchise developed over multiple reforms; secret ballots and anti-corruption protections address intimidation that formal suffrage alone does not remove. Use the 1918 Act and equal terms for women in 1928, retaining the chapter’s opening 1919 discrepancy. The joint institutional/economic sequence does not identify an automatic income-to-democracy or elections-to-growth law. Require the complete reverse-transition reasoning, feedback, comparative statics and source chronology.

interactions.prompt_html:
O013-D1

O013-D1, item_version 1, full_capability_check. Prompt: A proposed reform would increase total output but remove an incumbent monopoly. New reformers promise to compensate its owner from future public revenue; the owner doubts that future governments will pay. Citizens have recently become better organized and resource distribution more equal, but rulers retain formal control and can repress. Explain why an aggregate gain need not secure agreement and distinguish this problem from a manufacturer repricing after a dedicated machine is installed. Reconstruct the full institutional feedback, compare checks/broad investment interests/limited rents with selective protection, and state how repression/coup incentives affect creation versus consolidation of democracy. Explain why Britain’s joint finance–industrialization–political-reform sequence cannot be replaced by “income alone causes democracy.”
interactions.solution_html: Complete solution and essential rubric: The incumbent can lose protected rents despite a larger aggregate pie, and future compensation may not be credible when recipients of power can renege. This is political commitment and distributional conflict, not ignorance of an efficient rule. The dedicated machine adds a sunk relationship-specific investment and hence hold-up; compensation failure does not require that investment. Better citizen organization and more balanced resources increase de facto influence without automatically changing formal de jure authority. At \(t\), political institutions and resources/organization generate those respective power channels; together they choose current economic institutions and future political institutions. Economic institutions affect current performance and next-period resources, which feed back into power. Balanced checks, a broad group with investment opportunities and limited coercive rents can support broad property protection; a small investing oligarchy may instead protect only its own assets. Temporary citizen leverage makes a revocable policy promise weak; durable rights can change tomorrow’s decision makers. Repression can be chosen when rents are valuable and costs low, but destruction, failure and army empowerment can reverse that ranking. Democracy’s creation is separate from its endurance; a later temporary coup opportunity can undo formal rights. In Britain, limits on monarchy helped property/finance and investment, industrial/urban changes strengthened organization, and further franchise/ballot/social reforms followed while early participation remained restricted. Neither income alone nor one reform is isolated as the causal driver. Require the surplus-versus-distribution/credibility distinction, complete feedback and conditional political/historical analysis; do not infer agreement, reform or a permanent path merely from the stated improvement.

interactions.prompt_html:
O013-D2

O013-D2, item_version 1, full_capability_check. Prompt: A resource-price windfall strengthens a ruler’s allied security firms. Formal voting rights do not change, independent associations are obstructed, and the ruler uses new revenue to grant allies exclusive licences. An adviser says that the present boom proves inclusive institutions and that greater repression is costless because the army is paid. Trace the full current/future feedback and distinguish both power channels. Evaluate commitment, current concessions versus durable political change, repression and a possible later coup. Compare resource rents with a broad human-capital-intensive investing economy, and explain the lesson of Britain’s early parliamentary constraints without calling them immediate mass democracy or treating prosperity/democracy correlation as causal proof.
interactions.solution_html: Complete solution and essential rubric: The windfall initially changes resources and effective/de facto power, not the unchanged legal/de jure franchise. Obstructed organization weakens challengers even where formal votes exist. Exclusive licences are current economic institutions that selectively channel returns; a current boom does not establish broad entry, secure rights or inclusion. Political rules at \(t\) allocate de jure power; resources and organization at \(t\) allocate de facto power; both shape current economic rules and future political institutions. Those economic rules affect current performance and future resources, potentially reproducing allied power. Ruler promises or temporary transfers can be reneged on once opposition leverage fades; durable political constraints alter tomorrow’s incentives. A dedicated investment followed by repricing would be the narrower hold-up case, rather than every political promise. Paid troops can still destroy assets, fail or acquire independent coup leverage, so repression is not costless. High extractive rents raise the stakes of monopoly; broad investors, balanced power/checks, mobile capital and reliance on skilled effort can change the costs and benefits of inclusion or repression. Democratization and consolidation remain distinct; neither windfall nor human-capital structure guarantees one outcome. Britain’s monarchical constraints supported property/finance before industrialization and organized excluded groups prompted further changes; early parliamentary rights were narrow. Subsequent reforms and reciprocal economic/political effects preclude a simple one-way correlation claim. Require all power/time channels, the selective-rights diagnosis, commitment and conditional transition/reversal/history reasoning.

sections.html:
Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Liberty, Leviathans and the cage of norms; fingerprint d8467cfbbfbf327692a52af4dc0f820dd58507e3cfb3e430d35147ed2b8a3ce3. Heading depth and required relative figure-path relocation alone are adapted.

Liberty, Leviathans and the cage of norms

Source: Acemoglu Robinson - The Narrow Corridor - chapter 1 Source: Week II - lecture - large slides Source: Week III - lecture - large slides

  • Liberty means freedom from domination
  • Hobbes's Warre and the economic mechanism
  • Capacity can be used for repression
  • Norms can create order and a cage
  • The Shackled Leviathan
  • What the chapter's final outline does—and does not—supply

Can a powerful state protect liberty, and can a society without a state avoid domination? Chapter 1 of The Narrow Corridor rejects a simple choice between total anarchy and an all-powerful ruler. Liberty requires the capacity to control violence and effective constraints on how that capacity is used. The lecture's corridor is a balance between state and societal power, not a formula that state power alone or social cohesion alone creates freedom. The Narrow Corridor, chapter 1, physical PDF pp. 1–3, 23–26 Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 5–8

This map represents the chapter's three types and two objections to Hobbes. It is a conceptual comparison, not a causal experiment or a country-classification index. The Narrow Corridor, chapter 1, physical PDF pp. 7–11, 16–18, 23–26

Liberty means freedom from domination

The chapter starts with competing visions: Fukuyama's liberal convergence, Kaplan's anarchy and Harari's technology-enabled dictatorship. The authors propose diversity and historical contingency rather than one inevitable “end.” Their Congo “Article 15—fend for yourself” is explicitly a joke, not an actual constitutional provision. The real constitutional promises illustrate the gap between written rights and protection in practice. The Narrow Corridor, chapter 1, physical PDF pp. 1–3

Soyinka's journey through Lagos depicts gangs, predatory roadblocks, missing services and insecurity. The central idea, developed through Pettit's non-domination, is that a person can be unfree even without an actual assault today: another person's arbitrary ability to threaten, punish or withdraw essential protection alters behaviour. A subordinate spouse, worker or debtor may anticipate retaliation and self-censor. Freedom is therefore more than an abstract permission; it includes the practical ability to act without arbitrary domination by state or private actors. These are the book's historical narratives and conceptual examples, not current conditions certified for whole populations. The Narrow Corridor, chapter 1, physical PDF pp. 3–7

Hobbes's Warre and the economic mechanism

Warre includes both actual fighting and the known persistent possibility of violence when no common authority reliably protects people. If harvests, possessions and life can be taken, effort and investment have uncertain private returns. People divert resources into self-protection and avoid travel, commerce and long-lived projects. The economic harm can arise from credible threats even when violence is off the observed path. The Narrow Corridor, chapter 1, physical PDF pp. 7–10

Hobbes's solution is a powerful Leviathan, a state with overwhelming authority to impose order. He allows formation by agreement or conquest and regards monarchy, aristocracy and democracy mainly as different conveniences for wielding sovereign power. The authors accept his insight that avoiding Warre is crucial and that monopolizing violence can reduce killings. They reject two further steps: statelessness does not always mean uncontrolled violence, and a capable state does not automatically protect liberty. The Narrow Corridor, chapter 1, physical PDF pp. 9–11

Capacity can be used for repression

State capacity is the ability to achieve objectives: enforce rules, resolve disputes, tax, regulate, build services or wage war. Bureaucratic means and motivation are crucial; capacity is analytically distinct from the desirability of the objective. The Nazi expulsion machinery and mass murder illustrate capable organization used to dispossess and kill. The Mao-era famine account describes procurement and suppression of criticism; later re-education accounts show coercion is not merely a failure to provide order. They demonstrate why an efficient administrative mechanism need not be welfare-improving. The Narrow Corridor, chapter 1, physical PDF pp. 11–16

The Despotic Leviathan is defined by the absence of effective societal control over state power, not by a threshold number of murders. Repression is possible because the state is unaccountable. The Janus metaphor captures two faces: protection/services and predation/domination. Even a state that suppresses private violence can replace it with state violence. Source-reported atrocity estimates and historical incarceration examples are context for this argument, not newly verified demographic measurements or present-day legal descriptions. The Narrow Corridor, chapter 1, physical PDF pp. 16–17

Norms can create order and a cage

An Absent Leviathan lacks effective centralized authority, but social norms can still coordinate conflict resolution, reciprocity, sanctions and collective defence. The chapter's Akan accounts describe safe commerce and community hearings mediated by elders and shared expectations. These cases refute an automatic equation of statelessness with chaos. They do not establish the absence of hierarchy or coercion. The Narrow Corridor, chapter 1, physical PDF pp. 17–18

The same norms become a cage when conformity, subordination and prescribed roles cannot be freely challenged. In the Asante protection account, attachment to a lineage or powerful person helps guard against raiders but requires obedience; leaving that dependency can expose someone to enslavement. Goi's experience shows slavery and insecurity, while Bwanikwa's pawning illustrates how a nominally redeemable dependency can become lasting bondage. Wards, wives and dependants may receive protection while lacking independent voice. This is the supplied example of one norm system simultaneously reducing danger and restricting liberty. The Narrow Corridor, chapter 1, physical PDF pp. 18–21

The authors also discuss how powerful interpreters can tilt inherited norms in their own favour, including gender hierarchies. Their Pashtunwali example combines hospitality and generosity with revenge obligations and restrictions on women. Read these as the authors' specified historical/social accounts, not as a claim that every member of an ethnic or religious population behaves identically. The mechanism is compulsory unequal dependence, not a judgment inferred from a group label. The Narrow Corridor, chapter 1, physical PDF pp. 22

The Week III lecture adds the Tiv illustration: witchcraft accusations can constrain would-be dominant individuals yet inhibit initiative and centralization. That particular example is supplied by the lecture; detailed later book chapters were not supplied or audited here. The lecture's prebendalism discussion similarly explains officials financing themselves through office revenues/rents: it reduces the ruler's cash-wage needs but can encourage predation. These are institutional trade-offs, not proof that all premodern officials had identical arrangements. Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 21–23

The Shackled Leviathan

The answer is a state capable of enforcing law and controlling private violence that is itself constrained by an organized, vigilant society. Formal constitutions, elections and review matter, but effective societal ability to complain, organize, contest and remove rulers matters too. This Shackled Leviathan can also loosen oppressive customary constraints. Its coercive potential remains Janus-faced; constraints restrain it rather than erase that potential. The Narrow Corridor, chapter 1, physical PDF pp. 23–26

The Wyoming example links frontier violence, vigilante justice and the 1892 Johnson County conflict to state intervention, then women's voting rights to changes in customary restrictions. Two historical source labels need care: the chapter names William Henry Harrison for 1892, although it was Benjamin Harrison's presidency; its claim that Wyoming was the world's first place to grant women suffrage is too broad. Wyoming's 1869 territorial suffrage and later retention are the relevant institutional example, not an unqualified global-first claim. The Library of Congress Benjamin Harrison guide, Introduction, confirms his 1889–1893 presidency; its Women’s Suffrage classroom passage, “Early Rights,” notes earlier property-qualified female voting in New Jersey until 1807 and Wyoming territorial suffrage in 1869. These bounded checks correct the labels without treating the Johnson County intervention as a neutral, unqualified success. The Narrow Corridor, chapter 1, physical PDF pp. 23–25

The lecture diagram puts state power on the vertical axis and societal power on the horizontal. Moving upward alone can favour despotism; societal constraints without state capacity do not automatically supply security. A balance inside the corridor can support expansion of both. The following empirical illustration plots state capacity and civil society for the US, Japan, Honduras and Russia from 1855 to 2015. Its standardized/abstract axes and selected cases do not themselves identify a causal law or certify all conclusions of the cited Murphy–O'Reilly paper, which is a bibliography lead here. Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 7–8

What the chapter's final outline does—and does not—supply

The ending surveys later chapters: state-society coevolution, the will to power, economic incentives, European/Chinese/Indian contrasts, conditional structural effects, uneven US capacity and slavery, “Paper” Leviathans, Middle Eastern norms, zero-sum conflict, entry to the corridor and maintaining it as responsibilities expand. These are pointers in the supplied chapter, not ingestion of the later chapters' detailed evidence. The common implication is that building and defending accountable capacity is continuing work; geography or a historical shock does not have one unconditional political effect. The Narrow Corridor, chapter 1, physical PDF pp. 26–30

The core concepts answer the supplied questions: Warre discourages economic activity through insecurity; Hobbes is right about the importance of order but overstates the necessity and benignity of sovereign power; Absent, Despotic and Shackled types differ in effective capacity and constraints; the cage can protect people while binding them to unequal roles. The historical cases make those distinctions usable without turning them into inevitable country destinies. Week II lecture, physical PDF pp. 3 Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 5 The Narrow Corridor, chapter 1, physical PDF pp. 7–26

The lecture’s selected four-country trajectories use state-capacity and civil-society indices. Treat the curves as the cited illustration; they are not an independently audited identification design. Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 8

sections.html:
O014-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: Compare hypothetical communities Alder (no central authority, safe trade through elders but compulsory dependent status), Birch (effective coercive bureaucracy without accountability), and Cedar (capable enforcement with organized citizens able to challenge rulers and oppressive custom). Classify Leviathans and explain non-domination, Warre and investment, capacity’s two faces, the cage of norms/Asante protection, corridor axes and continuing contestation. Qualify historical examples, source corrections, later-chapter leads and the four-country graph.

Complete solution and essential rubric: Alder illustrates an Absent Leviathan: norms can provide order while caging dependants, so statelessness need not mean constant violence. Birch illustrates a Despotic Leviathan: capacity can protect or repress and is distinct from desirable objectives. Cedar illustrates a Shackled Leviathan: state capacity controls private violence while organized society constrains state power and can loosen customary domination. Liberty is practical freedom from arbitrary domination even without an assault today. Hobbes’s Warre includes persistent credible threats that discourage travel, commerce and long-lived investment and divert resources into protection. Order matters, but unaccountable sovereignty need not be benign. Asante attachment can reduce enslavement risk while demanding obedience; exit may expose vulnerability. Akan, Pashtun, Tiv and prebendalism examples are bounded accounts, not uniform ethnic/current-country claims. State power is vertical and societal power horizontal in the corridor; increasing state power alone can favour despotism, while society alone need not ensure security. Continuing organization matters alongside written rights. Congo Article 15 is a joke, not a constitutional law. The 1892 Wyoming context concerns Benjamin Harrison, not William Henry Harrison; 1869 territorial suffrage is not an unqualified world first. The 1855–2015 four-country index trajectories are a cited illustration, not an audited causal design. Later chapters remain pointers; no necessary country development sequence follows. All requested calculations, derivations and qualifications are essential; the component map above applies to every full form.

interactions.prompt_html:
O014-I1

O014-I1, item_version 1, full_capability_check. Prompt: A constitution promises speech and a bureaucracy efficiently collects taxes. In practice, officials may withdraw a worker’s permit arbitrarily; independent associations cannot challenge them. No permit has been withdrawn this month, so an analyst declares liberty secure and places the country inside the corridor using state capacity alone. Diagnose the claim using non-domination and Warre’s investment mechanism. Identify the most consistent Leviathan and distinguish what evidence would support the other two types; explain why orderly norms can still cage people, using Asante dependency. Correct the corridor axes and the Wyoming 1892/1869 source labels, and state what the four-country illustration and later-chapter outline can establish.
interactions.solution_html:
Complete solution and essential rubric: The worker’s anticipation of arbitrary permit withdrawal can constrain action without a withdrawal today: non-domination is more than written permission or the current assault count. Persistent threats to returns discourage travel, trade and long-lived investment and induce self-protection, the economic logic of Warre. Tax collection shows a capacity, but the lack of effective challenge makes the Despotic Leviathan most consistent; capability does not imply benign use. An Absent Leviathan would lack effective central authority, potentially with norm-based order; a Shackled one would combine capable protection with effective societal constraints, not just a constitution. Norms can coordinate safety yet impose compulsory status: Asante protection through a lineage/patron can reduce raiding danger while requiring obedience and making exit risky. Thus order alone does not settle liberty. State power is the vertical axis and societal power horizontal; an upward move alone cannot establish the corridor. Janus-faced capacity can supply services or repress. Wyoming’s 1892 presidency was Benjamin Harrison’s, and 1869 territorial suffrage is not an unqualified world first; these corrections do not turn the intervention into a neutral success proof. The 1855–2015 four-country index paths are a cited illustration, not an audited causal design, and later chapter details remain pointers. Require the permit-specific threat analysis, all three type distinctions, norms/capacity mechanism and evidence/scope corrections.

I1/I2 are immediate checks; D1/D2 are distinct parallel variants reserved where possible for delayed checks. A delayed success requires an unused form before recap, no help/solution access, and at least 24 actual elapsed hours after acquisition and the most recent relevant teaching/solution exposure. Record intervening exposure. A calendar-date change alone is insufficient; an early D attempt is immediate evidence only.

interactions.prompt_html:
O014-I2

O014-I2, item_version 1, full_capability_check. Prompt: A stateless trading community settles disputes through elders and has little street fighting, but dependants must obey a patron to keep protection from raiders. A reformer concludes both that no state is ever needed and that these norms prove liberty. Contrast that claim with a proposal for courts capable of protecting exit while open associations can contest officials. Explain Warre even during quiet periods, non-domination, the three Leviathans and capacity’s Janus character. Use the source’s Asante and Tiv/prebendalism examples without ethnic generalization, identify both corridor axes, and audit the Congo Article 15 and later-chapter/four-country evidence claims.
interactions.solution_html: Complete solution and essential rubric: Quiet commerce without central authority shows that an Absent Leviathan need not mean constant chaos; it does not establish liberty or the universal dispensability of state capacity. Protection conditional on patron obedience is a cage: arbitrary dependence and dangerous exit constrain conduct before an attack occurs. Warre includes the known possibility of violence that makes investment and travel unsafe. Courts with real protective capacity plus effective open societal contestation could move toward a Shackled Leviathan; mere administrative power without constraints could instead be Despotic. Capacity has protective and predatory faces, so the proposal must be assessed on actual enforcement and challenge, not its stated benevolence alone. The Asante account joins protection with subordination; Tiv accusations can constrain aspiring dominance yet inhibit initiative/centralization, and prebendal finance can reduce cash-wage needs while encouraging predation. These are bounded source accounts, not uniform ethnic or timeless rules. On the diagram, state power is vertical and societal power horizontal; organized norms alone do not replace capable public protection, nor does upward capacity alone secure freedom. Congo Article 15 is explicitly a joke, not law. The four-country trajectories cannot identify the proposed court reform’s causal effect; later chapters are only surveyed leads. Wyoming’s 1869 example and the Benjamin Harrison correction likewise remain qualified historical illustrations. Require the stateless-order-versus-liberty diagnosis, prospective institutional contrast, full type/capacity distinctions and scope/attribution limits.

interactions.prompt_html:
O014-D1

O014-D1, item_version 1, full_capability_check. Prompt: Citizens freely organize and obtain paper rights, but police cannot reliably protect roads and merchants avoid long trips because gangs could seize cargo. A graph shows high societal organization but low effective state capacity; a minister calls this a Shackled Leviathan merely because elections exist. A later proposal adds effective courts and accountable policing while permitting challenges to forced customary roles. Assess both stages and the investment mechanism without assuming any increase in policing is liberating. Contrast Absent, Despotic and Shackled arrangements, explain Asante-type protection/dependency and the corridor axes, and identify the historical and empirical qualifications needed before claiming a proven national transition.
interactions.solution_html: Complete solution and essential rubric: Effective road protection is missing despite formal rights and organization. Merchants respond to a credible threat even when a particular trip has not been attacked; insecure returns discourage commerce and long projects and divert resources to defence. The first stage does not meet the combined-capacity-and-constraint requirement for a Shackled Leviathan; it has an absent/ineffective central-protection feature, and the qualitative model is not determined by the election label alone. Courts and policing under effective societal control can support a Shackled arrangement and loosen arbitrary customary dependency. The same capacity without challenge could be Despotic, so increased enforcement alone is not sufficient. Absent states can have norm-based order, but Asante-type patron protection may require unequal obedience and dangerous exit; protection and non-domination differ. State power is vertical and societal power horizontal; improvement in both can be compatible with the corridor without making a trajectory inevitable. Janus-faced capacity requires continuing contestation, not merely adopting the proposal. Wyoming’s 1869 suffrage is not an unqualified world first, its 1892 president was Benjamin Harrison, and source intervention narratives remain qualified. The four-country 1855–2015 indices illustrate selected trajectories rather than identify this reform, while later book chapters are pointers. Require the stage-specific diagnosis, threat/returns mechanism, all type/norm distinctions and limits on inferred transition success.

interactions.prompt_html:
O014-D2

O014-D2, item_version 1, full_capability_check. Prompt: An essay uses three pieces of evidence: the Nazi state’s organizational effectiveness supposedly proves low violence is the definition of despotism; an Asante protection relationship supposedly proves customs cannot dominate; and Wyoming’s institutions supposedly prove every state automatically liberates women. Build a corrected argument linking liberty, capacity and societal constraint. Explain Warre’s known threat rather than only observed battles, distinguish all three Leviathans and the cage of norms, and interpret a vertical-only rise on the corridor diagram. Audit the source’s Harrison/global-first labels, Congo joke, four-country graph and later-chapter leads without replacing them with a universal country destiny.
interactions.solution_html: Complete solution and essential rubric: The Nazi example demonstrates capable machinery used for dispossession and killing, not a definition based on a murder threshold or low observed violence. Despotic power is unaccountable to effective societal control; a state can suppress private attacks while dominating people itself. Liberty means freedom from arbitrary dependence, including anticipated retaliation without an attack today. Warre’s persistent known danger undermines expected returns, commerce and investment even between battles. An Absent Leviathan lacks effective central authority but can have orderly norms; Asante protection can simultaneously reduce danger and cage dependants through obedience and costly exit. A Shackled Leviathan combines public capacity with organized continuing constraints and can challenge oppressive custom; Wyoming is a qualified illustration of that possibility, not automatic emancipation by any state. State power is vertical, societal power horizontal; rising only vertically can increase unaccountable capacity rather than secure the corridor. Its Janus faces must be judged separately from administrative effectiveness. Correct 1892 to Benjamin Harrison and qualify the 1869 world-first statement; Congo Article 15 is a joke. The four-country index illustration is not an identified causal law and the later-chapter outline is not supplied detailed evidence. Require corrections tied to each essay claim, full type and norm distinctions, threat/investment reasoning and empirical/historical restraint.

sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Embedded economies, reciprocity and the Kula ring; fingerprint 400fa27117a34f59293450de25852717ea932ca25ca96a5066d709d769df66fe. Heading depth and required relative figure-path relocation alone are adapted.

Embedded economies, reciprocity and the Kula ring

Source: Polanyi 1944 Great-Transformation chapter 4 Source: ADDITIONAL - Economic Pursuits of the Trobriand Islanders Source: Week III - lecture - large slides

  • Social motives and economic organization
  • Reciprocity and symmetry
  • Redistribution and centricity
  • Householding and production for use
  • The 1920 Trobriand report

Can a complex economy operate without market prices governing the whole system? Polanyi's chapter distinguishes the existence of trade, money and markets from a self-regulating market economy in which prices organize economic life as a whole. His historical thesis is that such a system is an exceptional development, rather than the natural expression of an invariant propensity to barter. This is the author's interpretation; it should not be turned into a claim that earlier societies had no trade or no individual motives. Polanyi, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 1–3 Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 13–16

This map separates principles of behaviour from the institutional patterns that support them. It follows Polanyi's argument rather than equating every gift economy with modern socialism or every exchange with capitalism. Polanyi, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 5–13

Social motives and economic organization

Polanyi argues that social standing, obligations, kinship and community membership can organize production and distribution. Reputation and public recognition reward effort; ostracism and sanctions discipline noncompliance. The relevant contrast is the dominant coordinating institution and motive, not an assumption that people in one society are inherently generous and those in another inherently selfish. He explicitly rejects replacing a stereotyped “capitalistic” psychology with an equally simple “communistic” psychology. Polanyi, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 2–5

The lecture groups traditional systems around slowly coevolved family, customary and religious institutions—“familistic groupism”—and contrasts that embedding with the greater subordination of social frameworks to economic calculation in stylized market/command systems. It also warns that traditional systems are diverse. This is a comparative organizing distinction, not a literal claim that modern economies lack norms or that every traditional economy has the same religion or technology. Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 12–16

Reciprocity and symmetry

Reciprocity organizes giving and receiving through continuing social obligations. Returns can be delayed and may come through a network rather than the same person immediately. Symmetry—recognized paired partners, kin groups or villages—helps those obligations remain legible without a spot-market contract for every exchange. Polanyi's matrilineal example has a man delivering produce to his sister's household while his own wife's relatives provide reciprocal support. Public displays of good gardening protect reputation; the pattern coordinates provision without a wage for each act. Polanyi, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 5–7

The lecture's Kula example is a ceremonial network across at least 18 island communities. Red shell-disc necklaces (soulava/veigun) circulate clockwise, and white arm-shells (mwali) counterclockwise; “north” and “south” in a ring are simplified local directions, not global compass rules. Objects have prestige linked to history and former owners, and ownership is temporary. Their limited practical use does not mean they have no social value. Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 19–20 Polanyi, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 7–8

Partners undertake dangerous long-distance voyages and exchange under ritual rules, rather than bargaining for immediate monetary profit. Polanyi describes circulation over years, sometimes up to a decade; an object may return after gaining history. Complex specialization and exchange therefore do not logically require a system wholly governed by market prices. The example demonstrates organizational complexity rather than proving that modern markets could never handle ceremonial valuables. Polanyi, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 8

Redistribution and centricity

Redistribution collects products at a centre, stores them and reallocates them. Centricity is the institutional arrangement that makes the centre available: a chief, temple, court or administration. Hunters sharing through a headman, Trobriand chief stores supporting feasts/expeditions, and large ancient granary systems are different scales and political forms of the principle. Redistribution can connect geographically specialized producers. Polanyi, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 6–10

It need not imply equality or voluntary cooperation. A chief may create dependency through gifts; a despot may collect tribute by coercion. Polanyi's “communistic” description of ancient household-like distribution explicitly permits sharply graded rations. His second use rejects the simplistic attribution of an innate communistic psychology to early people. The adjective therefore does not certify modern egalitarian communism. Polanyi, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 2, 9–10

Householding and production for use

Householding means producing and storing for a group's own use, with a closed-group/self-sufficiency pattern. The group can be a family, village or manor, with democratic or despotic internal relations. Polanyi rejects an isolated self-sufficient “savage” as the universal original economic unit; household provision develops within social organization. Polanyi, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 11

Aristotle's distinction between household provisioning and unlimited money-making supplies the interpretive contrast. Selling an incidental surplus need not transform a household into production organized primarily for gain. Polanyi recognizes that Greek commerce, loans, insurance and banking were highly developed, even while he argues that market organization did not govern the whole social economy. The presence of money is therefore insufficient to classify the whole system. Polanyi, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 11–12

The chapter characterizes the Greco-Roman economy as householding combined with large-scale grain redistribution. Feudal arrangements likewise combine collection, tribute, protection and distribution, often with exploitation and unequal status. Its conclusion groups premodern economies under combinations of reciprocity, redistribution and householding. Sixteenth-century mercantilist governments made markets important objects of regulation; that is still different from a nineteenth-century ideal of a self-regulating market. These broad historical propositions remain attributed to Polanyi, rather than presented as uncontested findings from a newly audited history literature. Polanyi, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 9–13

The 1920 Trobriand report

The two-page Nature item reports Malinowski's presentation to the Royal Anthropological Institute and the subsequent discussion. It rejects a view of Indigenous economies as merely individual subsistence. In its account, organized agriculture depends on chief authority and garden magic: the chief allocates land and finances communal work, while the magician directs ceremonial stages. Kayasa organizes communal gardening, fishing, construction, sports and games through announced enterprises and feasts. Trobriand report (1920), physical PDF pp. 1

Producers receive a share, while chiefly collection—reported as about 30–50% of tribal wealth—supports collective projects and accumulation of ceremonial valuables made by dependent specialists. The report distinguishes a common measure of value, tokens of stored wealth and a general medium of exchange; it says no single article performs the latter role in the described setting. Gift/counter-gift obligations also support authority, warfare/peace and penalties. This reinforces the connection between political organization and economic institutions, not an image of a society without power or conflict. Trobriand report (1920), physical PDF pp. 1

The Kula description emphasizes opposite-direction circulation, temporary ownership and repeated overseas expeditions. In discussion, Seligman asks whether elaborate garden organization depends on chiefs; Malinowski replies that Southern Massim/Dobu garden magic existed without the same elaborate distribution. Frazer, Routledge and Ray offer comparative comments about agriculture, magic and chiefly origin, which remain discussion suggestions rather than settled causal tests. Unrelated material on fungi/canvas and scientific services printed around the article is outside the academic item and is not imported into course notes. Trobriand report (1920), physical PDF pp. 1–2

Traditional systems matter here because they expose the institutional assumptions behind apparently universal economic motives. The lecture then asks how “new traditional” movements might combine modern technology with religiously derived social organization. That is an ideal/political perspective with diverse forms, not proof that a complete third system has been realized everywhere. Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 24–26

The lecture locates the islands surrounding the Kula network. The spatial figure supplies context for the opposite directions of ceremonial circulation; the diagram does not label every exchange as ordinary barter. Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 18

sections.html:
O015-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: A hypothetical network includes paired coastal kin: paired families send produce with delayed returns; central granaries: a chief collects stores and distributes unequal rations for expeditions; garden households: a household produces for use and sells occasional surplus. Classify principles and institutional patterns; distinguish exchange/money from a self-regulating market economy. Explain incentives/power, Kula circulation/prestige/ownership and the 1920 report’s agriculture, kayasa, collection and value instruments. Do gifts imply egalitarian socialism or modern machines determine one system?

Complete solution and essential rubric: paired coastal kin is reciprocity supported by symmetry and recognized partners; delayed network obligations differ from immediate spot barter. central granaries is redistribution supported by centricity and can be coercive/unequal. garden households is householding within a group, compatible with incidental surplus sales. Trade, money and specialization can exist without prices organizing the whole economy. Polanyi’s attributed historical thesis does not deny all premodern trade or individual motives. Reputation, status, kinship, obligations and sanctions coordinate effort; no innate communist psychology follows. Kula links at least 18 island communities: red necklaces circulate clockwise, white arm-shells counterclockwise; simplified north/south labels are not global compass rules. Prestige/history and temporary ownership give objects social value; ritual voyages and returns can span years. The 1920 report links agriculture to chief authority/garden magic, kayasa to announced communal enterprises and feasts, and roughly 30–50% chiefly collection to projects and dependent specialists. A measure of value or store of wealth need not be a general medium of exchange; the report denies a single general-medium article there. The discussion’s Southern Massim/Dobu contrast shows garden magic without identical elaborate distribution; comments are not causal tests. Other institutions can coordinate complex exchange, without proving markets could never handle ceremonial goods. Modern technology does not select one ownership/allocation model, and chiefly gifts need not be egalitarian or voluntary. interactions.prompt_html:
O015-I1

O015-I1, item_version 1, full_capability_check. Prompt: A visitor sees ceremonial shell valuables circulating for years without bargaining, ordinary goods bought on another market, unequal chief-organized grain distributions and families selling occasional surplus from production for use. She says the shells are valueless, every gift is spot barter and the presence of a market proves a self-regulating market economy. Diagnose these claims, classifying all three Polanyi principles and their supporting patterns. Reconstruct the Kula directions/ownership/history and explain how the 1920 report’s agriculture, kayasa, chiefly collection and value instruments relate to power. Distinguish source interpretation from a claim of universal altruism or modern egalitarian socialism.
interactions.solution_html:
Complete solution and essential rubric: The visitor confuses practical use with social value: Kula objects carry prestige and histories, with temporary ownership and delayed ritual returns. Red shell-disc necklaces move clockwise and white arm-shells counterclockwise across at least 18 island communities; local north/south simplifications are not global compass rules. Such reciprocal obligations rely on symmetry/recognized partners, not immediate bargained barter. Chiefly grain collection and reallocation are redistribution supported by centricity and can be unequal/coercive. Family production for its own use is householding with a closed-group pattern; incidental sales do not automatically make gain the organizing aim. A market for ordinary goods establishes exchange, not that prices govern economic life as a whole. The 1920 report links organized gardening to chief authority/garden magic and kayasa to announced communal enterprises and feasts. Its roughly 30–50%chiefly collection supports projects and dependent specialists and is not an equality measure. A common value measure or stored wealth need not be one generally accepted medium of exchange; the report finds no single general-medium article there. Its Southern Massim/Dobu discussion separates garden magic from identical elaborate chiefly distribution, not a causal test. Reputation, obligations, sanctions and power coordinate work without universal altruism; Polanyi rejects simple capitalist or communist psychologies. These attributed historical mechanisms neither prove modern egalitarian socialism nor deny that markets could handle ceremonial objects. Require each visitor-claim correction, all principles/patterns and Kula/report/power qualifications.

I1/I2 are immediate checks; D1/D2 are distinct parallel variants reserved where possible for delayed checks. A delayed success requires an unused form before recap, no help/solution access, and at least 24 actual elapsed hours after acquisition and the most recent relevant teaching/solution exposure. Record intervening exposure. A calendar-date change alone is insufficient; an early D attempt is immediate evidence only.

interactions.prompt_html:
O015-I2

O015-I2, item_version 1, full_capability_check. Prompt: A comparative account describes garden magic in a community without the Trobriands’ elaborate chiefly distribution, then concludes that magic alone causes central redistribution. Elsewhere a temple collects tribute into stores, two kin groups exchange harvest gifts on delayed obligations, and a manor produces for use while selling incidental excess. The author reverses the Kula directions and calls temporary possession permanent investment ownership. Evaluate the inference and classify each arrangement/pattern; explain the 1920 discussion and kayasa, value instruments and power, and whether complex specialization, money or modern machinery alone establishes a self-regulating market economy.
interactions.solution_html: Complete solution and essential rubric: The reported Southern Massim/Dobu contrast is precisely a warning that garden magic need not entail the same elaborate chiefly distribution; the discussion supplies comparison/questions, not a magic-causes-redistribution test. Temple tribute collection/storage/reallocation is redistribution with centricity; delayed kin-group obligations are reciprocity with symmetry; manor production for its own group is householding, not converted automatically by occasional surplus sales. None requires equality or voluntary relations. Kayasa coordinates announced communal work/enterprises through feasts; the 1920 report links chief land allocation/financing and garden ceremonial organization, and reports roughly 30–50%chiefly collection supporting projects/ceremonial specialists. Value measurement and storing wealth are distinct from a general medium; no single article performs the latter universally there. Correct Kula to red necklaces clockwise and white arm-shells counterclockwise; objects circulate over years, have histories/prestige and temporary rather than permanent exclusive possession. Opposite ritual circulation is not just immediate barter or proof of no social value. Specialized exchange and developed money/markets can coexist with householding/redistribution/reciprocity; self-regulating market organization concerns what governs the whole system. Machinery does not choose an institutional form or universal motive. Polanyi’s broad historical thesis and the 1920 discussion remain attributed, while chiefs, tribute and dependency make power/inequality visible rather than certifying communal egalitarianism. Require the false causal/ownership/direction corrections and complete institutional/whole-system contrast.

interactions.prompt_html:
O015-D1

O015-D1, item_version 1, full_capability_check. Prompt: An ethnographer declares a prestige object “general money” because participants use it to compare values and preserve wealth, although sellers do not accept it generally for ordinary goods. Her notes also record paired obligations between villages, compulsory collection by a ruler, and household provisioning supplemented by occasional sales. She argues that an object’s limited practical use means it cannot coordinate complex exchange, and that adopting modern boats would necessarily turn the system into market capitalism. Assess the claims using all three principles/patterns, the Kula mechanism and 1920 Trobriand organization/discussion; separate attribution, power and whole-system organization.
interactions.solution_html: Complete solution and essential rubric: A unit of comparison and a store of wealth do not by themselves establish a generally accepted medium of exchange; the observed refusal for ordinary goods directly defeats that inference. The 1920 report makes those functions distinct and describes no single general-medium article. Paired continuing village obligations exemplify reciprocity/symmetry; compulsory collection and reallocation exemplify redistribution/centricity, with coercion possible; household provisioning is production for group use/closed-group self-sufficiency, compatible with incidental sales. Kula valuables can coordinate prestige relations and risky voyages despite limited practical use: red necklaces move clockwise, white arm-shells counterclockwise, temporarily possessed with histories and delayed returns over years. At least 18 island communities demonstrate network complexity, not universal barter or altruism. The report’s chief allocates land/finances communal work, garden magic organizes stages, and kayasa announces collective enterprises/feasts; reported 30–50%collection supports projects and dependent specialists, showing authority rather than equal ownership. Its discussion notes garden magic without the same distribution elsewhere, so no one-factor origin claim follows. Modern boats change technology, not logically the ownership/allocation/obligation rules; complex exchange or some markets do not establish a whole self-regulating market economy. Polanyi’s attributed history permits mixed principles and rejects a simple innate communist psychology. Require the money-function test, every institutional classification, prestige/organization reasoning and limits on technological or egalitarian conclusions.

interactions.prompt_html:
O015-D2

O015-D2, item_version 1, full_capability_check. Prompt: A textbook summary quotes Polanyi’s word “communistic” and infers that all premodern economies had equal rations, no markets and no individual status motives. It also says Greek banking disproves householding and that ceremonial redistribution cannot support specialization. Construct a corrected comparison using reciprocity/symmetry, redistribution/centricity and householding/production for use, then use Kula and the 1920 report as explicit counterexamples to those inferences. Include circulation directions, possession/value, kayasa/authority, the report’s discussion limits and why neither modern socialism nor a universal motive follows.
interactions.solution_html: Complete solution and essential rubric: The inferences confuse institutional principles, distribution and psychology. Polanyi’s description permits sharply graded rations in household-like central distribution and expressly rejects an innate communist psychology; status, reputation, obligation and sanctions still motivate. Reciprocity relies on recognized symmetric partners and delayed giving/return; redistribution collects/reallocates at a centre and can sustain coercive unequal authority; householding organizes production for the group’s use, not an isolated universal original individual. Incidental selling and sophisticated Greek commerce/loans/insurance/banking can coexist with householding plus grain redistribution, so their presence does not settle whole-system market dominance. Kula spans at least 18 communities with red necklaces clockwise and white arm-shells counterclockwise; temporary possession, prestige/history and delayed ritual voyages show nontrivial coordination without reducing objects to useless goods or spot barter. The 1920 report describes chief land allocation and financed communal work, garden magic, kayasa announced enterprises/feasts and roughly 30–50%collection supporting projects and dependent specialists: specialization can coexist with redistribution. It distinguishes value measure, stored wealth and general exchange medium, finding no single universal article for the latter. The Southern Massim/Dobu discussion raises comparative alternatives rather than proving chiefly power caused all organization. These attributed historical arguments establish neither equal voluntary sharing nor identity with modern socialism; a self-regulating market economy is a distinct organizing claim, and technology alone does not choose it. Require a correction linked to every summary assertion plus all mechanisms and source limits.

sections.title: Motivation, intuition, and definitions

sections.html:
Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Religion and economic organization; fingerprint d251fd4c2dea68517f51f376ccccfd7a1ad3f7b9306eb7b70e46c6ebca9a25f2. Heading depth and required relative figure-path relocation alone are adapted.

Religion and economic organization

Source: Comparative Economics - Islamic Economics and the Economics of Other Religions Source: Week III - lecture - large slides

  • Embedded economies and the proposed “New Traditional Economy”
  • Religious traditions and economic conduct
  • The six lecture reading questions
  • Diversity within the source’s Protestant comparison

The lecture makes traditional organization and its possible modern revival a core comparison. Definitions of embeddedness in Embedded economies and the Kula ring explain why modern technology need not determine one set of social obligations.

Embedded economies and the proposed “New Traditional Economy”

Rosser and Rosser use Karl Polanyi’s idea of embeddedness to distinguish economic organization. In market and command systems, they say, production and distribution decisions are largely made on economic grounds; in traditional economies, decisions are embedded in social and cultural relationships and inherited practices. They identify three “Old Traditional Economy” forms: household sharing, reciprocal gift exchange between groups, and redistribution by a central authority or “Big Man.” The authors note controversy over this taxonomy: formalist economists argue that economies follow universal market principles, while substantivist scholars associated with Polanyi emphasize institutional and cultural variation; another position is that all economies are embedded, but differently. They also qualify Polanyi’s original ordering of household and reciprocal forms. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 85–86.

The “New Traditional Economy” aims to restore religious and social priorities while retaining modern technology. Its advocates present it as a “Third Way” that would combine the efficiency associated with markets, the social concern associated with socialism, and a renewed sense of ethical community. Rosser and Rosser describe this as an aspirational program rather than an established outcome: it looks nostalgically to old communities while seeking to operate in modern settings and use modern communications. The claimed benefits include family and social cohesion; the source also suggests that this can be interpreted as an attempt to build social capital. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 86–87.

Religious traditions and economic conduct

The authors distinguish religious economics—an advocacy program that seeks to organize society according to a religion’s economic teaching—from the economics of religion, the scholarly study of religion’s effects on economic behavior and institutions. Their comparative tour stresses that no single religious tradition yields one uncontested economic model. Teachings, institutions, political movements, historical settings, and interpreters differ within each tradition. Their examples should therefore be read as the authors’ historically situated comparisons, not as exhaustive descriptions of contemporary religions. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 87–88.

In Schumacher’s influential account, Buddhist economics emphasizes spiritual liberation, moderation in consumption, harmony with nature, resource conservation, local production, and self-sufficiency. The authors question whether this ideal describes Buddhism as practiced across diverse societies. They contrast Thailand’s more individualistic religious and market-oriented trajectory with Burmese Buddhist socialism and merit-making practices that may encourage both wealth accumulation and spending on temples rather than productive investment. They also discuss the different political histories of Theravada and Mahayana traditions. The economic implications are presented as varied and historically contingent, not as a single Buddhist prescription. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 88–89.

Confucianism is treated as a philosophy and cultural influence rather than straightforwardly as a religion. Rosser and Rosser outline benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and faithfulness, with particular emphasis on hierarchical relationships and education. They describe mixed historical attitudes toward commerce: some passages permit markets under benevolent rule, while later neo-Confucianism opposed commerce, industrialization, and foreign trade. Modern revivals, in their account, tend to support market activity alongside authoritarian governance and state planning. They present claims that Confucian values foster growth together with concerns about cronyism and corruption, especially in light of the East Asian financial crisis of 1997. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 89–90.

The discussion of Hindu economics centers on caste, village-based specialization, and the jajmani system, then turns to Gandhi’s Hind Swaraj: self-rule and self-sufficiency nationally and locally, village production, restrained consumption, and skepticism toward industrialization and urbanization. Gandhi’s vision included reform of caste practices, especially the oppression of “Untouchables,” while retaining a reformed caste structure. Deendayal Upadhyaya’s later “Integral Humanism” is presented as a New Traditional adaptation that accepts appropriate modern technology while preserving decentralized villages. This is a description of particular thinkers and political tendencies; it must not be taken as an endorsement of caste hierarchy or as a complete account of Hindu thought. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 90–91.

For Judaism, the authors discuss biblical economic rules concerning property, tithes, interest, Sabbath observance, and the Jubilee Year’s debt, land, and emancipation provisions. They describe different modern interpretations, including proposals for redistribution and debt relief, and note that Israel’s economic institutions also reflect secular socialist and state-building influences, not simply religious doctrine. For Christianity, they contrast Aquinas’s just price and opposition to usury; Catholic social teaching’s later support for markets combined with concern about poverty; Christian Democratic welfare-state politics; and Protestant currents ranging from Calvinist associations with capitalism to Anabaptist communalism, the Social Gospel, and divergent American fundamentalist positions. Their box on U.S. Protestant fundamentalism displays internal disagreement between laissez-faire, anti-market, and redistributive views. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 91–94.

The chapter concludes that these examples resist simple religion-to-system mappings. Buddhist traditions range from ecological critique to support for market activity; Confucian-influenced systems combine markets and hierarchy; Hindu economic visions include village self-sufficiency and contested caste reform; Judaic and Christian interpretations range across market, welfare, and redistributive positions. This is the comparative lesson: a tradition can shape economic arguments, but historical institutions and competing interpretations mediate its effects. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 109–110.

Discussion questions and reasoned answers Rosser & Rosser, printed p. 110.

  1. In what sense can Buddhist and Hindu economics support modern “green” movements? Schumacher’s Buddhist economics favors moderate consumption, conservation, harmony with nature, local production, and reduced long-distance transport. Gandhi’s Hindu economic vision favors restrained consumption, self-sufficient villages, and decentralized, appropriate technology. Both can support ecological aims by questioning materialism and resource-intensive growth. The source gives these as intellectual affinities, not evidence that all Buddhist or Hindu communities act uniformly or that the traditions offer identical environmental programs. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 88–91.

  2. Compare Buddhist, Confucian, and Hindu views of the state. The chapter’s Buddhist examples range from individual responsibility under Thai royal reforms to Burmese welfare-state ideals and socialist central planning. Confucian political thought emphasizes benevolent hierarchy, educated elites, order, and—in modern revivals—market activity combined with an authoritarian state and some planning. Gandhi’s model is more decentralized, emphasizing village self-rule and self-sufficiency; Upadhyaya adapts this to modern small-scale technology. These are contrasting cases and thinkers, not universal doctrines. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 88–91.

  3. Compare Judaic, Catholic, Protestant, and Islamic views of market capitalism. Rosser and Rosser present Judaic scripture as containing both market-compatible private-property rules and redistributive or interest restrictions, with contemporary interpretations varying. Catholic thought historically includes just-price and usury concerns, later combines support for markets with social protection, and has Christian Democratic welfare-state expression. Protestant traditions range from Calvinist and fundamentalist pro-market positions to communal, Social Gospel, and redistributive alternatives. The Islamic chapter sections likewise show approval of trade and private property alongside zakat, restrictions on riba and other conduct, and arguments for both market capitalism and redistribution. None of these traditions has one uncontested stance. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 91–94 and 105–110.

  4. Why does Islam seem to have a more fully developed economic system than other major religions? The authors suggest that Islam’s founder Muhammad was a merchant, that the tradition developed a legal framework (Shari’a) with rules relevant to transactions, and that modern Islamic movements have articulated a more explicit program, including zakat, fair dealing, profit-sharing finance, and riba restrictions. They also describe political and institutional reasons for the program’s visibility. This is a claim about the comparative elaboration and public prominence of a modern movement in the authors’ account, not proof that other religions lack economic thought or that Muslims agree on one system. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 87–88, 94–95, 97–100, 101–104.

Limitations and terminology. The chapter’s publication context predates many subsequent developments and uses country labels, political descriptions, demographic claims, and present-tense assertions that are dated. Do not restate its current-sounding numbers, election results, country lists, or claims about political conditions as current facts. The source itself notes scholarly disputes over Polanyi’s categories and diversity within religious traditions. Older terms such as “Hinayana,” “Mohammedan,” “fundamentalist,” and some country/place names require attribution and care; use contemporary neutral labels in explanatory prose while retaining historical source wording only when necessary. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 85–110.

The six lecture reading questions

Schumacher and environmentalism: moderation, local production, reduced transport, conservation and respect for nonrenewable resources explain the affinity. The ideal does not establish that every Buddhist economy implements it. Rosser & Rosser, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 3–5

Crucial Confucian elements: benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom and faithfulness; relationships of hierarchical duty, educated leadership and reciprocal obligations, with benevolent rule rather than an automatic commitment to one ownership system. The chapter contrasts older anti-commercial currents with modern market/authoritarian combinations. Rosser & Rosser, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 5–6

Jajmani: a local, relatively self-sufficient village arrangement in which hereditary caste-based occupations provide complementary goods/services through a stable division of labour and customary relations. It is neither simply a freely entered modern labour contract nor identical to every form of Indian village organization. Rosser & Rosser, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 6

Jubilee: the chapter connects seven Sabbath-year cycles (49 years) to a Jubilee, when property returns to its original owner and recently acquired slaves are freed, including debt release. Modern proposals extend this idea to debt relief, but the biblical rule and a contemporary policy are distinct. The source uses the 49-year cycle; do not confuse it with an annual tax or claim it describes actual current practice. Rosser & Rosser, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 7–8

Judaism and interest: the chapter reports a restriction on charging interest among Jews with a different rule for lending to non-Jews, plus a footnoted qualification for destitute borrowers. Describe the distinction and interpretive context; “all interest everywhere forbidden by Judaism” would erase the supplied rule’s boundary. Rosser & Rosser, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 7

Aristotle’s ideas in Christianity: the chapter identifies a just price and an abhorrence of interest as ideas Aquinas reconciled with Christian theology. This historically situated synthesis is different from a claim that every Christian movement has adopted one identical stance on finance. Rosser & Rosser, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 8

The Week III assignment asks for oral discussion rather than written submission. Its alternative Rosser–Rosser title is a reading lead, not a second supplied chapter audited here. Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 3

Diversity within the source’s Protestant comparison

Position in Box 4-1 Economic stance described in the historical source
Strict fundamentalists Avoid extensive political/economic theorizing or emphasize individual spiritual conduct.
New Christian Right Endorse a pro-market Chicago-style approach alongside moral/religious political aims.
Christian Reconstructionists Prefer an Austrian/libertarian framework, a flat tax and gold-based money, oppose income redistribution and broad state intervention.
Evangelical left Accept markets more conditionally and support greater redistribution on the basis of social concern.
Radical evangelicalism Advocates a socialist alternative.

These are the authors’ categories and examples, not an exhaustive contemporary typology. Their variation is the point: a religious label alone does not identify a policy package. Rosser & Rosser, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 10
sections.title: Explanation steps

sections.html:
O016-W1, item_version 1, worked_example. Prompt: A hypothetical movement proposes community obligations and modest consumption while retaining modern communications. Explain New Traditional aspirations and embeddedness debates, religious economics versus economics of religion, the six lecture prompts (Schumacher, Confucian elements, jajmani, Jubilee, Judaism/interest, Aristotle/Aquinas), environmental/state contrasts and market interpretations across religions. Explain the Protestant comparison and why a label does not identify a current policy bundle.

Complete solution and essential rubric: The movement seeks religious/social re-embedding with modern technology: an aspirational Third Way, not proven efficiency, equality or cohesion. Religious economics advocates a normative program; economics of religion studies behaviour/institutions. Formalists emphasize universal market principles, substantivists institutional variation, and another position says all economies are embedded differently. Schumacher’s moderation, local production, conservation and reduced transport, and Gandhi’s restrained consumption/village self-rule, give environmental affinities rather than uniform religious conduct. Confucian elements are benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom and faithfulness with hierarchy, reciprocal duty and education; older anti-commercial and modern market/authoritarian positions differ. Jajmani is hereditary caste-linked village specialization/customary exchange, not a freely entered modern labour contract. Gandhi sought reform of oppression with a reformed caste structure; Upadhyaya accepted appropriate modern technology. Jubilee follows seven Sabbath-year cycles/49 years and concerns restoration, debt and emancipation, not an annual tax or universal present practice. The chapter reports differing interest rules for in-group/out-group, with a destitute-borrower qualification; no uniform all-interest prohibition follows. Aquinas reconciled just-price and anti-usury ideas with Christianity; later Catholic teaching combines markets and social protection. Buddhist state examples range from Thai individualism to Burmese welfare/socialism; Confucian hierarchy differs from Gandhi’s decentralization. O016-I1

O016-I1, item_version 1, full_capability_check. Prompt: A modern ethical charter proposes local low-resource production with advanced communications.
