Complete solution and essential rubric: The charter can express New Traditional aspirations: restored ethical/social priorities with modern technology, not a demonstrated efficient/equal Third Way. Religious economics advocates the program, whereas economics of religion analyses behaviour/institutions. Formalists emphasize universal market principles, substantivists institutional/cultural variation, and another view sees all economies embedded differently. Schumacher’s moderation, conservation, local production and reduced transport contradict maximal-consumption language and give an environmental affinity; Gandhi’s restraint/village self-rule has a related but distinct affinity, not uniform Buddhist/Hindu conduct. Confucian benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom and faithfulness emphasize hierarchy/reciprocal duty/education; older anti-commercial and modern market/authoritarian currents refute always-bans-markets. Jajmani is hereditary caste-linked complementary village occupations/customary exchange, not freely chosen modern employment; Gandhi’s reformed caste vision and Upadhyaya’s appropriate technology remain specific programs. Aquinas reconciled Aristotelian just price/anti-usury with Christianity; later Catholic market/social-protection positions differ. Buddhist state examples vary Thai individualism/Burmese planning, Confucian educated hierarchy differs from Gandhian decentralization, and Judaic/Christian/Islamic property/redistribution arguments vary. O016-I2

O016-I2, item_version 1, full_capability_check. Prompt: An archive juxtaposes Thai market-oriented examples with Burmese Buddhist planning; older anti-commercial Confucian passages with modern market/authoritarian combinations; Gandhi’s village ideal with Upadhyaya’s modern appropriate technology; and a contemporary debt-relief proposal inspired by Jubilee. A researcher concludes these contrasts are transcription mistakes because each religion must imply one policy. Explain each contrast, including Schumacher’s environmental mechanism, the five Confucian virtues, jajmani’s institutional form, the 49-year Jubilee rule versus modern proposal, the Judaism interest boundary and Aquinas’s Aristotelian synthesis. Locate the study/program distinction and New Traditional/embeddedness debate; test the one-policy thesis with the Protestant box and other market/state interpretations.
interactions.solution_html: Complete solution and essential rubric: The contrasts are the chapter’s evidence of competing historically situated interpretations, not contradictions removable by selecting one true policy label. Thai and Burmese examples show differing Buddhist state/economic paths; Schumacher’s moderation, conservation/local production and reduced transport are an ideal with green affinity, not a description of all practice. Confucian benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom and faithfulness combine hierarchy, education and reciprocal obligations; old anti-commerce and modern market/planning mixtures are distinct currents. Gandhi’s restrained, self-governing village ideal and Upadhyaya’s appropriate modern technology differ without making hereditary caste-based jajmani a free modern contract. A Jubilee-inspired debt proposal is a new policy application; the source’s seven Sabbath cycles/49-year restoration, debt/emancipation rule is neither an annual tax nor proof current universal practice. Its Judaism lending distinction is in-/out-group with a destitute qualification, while Aquinas reconciles Aristotle’s just price and anti-usury with Christianity, not every later Christian view. Economics of religion analyses these effects; religious economics advocates a normative organization. New Traditional advocates seek ethical community with modern technology, an aspiration rather than proven synthesis. Formalists stress universal market principles, substantivists institutional variation and an alternative all-embedded view differing forms. Protestant Box 4-1 supplies spiritual-focus, pro-market New Christian Right, libertarian Reconstructionist, redistributive evangelical left and socialist alternatives; Judaic property/redistribution, Catholic markets/social protection and Islamic trade/property with zakat/riba constraints likewise resist one mapping. No current country/rule follows from dated examples. Require explanation of every archive contrast, all six reading mechanisms and the normative/analytic/diversity boundaries.

O016-D1

O016-D1, item_version 1, full_capability_check. Prompt: A grant committee must assess a village project combining modern small-scale machinery, customary reciprocal services and an ethical claim of restrained consumption. One reviewer calls it automatically an efficient New Traditional Third Way; another says hereditary occupations are free contracts because money sometimes changes hands. A financial annex treats every Jubilee-inspired debt cancellation as the chapter’s actual annual rule and charges that Aquinas and every Protestant share one pro-market interest doctrine. Give an evidence-based assessment: distinguish advocacy from analysis and embedding debates; address Schumacher/green affinity, Confucian virtues/state variation, jajmani, Jubilee, the Judaism lending boundary and Aristotle/Aquinas. Use the source’s religious/state/market contrasts and Protestant box to specify which conclusions the committee cannot infer.
interactions.solution_html: Complete solution and essential rubric: The project resembles an aspiration to re-embed modern production in social/ethical priorities, but machinery plus community aims does not demonstrate efficiency, equality or social-capital outcomes. Advocacy is religious economics; analysing its consequences is economics of religion. Formalist universal-market, substantivist institution-sensitive and all-economies-differently-embedded positions disagree about interpretation, so exchanging some money does not settle the organizing institution. Schumacher’s moderation, conservation/local production/reduced transport and Gandhi’s restraint/decentralization give ecological affinities, not measured project success. Confucian benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, faithfulness, reciprocal hierarchy and educated leadership do not choose one ownership model; older anti-commerce and modern market/authoritarian cases differ, as do Thai/Burmese Buddhist state paths. Jajmani’s hereditary caste-linked complementary services differ from a freely entered wage contract even with payments; Gandhi’s reform and Upadhyaya’s appropriate technology are specific visions. Jubilee’s seven Sabbath cycles/49-year restoration/debt/emancipation differs from annual cancellation or any contemporary policy. The chapter’s Judaism interest rules distinguish in-/out-group with a destitute-borrower qualification. Aquinas’s Aristotelian just-price/anti-usury synthesis cannot be equated with all later Christian markets/social protection or Protestant positions. Box 4-1 contrasts spiritual-focus, pro-market New Christian Right, libertarian Reconstructionist, evangelical left redistribution and radical socialism; Judaic, Catholic and Islamic interpretations also combine property/trade and social obligations differently. Require the project/annex-specific corrections, all six concepts, study-versus-program/embeddedness distinctions and explicit historical/diversity limits; no universal current policy conclusion follows.

interactions.prompt_html:
O016-D2

O016-D2, item_version 1, full_capability_check. Prompt: A forecasting memo quotes largely correct source details but makes new deductions: Schumacher’s conservation ideal allegedly proves every Buddhist state achieves green outcomes; Confucian educated hierarchy allegedly selects private ownership alone; Upadhyaya’s acceptance of appropriate technology allegedly makes his program identical to Gandhi’s; a 49-year Jubilee account allegedly orders cancellation of every present loan today; reported variation in Judaism allegedly means the chapter supplies no lending boundary at all; and Aquinas’s anti-usury synthesis allegedly makes later Catholic acceptance of markets impossible. Evaluate all six deductions. In evaluating the third deduction, define jajmani and explain whether adopting modern technology by itself converts hereditary village services into freely entered wage contracts. Compare the state/market alternatives and Protestant box; distinguish study from advocacy and New Traditional aspirations/embedding debates. Finally assess whether Islamic economics’ visibility establishes exclusive economic thought or a predictable present policy ranking.
interactions.solution_html: Complete solution and essential rubric: The memo confuses a source definition, an advocated ideal, a historical institution and an empirical forecast. Schumacher’s moderation, conservation, local production and reduced transport have green affinities, but Buddhist practice/state forms vary, including Thai individualistic/market and Burmese welfare/planning examples; no measured universal outcome follows. Confucian benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom and faithfulness with education/hierarchical reciprocity do not select private ownership: older anti-commerce and modern market/authoritarian mixtures differ. Upadhyaya’s appropriate modern technology is an adaptation, not identity with Gandhi’s restrained self-governing village ideal; jajmani remains hereditary caste-linked complementary village services, not necessarily voluntary modern employment. Installing modern technology does not by itself change inherited obligations or freedom to enter and leave a wage contract; the institutional terms must actually change. The chapter’s seven Sabbath-year cycles/49-year Jubilee concerns restoration/debt/emancipation; it does not itself issue a present legal instruction for every loan or define an annual tax. Interpretive variation does not erase the reported Judaism in-group/out-group interest distinction and destitute-borrower qualification. Aquinas’s Aristotelian just-price/anti-usury synthesis is historically distinct from later Catholic markets with social protection. Protestant Box 4-1 likewise spans spiritual focus, pro-market New Christian Right, libertarian Reconstructionists, evangelical left redistribution and radical socialism; Judaic/Christian/Islamic property and welfare arguments resist a single ranking. Religious economics advocates a normative program; economics of religion studies its effects. Formalist universal-market, substantivist institutional and all-economies-differently-embedded positions frame the disagreement. New Traditional movements seek ethical re-embedding with modern technology, an aspiration rather than demonstrated Third Way benefits. The authors’ merchant/legal/modern-movement account explains Islamic economics’ comparative visibility, not exclusive economic thought or unanimity. Require a separate reason rejecting each memo deduction, the six underlying concepts, historical/state/market contrasts and bounded source/current-policy distinction.

sections.html:
Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Trade, protection and historical Islam; fingerprint 032f26f0359d18357f1a3a165f3d83f86d6e698b9c2e75d6f4a468ed05f10d70. Heading depth and required relative figure-path relocation alone are adapted.

Trade, protection and historical Islam

Source: ADDITIONAL - Bernstein - chapter 3 Source: Week III - lecture - large slides

  • Trade infrastructure before Islam
  • The political problem of exchange
  • Muhammad, early Islam, and commercial norms
  • Political consolidation and commercial networks
  • Commercial instruments in the lecture

Bernstein’s supplied additional excerpt supplies historical context for the lecture’s links between commerce, political protection and Islam. It is interpretive background rather than a timeless account of religious conduct.

Trade infrastructure before Islam

Bernstein’s chapter begins with the camel as a transport technology that made long-distance exchange across arid regions practicable. The camel’s evolutionary adaptation to dry climates, its domestication, capacity to carry heavy loads, and development of specialized saddles together made it more useful than a donkey for bulk transport across trackless desert. The account contrasts dromedaries, Bactrians, and strong first-generation hybrids used along routes linking the Middle East and Central Asia. It emphasizes that trade capacity depended on animal biology, breeding, equipment, water access, and terrain rather than on distance alone: caravanserais and oases constrained routes, while steep mountain passes still required donkeys. Bernstein, supplied chapter 3, physical PDF pp. 1–5

The Arabian incense trade illustrates how a valuable export can support a long supply chain. Frankincense and myrrh from the relatively fertile southwest of Arabia and neighboring Somalia served ritual, medicinal, cosmetic, and other uses in ancient markets. Harvest season and monsoon timing affected the choice between camel caravans and sea transport. The text describes local production, protective packaging, caravan services, intermediary markets, transit charges, and destination demand as linked stages in the trade. It also presents evidence of organized market exchange: the “silent trade” described by Theophrastus, in which sellers left measured goods and marked prices for merchants, with a priest taking a stated share. Bernstein, supplied chapter 3, physical PDF pp. 5–12

Geography, political control, and transaction costs shaped the commodity’s route. The account traces incense through Shabwah and Thomna toward Gaza and Mediterranean markets, describing tolls, gate control, guards, water, fodder, lodging, and protection payments. It contrasts relatively trusting transactions at the production end with costly controls and theft prevention at processing and consumer centers. Under Roman rule, some routes became safer and cheaper, while demand and cultivation patterns changed. The author estimates large trade volumes and compares costs, prices, wages, and revenues using ancient monetary units. These are the author’s reported historical calculations, not contemporary values or independently updated estimates. Bernstein, supplied chapter 3, physical PDF pp. 8–14

The political problem of exchange

Bernstein frames the desert economy through a “trade, protect, or raid” trilemma: where enforceable authority is absent, a trader must secure a route and cargo, or risk predation. In his account, family and tribal ties supplied protection in a setting with weak central authority. Collective responsibility and retaliatory violence could deter attacks, but also perpetuate cycles of revenge and insecurity. Raiding, called ghazu, could become an economic strategy when no authority beyond the tribe protected trade. This is the author’s broad explanatory frame, not a universal law of desert societies or an adequate description of present-day Muslim societies. Bernstein, supplied chapter 3, physical PDF pp. 14–15

Mecca’s rise as a commercial center is presented as uncertain. The text notes competing explanations: its relative position between larger powers, the possibility that the principal incense route bypassed it, its dependence on agricultural production at Taif, and the commercial and pilgrimage activity surrounding the Kaaba and nearby shrines. Bernstein describes Quraish leaders as making trade safer and more profitable by taxing merchants and selling safe conduct, shifting incentives away from raiding. This links political organization to the provision of protection and to the growth of exchange. Keep the uncertainty explicit: the source does not establish that Mecca sat on the main incense route or that incense alone caused its prosperity. Bernstein, supplied chapter 3, physical PDF pp. 15–16

Muhammad, early Islam, and commercial norms

Bernstein situates Islam’s emergence in a changing commercial and political setting. His narrative presents Muhammad as having merchant experience, including work for Khadija’s trading enterprise, and stresses that Islamic texts and traditions contain guidance on consensual exchange, truthful disclosure of defects, and fair dealing. The author connects these commercial norms to the religious community’s institutional unity. The historical details about Muhammad’s early life are qualified in the source: it says the surviving written biographies appeared more than a century after his death and that the historical record is uncertain. Treat the chapter as a historical interpretation, not as a settled account of Islamic doctrine or as a religious authority. Bernstein, supplied chapter 3, physical PDF pp. 16–19

The account of early expansion combines religious conversion, military conquest, and economic redistribution. Bernstein describes raids on caravans after the migration from Mecca to Medina, the treatment of conquered property, and the allocation of a share to the community and the remainder to participants. He argues that conversion and conquest together expanded the boundaries of the new polity. This passage is the author’s interpretation and is phrased in sweeping terms, including claims about relations with nonbelievers; it should not be turned into a timeless rule about Islam or Muslims. The text itself notes peaceful conversion as a distinct route of expansion. Bernstein, supplied chapter 3, physical PDF pp. 19–20

Political consolidation and commercial networks

The early caliphates are shown as both political powers and organizers of routes and supplies. The text describes efforts to move Egyptian grain to Arabia, including a Nile–Red Sea canal project and the strategic decision not to extend it to the Mediterranean. It recounts the Battle of the Masts in 655, the subsequent growth of Muslim naval control, and expansion into North Africa, Spain, Mediterranean islands, and Central Asia. These events connect trade to food security, naval capacity, and control over ports and sea lanes. A source-based map of incense lands and routes appears earlier in the chapter; a second teaching diagram could map the Red Sea, Persian Gulf, and Silk Road as an integrated network under the early caliphates. Bernstein, supplied chapter 3, physical PDF pp. 20–22

Bernstein characterizes the Umayyad and Abbasid domains as a large commercial zone in which barriers were reduced and the Red Sea, Persian Gulf, and Silk Road functioned as connected routes. He associates this network with Muslim seafaring, Arabic as a lingua franca, long-distance connections to China, Scandinavia, and sub-Saharan Africa, and the movement of goods such as gold, ivory, furs, amber, silk, pepper, and metalwork. He also notes an intellectual and cultural flourishing centered in cities including Damascus, Baghdad, and Cordova. The account does not imply that political unity produced frictionless trade or equal access for all populations. It explicitly says that the “Pax Islamica” was not an unmixed blessing: the Mediterranean could become a frontier of conflict, and the source describes a shift in the boundaries between Occident and Orient. Bernstein, supplied chapter 3, physical PDF pp. 22–23

The closing pages note a distinction between sophisticated commercial practices and state financial institutions: Bernstein says Muslim commercial networks used bills of exchange, lending arrangements, and futures markets, while no Islamic state established a national or central bank. He then traces later challenges to the commercial order, including Christian reconquest, Crusades, Mongol invasions, plague, and European entry into the Indian Ocean, while noting that Muslim traders remained important in long-distance trade into the early modern period. This is a historical narrative of changing routes and political conditions, not a claim that one factor alone explains later economic outcomes. Bernstein, supplied chapter 3, physical PDF pp. 23

Interpretive cautions. The chapter uses a vivid, sometimes polemical narrative voice and offers broad claims about tribal life, raiding, religious motivation, conquest, and economic decline. Present these as Bernstein’s explanatory propositions, preserve qualifications and contested points, and do not generalize them to all Muslim societies or the present. The text itself calls Mecca’s commercial importance and route position uncertain. Historical quotations and numerical estimates (including camel capacities, population counts, trade volumes, prices, wages, and silver outflows) are source-period claims; retain their attribution and dates rather than presenting them as current or independently verified. The chapter excerpt ends mid-book and contains no end-of-chapter discussion questions. Bernstein, supplied chapter 3, physical PDF pp. 1–23

The supplied incense-route map locates production areas, caravan routes and maritime alternatives. Read it alongside the chapter’s explicit uncertainty about whether the principal route passed Mecca. Bernstein, supplied chapter 3, physical PDF pp. 10

The Week III map depicts the medieval trade network. The associated three-route argument links the Red Sea, Persian Gulf and Silk Road; a map of connections alone does not measure trade volumes or prove a single cause of later decline. Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 31

Commercial instruments in the lecture

The lecture adds historical terms from Irfan (2015): suftaja as a transferable money order, hawala as a credit/transfer arrangement, sakk as an early cheque-like written instruction, musharaka as partnership and mudarabah as capital–management profit sharing. The lecture relates these instruments to extensive trading networks and later financial practices. Its genealogy is a reported historical interpretation; the supplied chapter does not establish an exact one-to-one invention lineage for every modern instrument. Distinguish that history from the contract mechanisms explained in Islamic finance and institutional diversity. Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 28–34

sections.html:
Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Islamic finance and institutional diversity; fingerprint 01147e8ee729e8caeb0839c93797a7233d349875f87f720597d5609822c4c504. Heading depth and required relative figure-path relocation alone are adapted.

Islamic finance and institutional diversity

Source: Comparative Economics - Islamic Economics and the Economics of Other Religions Source: Week III - lecture - large slides

  • Historical setting and diversity of Islamic interpretation
  • Chronology, succession and interpretation
  • Foundational principles and obligations
  • Gharar, qirad, and the problem of risk
  • Riba, competing economic arguments, and banking practice
  • Property, capitalism, socialism, and unresolved outcomes
  • Contract mechanisms, securities and the lecture’s corrections
  • Risk, liquidity and dated industry evidence

The lecture gives Islamic finance a central role in the proposed new traditional economy. The contract mechanisms need the broader distinction between ethical programs and observed institutions explained in Religion and economic organization.

Historical setting and diversity of Islamic interpretation

Rosser and Rosser begin the Islamic discussion with Muhammad’s life, the early community, the caliphate, and the development of the Qur’an, Hadith, and Shari’a. They describe the spread of Islam through conversion and political expansion and the later rise of multiple legal schools. They stress that even accepted foundational sources admit varying interpretations of economic questions, including differences between Shari’a schools. In the modern era, Islamic economics gained visibility amid anti-colonial nationalism, disappointment with post-independence economic models, concern about sovereignty, oil wealth, and appeals to a shared historical identity. Their account includes broad generalizations and political examples tied to its publication period; retain attribution and historical framing. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 94–99.

Chronology, succession and interpretation

The supplied lecture dates the beginning of Muhammad’s revelations to around 610, as part of the religious tradition it describes. The 622 Hijra—migration to Medina—marks year one of the Islamic calendar and the formation of the umma, a religious, political and economic community. After Muhammad’s death in 632, a caliph was chosen to lead that community without succeeding to prophetic status. The source traces early conquests, a large domain by 644, the confrontation at Tours in 732, and the Abbasid period based in Baghdad after 750, portrayed as a centre of science and commerce. Political fragmentation by the mid-900s did not end religious expansion: the chapter’s 900–1700 account includes conversion under existing rulers, successor-state conquests, and merchant/missionary networks in different regions. These are source-attributed historical sequences; they do not mean all expansion occurred by one mechanism. Physical PDF pp. 29 Physical PDF pp. 10–13

The chapter connects the Sunni–Shi’a distinction to struggles over succession, including Ali, Mu’awiya and the 680 killing of Husayn at Karbala. That conflict concerns political and religious authority, which helps explain why a shared faith need not produce one legal or institutional practice. Its modern population shares and country-political descriptions are dated and are not adopted as present facts. Physical PDF pp. 12

The chapter describes the Qur’an and Hadith as foundational for Shari’a, with interpretation shaped by language, the authenticity of reported sayings, local traditions and legal scholarship. Its four named Sunni schools are Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i and Hanbali. Naming them identifies organized traditions of interpretation; the source’s compressed strict/liberal country rankings are not timeless rules for every financial contract. Physical PDF pp. 11–13

Ijtihad refers here to interpretation/reasoning about new practices. The chapter’s footnote reports the historical “closed gate” thesis after the tenth century and a claimed link to institutional ossification. Treat that as the authors’ reported interpretation: this excerpt does not establish that all subsequent Islamic interpretation universally stopped or that one legal development proves the cause of economic decline. The continuing disagreements about gharar, land rent, banking and property later in the same chapter show why interpretive diversity remains central to the economic analysis. Physical PDF pp. 13

The “New Traditional Islamic Revival” is presented as a movement seeking to re-embed economic life in religious and social obligations while retaining modernity. The authors associate its political prominence with demands for Shari’a-based law and with the search for identity after colonial rule and failed or disappointing alternatives. They mention the oil shocks of the 1970s and the influence of wealthy states in funding movements. This is the authors’ account of political-economic context, not a statement that Islamic revival has one cause or that Muslims uniformly support fundamentalist politics. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 98–100.

Foundational principles and obligations

Three concepts frame the authors’ account of Islamic economics. Tawhid means divine unity and requires economic activity to conform to divine commands. Khilafah means human vicegerency or stewardship in managing the world and its resources, and is associated with universal brotherhood. Adalah means justice and concern for others’ welfare, with cooperation as a principle of organization. Umer Chapra’s proposal of employee stock ownership plans is given as one way to express cooperation. These are the authors’ summary of central concepts; theological and legal interpretations vary. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 100–101.

Zakat is the major positive injunction discussed. The chapter describes it as almsgiving that developed in practice into a religious tax used by Islamic governments for redistribution. It gives a conventional 2.5 percent rate on many forms of wealth above basic needs and higher agricultural rates called ‘ushr or tithe. It notes debate over which assets are covered, how newer forms of wealth should be treated, and how rules differ among legal schools. State-collected zakat is discussed for Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, and Sudan, with divergent assessments of its poverty effects. Zakat should therefore be explained as a religious obligation with historically and legally varied implementation; neither the rate nor outcomes should be presented as uniform or timeless. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 101–102.

Other positive principles include hard work, honest and fair dealing, accurate weights and measures, just wages and prices, and avoidance of waste and conspicuous consumption. The chapter distinguishes these norms from restrictions on consumption and conduct, including pork, non-ritually slaughtered meat, alcohol, prostitution, and gambling. It is describing the authors’ summary of Islamic economic principles, not issuing religious guidance. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 102–103.

Gharar, qirad, and the problem of risk

Gharar is discussed as a prohibition on certain kinds of chance or contractual uncertainty, rooted in the prohibition of gambling. Rosser and Rosser describe later juristic extension of the concept to contracts whose outcomes cannot be predicted, but they also emphasize controversy. Insurance is a central example: some interpretations accept pooled insurance as risk reduction, others classify it as gharar, and a third distinguishes life insurance from other forms. The authors report that these disagreements have led some to favor public insurance. This means gharar should not be simplified as a ban on all uncertainty or all risk-bearing economic activity. Rosser & Rosser, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 18–20

The chapter also describes disagreement about land rent and sharecropping. Some Islamic economists permit both; some oppose all rents; others regard fixed rent as riba but accept sharecropping as a form of qirad or profit-sharing; still others reverse these judgments. This diversity shows that legal conclusions depend on how gharar and riba are defined and applied, not on a single uncontested rule. Rosser & Rosser, printed p. 103.

Qirad denotes accepted profit-sharing in the chapter’s terminology. The authors frame an unresolved boundary between prohibited chance and acceptable shared entrepreneurial risk. They suggest that profit-sharing can be permissible when parties do not seek gratuitous uncertainty and agreements clearly specify how profits and losses are shared. The historical justification they report relies on traditions about the Prophet’s commercial practice rather than a direct Qur’anic rule, and legal schools allow different arrangements. Rosser & Rosser, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 18–20

Mudarabah is presented as a widely recognized form of qirad: a financier supplies money or goods, an entrepreneur manages the enterprise, and profits are split according to an agreed share. The financier bears the loss of invested capital if the venture fails, while the manager loses labor time; any service compensation is specified. This differs from an interest-bearing loan because the return is contingent on realized profits and the investor bears business risk. The chapter notes practical problems: investors may have difficulty verifying reported profits, creating incentives for fraud or misreporting. For this reason, the ideal of profit-and-loss sharing has not always dominated actual Islamic banking. Rosser & Rosser, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 18–20

Riba, competing economic arguments, and banking practice

Riba is treated in the chapter as the prohibition of interest, but the authors distinguish the religious rule from debates over its definition and economic implications. They present arguments made by Islamic economists that interest can transfer income from poorer borrowers to wealthier lenders, encourage rentier behavior, raise costs, and contribute to instability. Some argue that profit-sharing focuses finance on productive enterprise. The authors also summarize theoretical claims that prohibiting interest could reduce inflation or monetary cycles. These are arguments within the literature, not established empirical results. They set out counterarguments: a ban may reduce saving, capital investment, or growth, and eliminating the price of capital creates an allocation problem. They note proposals ranging from central planning to linking zakat to the opportunity cost of capital. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 104–105.

The chapter describes Islamic banking as seeking returns through permitted financing arrangements rather than explicit interest. In the idealized model, depositors become indirect participants in the ventures financed by a bank, for example through mudarabah. In practice, the authors say that murabaha became widely used: a financier purchases goods and resells them to a customer at an agreed higher price payable later. The justification described is that the financier owns the goods and bears some risk during that period. Because the ownership period can be very short, critics argue that this arrangement can closely resemble conventional interest and may undermine the ethical rationale. Murabaha is a cost-plus sale with deferred payment, not profit-sharing; mudarabah is the chapter’s example of profit-sharing. Keep that distinction explicit. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 106–107.

The chapter’s historical examples include Mit Ghamr savings institution (1963), Nasser Social Bank (1972), a Dubai Islamic bank (1975), and the Islamic Development Bank (1975). It discusses growth of Islamic banks across countries and contrasting practices in Iran, Pakistan, and Sudan. It also describes conflicts between banking contracts and legal enforcement in Saudi Arabia, alongside efforts to reconcile conventional banking with religious restrictions. These examples document the chapter’s period and should not be treated as a current inventory of institutions or regulations. The authors say problems with profit reporting, expertise, and bad loans pushed banks toward more predictable financing forms such as murabaha. Their portfolio figures for the Islamic Development Bank illustrate a historical shift away from mudarabah and toward murabaha; they should be attributed as dated data from the cited study. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 106–108.

Property, capitalism, socialism, and unresolved outcomes

The chapter rejects a simple classification of Islam as either capitalist or socialist. It reports that Qur’anic rules support trade and private property, while inheritance rules encourage division of wealth; charitable trusts (waqf) can preserve property across generations. Other Islamic thinkers call for stronger redistribution or public management, drawing on the premise that ultimate ownership belongs to Allah. The authors describe a socialist-oriented tradition and competing interpretations of scriptural passages, including divergent translations. They conclude that Islamic economics may support modified market capitalism, redistribution, or other institutional arrangements depending on political and legal interpretation. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 108–109.

Rosser and Rosser close by juxtaposing Chapra’s optimistic account of a coordinated Islamic socioeconomic program with Timur Kuran’s pessimistic warning that a political project claiming definitive religious answers could become repressive and mistake symbolic changes for reform. They decline to adjudicate between them. This unresolved evaluation matters: the chapter presents Islamic economics as an influential program, not as a proven economic model with settled effects. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 109–110.

Terminology and limits. Use riba for the source’s prohibited interest concept without implying that all contemporary Muslims or jurists define it identically; describe disagreement rather than deciding religious doctrine. Keep gharar bounded to contested forms of avoidable contractual uncertainty and chance rather than equating it with all risk. Keep qirad / mudarabah distinct from murabaha: the former are profit-sharing arrangements; the latter is a deferred-payment cost-plus sale which can approximate interest economically. The chapter repeatedly notes differences across Shari’a schools and interpretations. Its institutional data, laws, country conditions, and political claims are historical and dated; use them as examples from the authors’ period, not as current advice or facts. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 100–110.

Contract mechanisms, securities and the lecture’s corrections

Arrangement Mechanism Return and risk distinction
Mudarabah Investor supplies capital; manager supplies enterprise/management; profits split by agreed shares. Ordinary business capital loss belongs to the investor while the manager loses effort; this does not excuse manager misconduct or negligence.
Murabaha Financier buys an asset and sells it at disclosed cost plus markup, often payable in instalments. A sale obligation replaces a floating share of realized enterprise profit; brief ownership still differs from “no ownership at all.”
Ijara Financier owns an asset and leases its use to the customer. Rent compensates use; a separate purchase/transfer arrangement is needed if ownership will eventually pass to the customer. A lease alone does not automatically transfer title.
Sukuk Certificates represent the relevant ownership/beneficial interests and associated cash flows under their specified structure. The lecture’s rental/profit/redemption example is one arrangement; a certificate is not a universal guarantee of fixed income, principal or direct recourse to the physical asset.
Takaful Cooperative insurance-type risk pooling under the relevant institutional rules. Pooling does not make losses impossible; governance, underwriting and contract interpretation matter.

The lecture’s profit-sharing label “Murababa” conflates spellings: the relevant profit-sharing concept here is mudarabah, while its later mortgage cost-plus sale is murabaha. Its early Egypt date “193–1968” is a typographical truncation: the supplied chapter gives Mit Ghamr 1963, closed in 1968. “Do invest into forbidden” omits the intended negation: the slide’s argument is do not invest in prohibited activities. These corrections follow the chapter’s definitions and the lecture’s own context, rather than silently preserving contradictory labels. Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 38–41 Rosser & Rosser, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 19–23

The IMF Financial Soundness Indicators Compilation Guide (2019), Annex 7.4, §§7.85–7.86 and contract definitions, as actually available in its indexed definition passages, supports the qualification excessive uncertainty and the distinction between ordinary business loss and manager misconduct/negligence. This bounded clarification is not a survey of contemporary law or product compliance.

Risk, liquidity and dated industry evidence

Asset-linked financing, shared business exposure and restrictions on speculation may alter risks, but do not make every Islamic bank or security safer than every conventional one. Cost-plus obligations can resemble debt cash flows, profit-sharing exposes investors to enterprise performance and information problems, and securities can have market, credit and liquidity risks. The lecture’s cited Beck–Demirgüç-Kunt–Merrouche comparison reports stronger capital/asset indicators and crisis performance in its sample, which is an empirical association under that study’s design, not an unconditional theorem of safety. Irfan’s critique concerns divergence between ethical ideals and contracts made to resemble conventional products. Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 42–45

Liquidity management requires assets and facilities whose cash-flow structure is acceptable under the institution’s rules while meeting prudential needs. The Bank of England’s 2 December 2021 announcement, “The Alternative Liquidity Facility,” verifies that its non-interest deposit facility opened to deposits then. Deposits are backed by a fund of high-quality sukuk and earn the fund return net of costs; it complements, rather than removes, a bank’s regulatory liquidity obligations. This is a dated institutional example supporting the lecture, not a statement that a launch announcement in December 2020 and actual deposit opening in December 2021 were the same event.

The slide’s Saudi asset share is labelled 2014. Its S&P figures—10.6% growth in 2024 and sukuk above USD 1 trillion—and UK bank counts belong to the reports cited on the 2025 slide. They are supplied historical claims, not updated 2026 measurements or a verified present inventory. Its reference to a January 2024 Bank of England consultation is likewise a dated lead; the facility-opening fact above has direct bounded verification. The two YouTube references are optional leads, not viewed or imported as additional academic sources. Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 39–46

sections.html:
Source passage

Origin: reused complete checked passage Islamic finance and institutional diversity; fingerprint 01147e8ee729e8caeb0839c93797a7233d349875f87f720597d5609822c4c504. Heading depth and required relative figure-path relocation alone are adapted.

Islamic finance and institutional diversity

Source: Comparative Economics - Islamic Economics and the Economics of Other Religions Source: Week III - lecture - large slides

  • Historical setting and diversity of Islamic interpretation
  • Chronology, succession and interpretation
  • Foundational principles and obligations
  • Gharar, qirad, and the problem of risk
  • Riba, competing economic arguments, and banking practice
  • Property, capitalism, socialism, and unresolved outcomes
  • Contract mechanisms, securities and the lecture’s corrections
  • Risk, liquidity and dated industry evidence

The lecture gives Islamic finance a central role in the proposed new traditional economy. The contract mechanisms need the broader distinction between ethical programs and observed institutions explained in Religion and economic organization.

Historical setting and diversity of Islamic interpretation

Rosser and Rosser begin the Islamic discussion with Muhammad’s life, the early community, the caliphate, and the development of the Qur’an, Hadith, and Shari’a. They describe the spread of Islam through conversion and political expansion and the later rise of multiple legal schools. They stress that even accepted foundational sources admit varying interpretations of economic questions, including differences between Shari’a schools. In the modern era, Islamic economics gained visibility amid anti-colonial nationalism, disappointment with post-independence economic models, concern about sovereignty, oil wealth, and appeals to a shared historical identity. Their account includes broad generalizations and political examples tied to its publication period; retain attribution and historical framing. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 94–99.

Chronology, succession and interpretation

The supplied lecture dates the beginning of Muhammad’s revelations to around 610, as part of the religious tradition it describes. The 622 Hijra—migration to Medina—marks year one of the Islamic calendar and the formation of the umma, a religious, political and economic community. After Muhammad’s death in 632, a caliph was chosen to lead that community without succeeding to prophetic status. The source traces early conquests, a large domain by 644, the confrontation at Tours in 732, and the Abbasid period based in Baghdad after 750, portrayed as a centre of science and commerce. Political fragmentation by the mid-900s did not end religious expansion: the chapter’s 900–1700 account includes conversion under existing rulers, successor-state conquests, and merchant/missionary networks in different regions. These are source-attributed historical sequences; they do not mean all expansion occurred by one mechanism. Physical PDF pp. 29 Physical PDF pp. 10–13

The chapter connects the Sunni–Shi’a distinction to struggles over succession, including Ali, Mu’awiya and the 680 killing of Husayn at Karbala. That conflict concerns political and religious authority, which helps explain why a shared faith need not produce one legal or institutional practice. Its modern population shares and country-political descriptions are dated and are not adopted as present facts. Physical PDF pp. 12

The chapter describes the Qur’an and Hadith as foundational for Shari’a, with interpretation shaped by language, the authenticity of reported sayings, local traditions and legal scholarship. Its four named Sunni schools are Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i and Hanbali. Naming them identifies organized traditions of interpretation; the source’s compressed strict/liberal country rankings are not timeless rules for every financial contract. Physical PDF pp. 11–13

Ijtihad refers here to interpretation/reasoning about new practices. The chapter’s footnote reports the historical “closed gate” thesis after the tenth century and a claimed link to institutional ossification. Treat that as the authors’ reported interpretation: this excerpt does not establish that all subsequent Islamic interpretation universally stopped or that one legal development proves the cause of economic decline. The continuing disagreements about gharar, land rent, banking and property later in the same chapter show why interpretive diversity remains central to the economic analysis. Physical PDF pp. 13

The “New Traditional Islamic Revival” is presented as a movement seeking to re-embed economic life in religious and social obligations while retaining modernity. The authors associate its political prominence with demands for Shari’a-based law and with the search for identity after colonial rule and failed or disappointing alternatives. They mention the oil shocks of the 1970s and the influence of wealthy states in funding movements. This is the authors’ account of political-economic context, not a statement that Islamic revival has one cause or that Muslims uniformly support fundamentalist politics. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 98–100.

Foundational principles and obligations

Three concepts frame the authors’ account of Islamic economics. Tawhid means divine unity and requires economic activity to conform to divine commands. Khilafah means human vicegerency or stewardship in managing the world and its resources, and is associated with universal brotherhood. Adalah means justice and concern for others’ welfare, with cooperation as a principle of organization. Umer Chapra’s proposal of employee stock ownership plans is given as one way to express cooperation. These are the authors’ summary of central concepts; theological and legal interpretations vary. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 100–101.

Zakat is the major positive injunction discussed. The chapter describes it as almsgiving that developed in practice into a religious tax used by Islamic governments for redistribution. It gives a conventional 2.5 percent rate on many forms of wealth above basic needs and higher agricultural rates called ‘ushr or tithe. It notes debate over which assets are covered, how newer forms of wealth should be treated, and how rules differ among legal schools. State-collected zakat is discussed for Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, and Sudan, with divergent assessments of its poverty effects. Zakat should therefore be explained as a religious obligation with historically and legally varied implementation; neither the rate nor outcomes should be presented as uniform or timeless. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 101–102.

Other positive principles include hard work, honest and fair dealing, accurate weights and measures, just wages and prices, and avoidance of waste and conspicuous consumption. The chapter distinguishes these norms from restrictions on consumption and conduct, including pork, non-ritually slaughtered meat, alcohol, prostitution, and gambling. It is describing the authors’ summary of Islamic economic principles, not issuing religious guidance. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 102–103.

Gharar, qirad, and the problem of risk

Gharar is discussed as a prohibition on certain kinds of chance or contractual uncertainty, rooted in the prohibition of gambling. Rosser and Rosser describe later juristic extension of the concept to contracts whose outcomes cannot be predicted, but they also emphasize controversy. Insurance is a central example: some interpretations accept pooled insurance as risk reduction, others classify it as gharar, and a third distinguishes life insurance from other forms. The authors report that these disagreements have led some to favor public insurance. This means gharar should not be simplified as a ban on all uncertainty or all risk-bearing economic activity. Rosser & Rosser, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 18–20

The chapter also describes disagreement about land rent and sharecropping. Some Islamic economists permit both; some oppose all rents; others regard fixed rent as riba but accept sharecropping as a form of qirad or profit-sharing; still others reverse these judgments. This diversity shows that legal conclusions depend on how gharar and riba are defined and applied, not on a single uncontested rule. Rosser & Rosser, printed p. 103.

Qirad denotes accepted profit-sharing in the chapter’s terminology. The authors frame an unresolved boundary between prohibited chance and acceptable shared entrepreneurial risk. They suggest that profit-sharing can be permissible when parties do not seek gratuitous uncertainty and agreements clearly specify how profits and losses are shared. The historical justification they report relies on traditions about the Prophet’s commercial practice rather than a direct Qur’anic rule, and legal schools allow different arrangements. Rosser & Rosser, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 18–20

Mudarabah is presented as a widely recognized form of qirad: a financier supplies money or goods, an entrepreneur manages the enterprise, and profits are split according to an agreed share. The financier bears the loss of invested capital if the venture fails, while the manager loses labor time; any service compensation is specified. This differs from an interest-bearing loan because the return is contingent on realized profits and the investor bears business risk. The chapter notes practical problems: investors may have difficulty verifying reported profits, creating incentives for fraud or misreporting. For this reason, the ideal of profit-and-loss sharing has not always dominated actual Islamic banking. Rosser & Rosser, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 18–20

Riba, competing economic arguments, and banking practice

Riba is treated in the chapter as the prohibition of interest, but the authors distinguish the religious rule from debates over its definition and economic implications. They present arguments made by Islamic economists that interest can transfer income from poorer borrowers to wealthier lenders, encourage rentier behavior, raise costs, and contribute to instability. Some argue that profit-sharing focuses finance on productive enterprise. The authors also summarize theoretical claims that prohibiting interest could reduce inflation or monetary cycles. These are arguments within the literature, not established empirical results. They set out counterarguments: a ban may reduce saving, capital investment, or growth, and eliminating the price of capital creates an allocation problem. They note proposals ranging from central planning to linking zakat to the opportunity cost of capital. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 104–105.

The chapter describes Islamic banking as seeking returns through permitted financing arrangements rather than explicit interest. In the idealized model, depositors become indirect participants in the ventures financed by a bank, for example through mudarabah. In practice, the authors say that murabaha became widely used: a financier purchases goods and resells them to a customer at an agreed higher price payable later. The justification described is that the financier owns the goods and bears some risk during that period. Because the ownership period can be very short, critics argue that this arrangement can closely resemble conventional interest and may undermine the ethical rationale. Murabaha is a cost-plus sale with deferred payment, not profit-sharing; mudarabah is the chapter’s example of profit-sharing. Keep that distinction explicit. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 106–107.

The chapter’s historical examples include Mit Ghamr savings institution (1963), Nasser Social Bank (1972), a Dubai Islamic bank (1975), and the Islamic Development Bank (1975). It discusses growth of Islamic banks across countries and contrasting practices in Iran, Pakistan, and Sudan. It also describes conflicts between banking contracts and legal enforcement in Saudi Arabia, alongside efforts to reconcile conventional banking with religious restrictions. These examples document the chapter’s period and should not be treated as a current inventory of institutions or regulations. The authors say problems with profit reporting, expertise, and bad loans pushed banks toward more predictable financing forms such as murabaha. Their portfolio figures for the Islamic Development Bank illustrate a historical shift away from mudarabah and toward murabaha; they should be attributed as dated data from the cited study. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 106–108.

Property, capitalism, socialism, and unresolved outcomes

The chapter rejects a simple classification of Islam as either capitalist or socialist. It reports that Qur’anic rules support trade and private property, while inheritance rules encourage division of wealth; charitable trusts (waqf) can preserve property across generations. Other Islamic thinkers call for stronger redistribution or public management, drawing on the premise that ultimate ownership belongs to Allah. The authors describe a socialist-oriented tradition and competing interpretations of scriptural passages, including divergent translations. They conclude that Islamic economics may support modified market capitalism, redistribution, or other institutional arrangements depending on political and legal interpretation. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 108–109.

Rosser and Rosser close by juxtaposing Chapra’s optimistic account of a coordinated Islamic socioeconomic program with Timur Kuran’s pessimistic warning that a political project claiming definitive religious answers could become repressive and mistake symbolic changes for reform. They decline to adjudicate between them. This unresolved evaluation matters: the chapter presents Islamic economics as an influential program, not as a proven economic model with settled effects. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 109–110.

Terminology and limits. Use riba for the source’s prohibited interest concept without implying that all contemporary Muslims or jurists define it identically; describe disagreement rather than deciding religious doctrine. Keep gharar bounded to contested forms of avoidable contractual uncertainty and chance rather than equating it with all risk. Keep qirad / mudarabah distinct from murabaha: the former are profit-sharing arrangements; the latter is a deferred-payment cost-plus sale which can approximate interest economically. The chapter repeatedly notes differences across Shari’a schools and interpretations. Its institutional data, laws, country conditions, and political claims are historical and dated; use them as examples from the authors’ period, not as current advice or facts. Rosser & Rosser, printed pp. 100–110.

Contract mechanisms, securities and the lecture’s corrections

Arrangement Mechanism Return and risk distinction
Mudarabah Investor supplies capital; manager supplies enterprise/management; profits split by agreed shares. Ordinary business capital loss belongs to the investor while the manager loses effort; this does not excuse manager misconduct or negligence.
Murabaha Financier buys an asset and sells it at disclosed cost plus markup, often payable in instalments. A sale obligation replaces a floating share of realized enterprise profit; brief ownership still differs from “no ownership at all.”
Ijara Financier owns an asset and leases its use to the customer. Rent compensates use; a separate purchase/transfer arrangement is needed if ownership will eventually pass to the customer. A lease alone does not automatically transfer title.
Sukuk Certificates represent the relevant ownership/beneficial interests and associated cash flows under their specified structure. The lecture’s rental/profit/redemption example is one arrangement; a certificate is not a universal guarantee of fixed income, principal or direct recourse to the physical asset.
Takaful Cooperative insurance-type risk pooling under the relevant institutional rules. Pooling does not make losses impossible; governance, underwriting and contract interpretation matter.

The lecture’s profit-sharing label “Murababa” conflates spellings: the relevant profit-sharing concept here is mudarabah, while its later mortgage cost-plus sale is murabaha. Its early Egypt date “193–1968” is a typographical truncation: the supplied chapter gives Mit Ghamr 1963, closed in 1968. “Do invest into forbidden” omits the intended negation: the slide’s argument is do not invest in prohibited activities. These corrections follow the chapter’s definitions and the lecture’s own context, rather than silently preserving contradictory labels. Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 38–41 Rosser & Rosser, chapter 4, physical PDF pp. 19–23

The IMF Financial Soundness Indicators Compilation Guide (2019), Annex 7.4, §§7.85–7.86 and contract definitions, as actually available in its indexed definition passages, supports the qualification excessive uncertainty and the distinction between ordinary business loss and manager misconduct/negligence. This bounded clarification is not a survey of contemporary law or product compliance.

Risk, liquidity and dated industry evidence

Asset-linked financing, shared business exposure and restrictions on speculation may alter risks, but do not make every Islamic bank or security safer than every conventional one. Cost-plus obligations can resemble debt cash flows, profit-sharing exposes investors to enterprise performance and information problems, and securities can have market, credit and liquidity risks. The lecture’s cited Beck–Demirgüç-Kunt–Merrouche comparison reports stronger capital/asset indicators and crisis performance in its sample, which is an empirical association under that study’s design, not an unconditional theorem of safety. Irfan’s critique concerns divergence between ethical ideals and contracts made to resemble conventional products. Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 42–45

Liquidity management requires assets and facilities whose cash-flow structure is acceptable under the institution’s rules while meeting prudential needs. The Bank of England’s 2 December 2021 announcement, “The Alternative Liquidity Facility,” verifies that its non-interest deposit facility opened to deposits then. Deposits are backed by a fund of high-quality sukuk and earn the fund return net of costs; it complements, rather than removes, a bank’s regulatory liquidity obligations. This is a dated institutional example supporting the lecture, not a statement that a launch announcement in December 2020 and actual deposit opening in December 2021 were the same event.

The slide’s Saudi asset share is labelled 2014. Its S&P figures—10.6% growth in 2024 and sukuk above USD 1 trillion—and UK bank counts belong to the reports cited on the 2025 slide. They are supplied historical claims, not updated 2026 measurements or a verified present inventory. Its reference to a January 2024 Bank of England consultation is likewise a dated lead; the facility-opening fact above has direct bounded verification. The two YouTube references are optional leads, not viewed or imported as additional academic sources. Week III lecture, physical PDF pp. 39–46

Complete solution and essential rubric: Financier profit is \(0.6(20)=12.000000\) and manager profit is \(0.4(20)=8.000000\); under the stated successful return of capital the financier receives \(100+12.000000=112.000000\). In ordinary total business loss the investor loses invested capital and manager loses effort, absent misconduct/negligence; this does not immunize wrongdoing or guarantee a return. Profit verification can create fraud/misreporting incentives. Murabaha is asset purchase then disclosed cost-plus resale, with obligation \(100+10=110\), not a floating share of realized profit; brief genuine ownership differs from none, while critics note interest-like cash flows.
